Sections.title: Reconsider Afr Environments
Sections.description: Blood diamonds. Resource curses. Land grabs. Tragedies of the commons. Climate refugees. These concepts are often used to frame discussions about natural resource politics and environmental (mis)management in Africa. Time and again, we hear that corruption (in government) and overexploitation (by poor citizens) are preventing sustainable development, putting biodiversity conservation at risk, and providing fodder for ongoing conflict. This course prompts students to critically engage with these narratives through an appraisal of popular media, policy documents, and relevant scholarship in the fields of political economy, geography, anthropology, political ecology, and development studies. In doing so, we aim to uncover substantiations, deviations, and contradictions in cases across the African continent, and to interrogate the (often colonial) origins and racialized elements of the stories and stereotypes that shape our perceptions of African societies and environments. Students will leave the course better equipped to interrogate the ways in which ecological and development challenges are shaped and landscapes produced by the complex interplay of local, national, and global forces across time and space.

Sections.title: Read Africa Critical Perspect
Sections.description: This course seeks to introduce students to everyday life in urban Africa. The course is designed to equip students with basic and useful knowledge about the how urban residents – rich and poor, newcomers and old-timers, young and old, men and women – negotiate the challenges of living in cities. This course focuses on networks, associational life, and relationships that are the ties that bind urban residents together. Social organization, religious belief and practice, ethnicity, economic and political systems, the arts, and popular culture are some of the topics we will explore. We will be approaching these themes from a variety of disciplinary perspectives, including history, anthropology, literature, political science, sociology, and economics.

Sections.title: Stdnt Protest BlkPwr-Palestine
Sections.description:
The dramatic and powerful surge of student protest at the University of Michigan in 2023-2024 calling for divestment was part of a national wave of student organizing against the war in Gaza and in support of Palestinian liberation. It was also an extension of a rich history of student activism at U of M. This course explores that history, its connections to the contemporary moment, and the meanings of this legacy for current students. We will examine key movements and moments over the last 60 years in which students protested, issued demands, and called on the university to take action on a range of matters, from racial justice on campus to international wars. In each case, we will explore what the students were fighting for, how the university responded, and what the outcomes were. In some cases this involved changing university policy, other times it meant the creation of programs, cultural spaces, or an academic department–all  as a result of student activism. For example, students in this course will learn about:

  • the original teach-ins and the movement against the war in Vietnam in the 1960s 
  • the three Black Action Movements (BAM I, BAM II, and BAM III) of the 1970s and 80s that led to the creation of the Comprehensive Studies Program (CSP), the office of Academic Multicultural Initiatives (OAMI), the Office of Multi-Ethnic Student Affairs (MESA), and the Department of Afroamerican and African Studies (DAAS).
  • the #BBUM (Being Black at U of M) campaign in 2013 and the Black Student Union’s demand for the Trotter Multicultural Center, which opened in 2018
  • the TAHRIR coalition and the Encampment for Gaza in 2024. 

Over the course of the semester, students in this course will have the opportunity to critically assess the goals and impacts of student protests across decades, and we will take stock of the ways that student activism has shaped and reshaped the university.

Sections.title: Trauma/Memory/Memorialization
Sections.description:
Decisions about memory – what gets remembered and how – are political processes. This first-year seminar is designed to introduce students to the study of the politics of memory in Africa. Students will learn about the ways that politics shape how key moments of trauma are memorialized across the continent, including the slave trade, colonialism, political violence, genocide, and environmental disasters. We will consider specific events in African countries while also using social science concepts and methods to examine and explain broad patterns across the continent. We will interrogate how governments and other political actors decide what gets memorialized and how, and we will examine how different populations experience sites of memory commemorating traumatic events. 

In conducting this exploration, we will primarily rely on and build upon the work of political scientists, but will also draw on the contributions of journalists, anthropologists, psychologists, economists, and historians. Course material will be drawn from academic articles and books, as well as popular media, including novels, films, and music.  This course aims to develop students' skills of clear and cogent articulation and critical thinking with an emphasis on empirically-based argumentation and reasoning skills. Bi-weekly reading responses, in-class discussions, and a final project focusing on a site of memory of the students’ choice will all be used to evaluate student progress in developing these skills.

Sections.title: Intro to East African Culture
Sections.description:
CHECK IT OUT! - Video Description

Intercultural competence is crucial in navigating today’s world, and what better ways are there to achieve that competence other than by purposefully delving into learning about a culture other than your own? This course will introduce you to the ways of life in East Africa. We will discuss topics such as family life, economic activities, cultural celebrations, food, clothing, entertainment, education, and health among others. The exposure that you will gain from this course will not only place you at an advantage on matters regarding East Africa but will also help you draw comparisons with other cultures and to engage in critical analyses about issues that affect different parts of the world. The course will entail lectures, readings, classroom discussions, and presentations. Short, independent research tasks as will be assigned occasionally to encourage students to discover information on their own and to share that in class. I hope that through this introductory course to the East African culture, many students will develop further interest to take courses on Africa in general, and to also learn the African languages that are offered at the University of Michigan.

Sections.title: Nonviolence Montgomery - World
Sections.description:
When Rosa Parks refused to leave her seat on a city bus in Montgomery, Alabama one fateful afternoon in December 1955, the stage was set for what would later become the modern Civil Rights Movement, launching the public careers of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr., the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, and other civil rights leaders and organizations. What is less widely known, however, is how Black and white activists in the American South during the 1950s and 1960s have come to inspire nonviolent political and social movements, worldwide, to the present day. Utilizing historical literature, biography, and documentary film, this course will feature both an in-depth study of the origins, structure, and development of the American Civil Rights Movement, as well as focus on the success, and failings, of a select number of nonviolent struggles worldwide.

Course Requirements:

Regular attendance, active participation in class discussions, and keeping up with the reading for the course are all both expected and essential. Students will also write essays, undertake group projects, and take a final examination.

Intended Audience:

This class is open to all first year students.

Sections.title: Law, Race, Historical Process
Sections.description:
AAS 250 is the first half of a two-course sequence on the constitutional and legal history of African Americans. It covers the phase of this history that begins with European exploration of the western hemisphere, and ends as we set the stage for the advent of the Modern Civil Rights movement. A unique backdrop for our work throughout the term will be the historical significance of the year 2005. This is, among other things, the 50th anniversary of two pivotal events in the history of the Modern Civil Rights Movement — the murder of 14 year old Emmett Till in Money Mississippi, and the beginning of the Montgomery Bus Boycott in Montgomery, Alabama. It is the 40th anniversary year of the passage of the monumental Voting Rights Act of 1965. If the events of 1955, along with the historic Brown decision of the year before, represented the opening salvo in the Modern Civil Rights Era, the Voting Rights Act of 1965, combined with the other legislative foundation posts initiated in that era, and was the practical policy steps taken to usher in an era of operational equality in American life.

AAS 250 will look, however, at the origins of this central challenge of the 20th and 21st centuries. That challenge, essentially is to resolve the “birth conflicts” present as the North American colonies and later the United States take shape. In looking at the how and why questions of law in the time period from 1400-1900, AAS 450 will focus upon the conceptual underpinnings of the study of race and law in the U.S., the era of Constitutional formation, the dynamics of law in the antebellum period, the possibilities and limitations of law in Reconstruction and thereafter, and the halting nature of the quest for power and presence during the period of Jim Crow segregation.

Readings by Derrick Bell, Annette Gordon Reed, Thurgood Marshall, and others.

Course Requirements:

Two tests, final examination and writings analyses.

Intended Audience:

No data submitted

Class Format:

My online class will include both synchronous and asynchronous elements, but I will generally expect students to “attend” my class at its currently scheduled time.

Sections.title: The Political Economy
Sections.description: The course introduces students to the confluence of political and economic forces at the local, national, regional, and global levels that have helped shape the trajectory of African development. The course is divided into three parts: the first examines the meaning and evolution of the political economy of development in the context of Africa’s unfolding history from pre-independence through the era of structural adjustment. The second applies an understanding of political economy to topical development issues such as environment and climate change, causes and consequences of conflict, health and development, and international aid. The latter section applies the political economy framework to particular African country case studies.

Sections.title: Hoop Dreams Race Basketball
Sections.description:
From its first appearance in a school gymnasium in Massachusetts in 1891 until today, the game of basketball has proved to be both an arena, and a bellwether, for the expression of larger social issues and trends in American life, especially with regard to race. Not only has the game itself changed significantly during the past century, but so have the styles, ethos, and aspirations of those who play it. Ranging across the entire history of the sport, this course will focus on basketball's own particular racial narrative, highlighting not only the immense African American contribution to the development of the game, but also basketball's ever-changing role in American society.

The mini-course seminars will introduce students to a range of issues and experiences related to the topics and identity categories of specialized topics in Afroamerican, African, and/or Caribbean studies. The courses will explore and analyze major aspects of the subject matter:

  1. historical contexts for the interactions of African and the diaspora;
  2. personal experiences; and
  3. meanings and effects.

This is a combined short lecture/discussion course that is designed to function as an introduction to the subject matter. Students at all levels are welcome to enroll.

Course Requirements:

Regular attendance, active participation in class discussions, and keeping up with the reading for the course are all both expected and essential. Students will also write essays and take a final examination.

Intended Audience:

This course is geared towards students who have interests in Afroamerican, African, and/or Caribbean studies. The course meets the 200-level area course requirement for DAAS majors and minors.

Class Format:

Seminar

Sections.title: Intro Environmental Politics
Sections.description:
This course introduces students to global environmental politics, justice and development. This course will explore environmental issues around the world and the relatedness of nature to politics, development and culture. We will address historically unique social form that presents special challenges to our understanding of environmental politics, gender, race and culture by looking at case studies from around the world. Among the questions that we will examine are the following: How have local and global histories, memories, practices, values, gender, race and identities that derive from our understanding of politics intersect with nature? Are there environmental issues that are also issues of race, class and gender? For example, are there particular forms of knowledge and subjectivity that intersect or interact with race and gender difference, or ideas about civilization and primitivity that could be seen as distinctive instruments of environmental rule?

Sections.title: Black Feminism(s)
Sections.description:
What is Black Feminism? In this course, we will explore the history of Black women’s gendered and racial politics in the United States and, in particular, how their beliefs and experiences have differed from other groups. How have Black women pushed back against and attempted to reshape traditional, Eurocentric, “white feminist” politics? How have Black Feminist responses to racism diverged from and challenged mainstream and Black masculinist political scripts? We will explore these questions as well as representations of Black women’s sexuality and political activism. Course readings are drawn from a variety of disciplines and time periods with the goal of exposing students to the history of Black Feminist thought and the breadth of Black Feminist scholarship, activism, and methodologies. By the end of the semester, students will be conversant in the major concepts of Black Feminism and Black Women’s Studies and have developed the analytical tools to understand how race, gender, and class interact to produce the unique experiences of Black women in the United States.

Course Requirements:

Regular attendance and participation in class discussions is expected. There will a handful of discussion posts, three short papers (<5pg), and a final project. The three papers are worth 30% of the final grade and the final project is worth 25%.

Sections.title: Environ Governance African Dev
Sections.description: Environmental sustainability and economic development are two of the most pressing issues of our time. Nowhere is the imperative for both clearer than in Africa. In this course, we will explore the institutional structures that mediate human interactions with the environment in Africa, and consider how different approaches to natural resource extraction and use have shaped economic and ecological outcomes across the continent throughout history. Emphasis will be placed on both nonrenewable resources (e.g. extractive industries, from colonial exploitation to national development programs to multinational corporate operations) and renewable resources (e.g. forests and biodiversity, from community-managed commons to market-based conservation to protected areas managed by foreign NGOs). Moreover, we will examine the varied strategies individuals, communities, states, corporations, and organizations have used in seeking to gain and maintain control over resources for purposes of subsistence, profit, conservation, and/or development. In doing so, we will consult literature in political ecology, environmental history, and development studies, as well as popular media and policy documents.

Sections.title: Detroit Art in and out of UMMA
Sections.description:
What can we learn about Detroit through studying its art? What does it mean to study Detroit from outside of it, and particularly, from Ann Arbor? What do we miss when we’re not immersed in a specific place, community, and/or moment in time? This course will explore central patterns and themes of Detroit-based art and consider what happens when we take art out of its original place and context to put it on display elsewhere.

While this course will ask students to engage critically and analytically with the Detroit art we’ll see at UMMA, we will just as often consider what we’re not seeing in front of us, what’s missing, what’s outside the frame. Blending methods and strategies from cultural studies, history, critical theory, literary studies, gender studies, art history, and museum studies, we’ll bring an intersectional lens to the art we take up.

Course Requirements:

Assignments likely to include weekly readings and informal writing, visual and literary analyses, and a final cumulative project.

Intended Audience:

While open to any U-M undergraduate student, this course is affiliated with the Semester in Detroit (SiD) program. Students interested in this class and other course topics on Detroit should consider exploring the full SiD program at www.semesterindetroit.com.

Sections.title: From the Underground to Motown
Sections.description:
This course will explore the history of Detroit, focusing on its transformation during the twentieth century and continued evolution as a majority-black city. The course is intended to clarify how the city’s past has created the conditions and circumstances of the present. Potential topics and themes to be examined in the course include (but certainly are not limited to): the histories of indigenous peoples in the region before the founding of Detroit; practices of slavery and abolition; the persistence and impact of racial and ethnic conflicts across time periods; the ways in which class conflicts have shaped the urban landscape and the workplace; the Great Migration and the social and political development of Black communities; the impact of immigration on Detroit’s social and political development; profiles of specific neighborhoods; musical traditions such as Blues, Jazz, Motown, Techno, and Hip Hop; the interplay between the auto industry and the urban environment; the on-going struggles over political power and for control of the city; and the changing ways the city is represented, both among its citizens and in the broader American consciousness.

While open to any U-M undergraduate student, this course is part of the full curriculum for students accepted into the Semester in Detroit Program. Students interested in this class might want to consider applying to spend the entire fall semester off-campus in Detroit. More information at www.semesterindetroit.com.

Sections.title: Remaking the World
Sections.description:
In this seminar, we will explore the relationship between politics, mental health, and trauma in post-colonial Africa, primarily from an anthropological perspective. Having achieved independence from colonial powers, many African nations set out in the 1960s to develop psychiatric institutions and practices informed by “traditional” modes of therapeutic healing in a movement broadly referred to as “Africanization.” At the same time, African and foreign practitioners alike hoped to infuse African psychiatry with the knowledge of universalized approaches to the mind, illness, and healing. This course explores the tensions between these relativistic and universalist approaches to mental health developed in Africa during the post-colonial period, focusing in particular on the power relations they entailed. How do global psychiatric discourses travel and how do they resonate in African contexts with different traditions of healing and therapeutic practice? What does an “African” approach to mental health look like and how can we entangle the work of practitioners from colonial legacies of knowledge production, domination, and oppression? To answer these questions, we will examine several case studies from the 1960s onwards which provide perspectives on the formation of different therapeutic institutions in Nigeria, Senegal, and Ghana.

In the second half of the course, we will narrow our focus to explore the uptake of the concepts “trauma” and “PTSD” in post-conflict countries including Sierra Leone, Libera, South Africa, and Rwanda. Over the last several decades, trauma has gained global popularity as a way of discussing the effects of psychic harm. But what is trauma and how does it present across different cultural contexts? After briefly reviewing the history of trauma and PTSD, we will explore how understandings of trauma circulate in contemporary Africa, evaluating the limits and possibilities of trauma to explain and ameliorate the psychic effects of physical, historical, and metaphysical violence. We will take post-genocide Rwanda as a specific case study through which we can examine the complexities of victimhood and healing in a post-colonial and post-conflict environment. Through this case study and others, we will interrogate how foreign meanings of trauma and PTSD become incorporated into and/or transformed by local systems of knowledge; the ways in which economization of trauma and testimony can reproduce or create social and political tensions; and the ways in which artistic representations of trauma can serve as forms of political expression/protest.

Sections.description: In this course we will study some of the novels, short stories and essays of Africa’s newest Nobel Prize in Literature winner, Abdulrazak Gurnah (Nobel Prize 2021). Our discussions will center on close readings of his writings as well as on the larger social and literary contexts in which they emerge. Among the topics to be discussed will be the politics of language in African literary production, the social power of literature, the representation of history in literary texts, the question of imported genres, the role of the writer in presenting a critique of colonial and postcolonial society, the experience of migration and the predicament of ethnic and sexual minorities. Texts studied will include Memory of Departure, Admiring Silence, Gravel Heart and Theft.

Sections.title: Cult, Class&Conflict South Afr
Sections.description: In 1994, observers proclaimed the end of apartheid in South Africa a "miracle" and applauded the creation of a vibrant, inclusive democracy. Nearly a quarter of a century later, vast economic inequalities remain, unemployment has worsened, corruption is rife, and voters are abandoning the ruling African National Congress. Why have social inequities and economic disparities persisted? How are South African citizens navigating hardship? How do they express their discontent? Is democracy in danger in South Africa? This course explores the institutionalization of racist and segregationist legislation under apartheid, as well as the protests and resistance that followed from such acts. It will investigate the legacy of apartheid and the resulting spatial compartmentalization of housing, neighborhoods, schools, clinics, and social life in South Africa. The course will also cover successive democratic elections since 1994 and discuss the contemporary challenges posed by the lack of jobs, housing, and other goods; the ANC as a dominant party; persistent educational inequities; and the strains of urbanization and immigration. Finally, we will examine the expression of hope and resistance in popular culture, from radio programs and blogs to student demonstrations. Where appropriate, we will draw on theoretical and empirical research in comparative politics to situate the South African experience in relation to other countries that have had a history of segregation and/or have undergone transitions to democracy.

Sections.title: De/Re-Imagining Black Progress
Sections.description: Since Africans were first brought to what would become the United States of America there has been extensive thought, rhetoric and action taken regarding their freedom - what it would look like, when it would be granted and how? In contrast to the amount of effort put into the subject and reality of black freedom, what the freedom would be used for/toward has received comparatively less attention (i.e., what end/idealized world was sought). What are these imagined ends/worlds? In answer to the question of what freedom could be used for and how well African Americans have done in achieving these alternatives, it is first necessary to know what African American ideas of progress were/looked/functioned/felt like, how people would pursue them, what they would be willing to do/not do and how well they have achieved these alternatives. In the final analysis, all freedom means is that blacks were no longer shackled and worked for no compensation. Black freedom itself says nothing about the world and life that could be created with that opportunity. Our class is geared toward identifying, understanding and building these conceptions of progress. Before new worlds can be created and enjoyed they must first be imagined. To achieve this objective, over the course of two semesters we will convene an educational dream team composed of visionaries, pragmatists, philosophers, political scientists, architects, poets, fine artists, sociologists and mental health experts. Together we will dream, plan and share.

Sections.title: Justice in Africa
Sections.description:
This course examines the quest for justice in Africa from three perspectives: concepts of justice and rights, institutions of law, and the experience of injustice. We shall consider issues pertaining to the historical quest for redress against injustice done to Africans by outsiders such as slavers, colonists, settlers, and their beneficiaries. We shall also examine the quests for justice when Africans perpetrate large-scale violence on each other. Thirdly, we shall focus on questions of how ordinary people in Africa seek justice in their everyday lives in the context of legal systems, often inadequate and incompetent, deriving from the colonial era and where courts of chiefs and “traditional” leaders co-exist with formal legal institutions and informal judicial forums as well as ad hoc mob justice. Central to our deliberations here will be questions of how notions of universal human rights clash with local concerns about the status and rights of women, occult violence such as “witchcraft,” sexual morality (specifically, homosexuality), and the causes of diseases such as AIDS.

Course Requirements:

The objective of the course is to produce a 20-page research paper of publishable quality on a topic of the student’s choosing. A series of research exercises will be assigned to assist in producing this paper.

Sections.title: Filming the Future of Detroit
Sections.description:
The goal of this course is to produce an exhibition based on “Filming Future City” films made over the last ten years in Detroit, Berlin, and Philadelphia (see filmingfuturecities.org).

Initiated in Detroit in 2014 through participatory filmmaking, the “Filming Future Cities” project has become a regular collaboration between students, young artists and activists from the three cities listed above.

Until now, the Filming Future Cities filmmakers have included refugees, migrants, urban residents, and students from Cameroon, the Congo, Syria, Ann Arbor, Detroit, Berlin, and Philadelphia making short films about topics ranging from noncitizen safety, to pity for refugees, to the displacement of long term urban residents, to access to transportation, to education and the disappearance of schools, to African perspectives on the future in American and European cities.

Our goal will be to identify key themes that run through the films of filmmakers who are often invisible to the public or academic discussion of urban futures which often includes ideas of “development” that displace precisely our filmmakers’ populations.

In addition to learning how to curate film, we will collaborate on how to display the medium in a museum and various other settings. We will learn about how to attract an audience, how to engage new publics, the problematics of the history of exhibition and what it might mean to exhibit these films now.

We will work in collaboration with visiting filmmakers, curators, architects, and artists. We will also visit and read about relevant exhibitions in nearby more removed urban contexts and ultimately produce our own exhibition.

Note: This class has some meetings in Detroit, transportation will be provided.

Sections.title: American Carceral State
Sections.description:
In this course we will study African American literature written from the end of the 19th century—known as the "nadir" (lowest point) in African American history—through the beginning of the 20th century, the moment that gave birth to the "New Negro" of the Harlem Renaissance. These decades represent a period of intense cultural production that reflected both pessimism about post-Civil War racial violence in the US and optimism over new opportunities for black artists. How did African American writers conceive of the role of letters and literature in the national debates over freedpeople’s rights to citizenship? How did they try to represent differences in the black community with dialect and invocations of the “folk,” and how did they mobilize these cultural forms in their search for new racial, political ideals? And finally, we will discuss the methods and issues pertaining to the periodization of African American literature and history in the Academy. Readings include novels, poetry and short stories by noted and less familiar authors, including Charles Chesnutt, Frances Ellen Watkins Harper, Paul Laurence Dunbar, Pauline Hopkins and Sutton Griggs, in addition to secondary critical material.

Intended Audience:

Attendance, participation, flexibility, and willingness to learn new skills, and open-mindedness and collaborative approach toward being part of a diverse intellectual community.

Sections.title: Interdiscip Appr to Afr Stds
Sections.description:
This course seeks to broaden our understanding of both historical and contemporary Africa, allowing a forum for the exchange of ideas among participants drawn from a diversity of disciplines. Course themes may include colonialism and its legacies; performance and culture; extractive resources and environmental degradation; nationalism, politics and development; and urbanization. Rather than treating ‘Africa’ as an undifferentiated place of socio-economic malaise, famine and war, failed states, and distorted urbanism, the course seeks to understand the complexity of processes at work that produce the “Africa” of today.

Besides focusing on substantive topics of contemporary relevance, the course also critically investigates the application and the ethics of diverse theoretical and methodological approaches to the study of Africa. We will explore the pitfalls and challenges of ethnography, fieldwork, controlled comparisons, survey research and experiments. We will also revisit debates about “area studies” and African exceptionalism that periodically resurface in the literature on Africa. Students will also have opportunities to assign and to teach works of scholarship that they find to be original or path-breaking

Sections.title: Histories of Gender in Africa
Sections.description:
When anthropologist Ifi Amadiume published Male Daughters, Female Husbands in 1987, it represented the first work of academic ethnography written by a West African woman about women and gender in West Africa. In her original introduction, Amadiume decried decades of Western scholarship, first by colonial-era ethnologists and then by modern feminists, essentializing sex roles and depicting West African society in terms of culturally-rooted patriarchy. In the decades since, scholars have sought to disrupt western frameworks and scholarship on the histories of gender in Africa have moved to explore, critique, and rewrite the roles of women, households, marriage, rites of passage, and motherhood, and, increasingly, the roles of men as gendered subjects. Recent works consider the construction and production of gender far beyond domestic realms to identify the “unmarked categories” (Lindsay and Miescher, 2003) of masculinity and femininity that appear across domains of life in historical contexts. This course surveys women’s and gender history in Africa in all regions of the continent and spanning the distant past to twentieth century. While the focus is on Africa, students from all fields are welcome. This is a readings course and culminates in a 15-20 page historiographical essay.

Class Format:

Seminar and discussion, with short introductory talks to orient the conversation

Sections.title: Building Communities
Sections.description:
This interdisciplinary first-year seminar provides us with opportunities to put our experiences of the COVID-19 pandemic, uprisings for racial justice, economic disruption, and political polarization into broader perspective by exploring what it means be a responsible member of a group, a community, and a society. Together, we will explore some fundamental questions about community functioning, community disruption, and community building:

  • what does it mean to be part of a community, and how do effective communities function?
  • what internal and external forces disrupt communities? What forces support them?
  • how can I engage with others in a community in ways that honor our differences and our commonalities?
  • how might I, as a member of a democracy, help to build communities that help to fight injustice, preserve our shared earth, and promote the well-being of all?

We will draw on a variety of materials to explore these topics, learning from journalists, philosophers, social scientists, musicians, novelists, activists, and poets.

By the end of the course, you should be able to draw on course materials and your reflections on your own experiences and observations to

  • describe key characteristics of strong communities;
  • describe factors that weaken communities;
  • describe and practice ways to manage difference and conflict in community;
  • identify specific real-world community builders and the characteristics they embody;
  • articulate a philosophy of community building that you can use in your daily life

We will achieve these goals by engaging with a variety of disciplinary approaches to understanding and building communities; by  talking and listening to each other and to guest speakers; and by writing/producing a variety of formal and informal projects.

Course Requirements:

This course is a “gameful” course, which means you can select from a menu of assignments, try different activities, and earn points as you move through the semester. Some options include writing shorter and longer traditional essays, designing and completing multimedia/multimodal projects, attending and reflecting on relevant campus events, and leading class discussions. Daily attendance and weekly journals are required.

Sections.title: Leading without Authority
Sections.description:
Leadership isn’t about titles, it’s about action, connection and collaboration. This course helps students discover how meaningful leadership often happens without formal authority. Through real-world case studies, peer interaction, and systems-focused thinking, students will learn how to influence outcomes, build trust, and initiate change even when they’re not “in charge.” This course is especially valuable for students leading from less visible roles or within systems that feel rigid. It culminates in the creation of a personal influence plan tailored to a real-life context they care about.

By the end of this course, students will be able to: Define leadership as influence, not position, and identify real-life opportunities to lead without formal authority, Develop strategies for initiating change in complex systems or groups where they lack direct power, Build policy and systems awareness, recognizing how informal power, credibility, and networks can be used to shape outcomes, Explore their identity and confidence in stepping into leadership roles that are less visible, less central, or less traditional, and Create a personal influence plan that outlines how they will take initiative and create impact in a specific area of their life.

Sections.title: Critical Issues-ClimateSolutio
Sections.description:
This fun and engaging minicourse enables students to explore pressing issues related to climate and sustainability, learn the tools to identify and define problems, and design creative solutions. 

Each week an expert who has dedicated a substantial portion of their career working in climate and sustainability will join us for the first hour of class to share their story, have an open discussion about the most pressing challenges they face in their work, and communicate lessons they’ve learned.

The second hour of class will involve engaging discussion based activities where you will work with your peers, challenge your own assumptions, and broaden your perspective. These discussion activities will be led by student course facilitators, ranging from small groups to full class discussion.

This course offers an introduction to Food Studies, an interdisciplinary field that explores the social, cultural, historical, and political aspects of food and eating. We'll read about and discuss questions like:

  • What should we do about the "obesity epidemic"?
  • What are the philosophical and practical implications of eating animals?
  • Is it really better to eat "local"?
  • Where did the association between African Americans and fried chicken come from?
  • And many more.

    In addition, we'll watch several recent documentaries and visit the Culinary Archive at the Clements.

    By the end of the class, you will be better equipped to develop research questions, find and evaluate evidence, and articulate nuanced arguments — not only about food but about any subject.

    Course Requirements:

    Grades will be based on reading quizzes, contributions to a class blog, presentations, and several short papers.

This course explores Intergroup Dialogue and facilitation through a psychological lens, giving you theory, hands-on practice, and research-backed tools to transform intergroup conflict into connection. You’ll learn how identity, bias, power, and emotional dynamics shape conversations across difference, and you’ll develop knowledge and skills to create safe, inclusive spaces for productive exchange. Through a review of various relevant theories, experiential exercises, case studies, and reflective assignments, you’ll practice active listening, conflict re-framing, and group design strategies from a psychological perspective that are effective in classrooms, communities, and organizations. This course is ideal for students in psychology, sociology, education, social justice, and anyone who wants practical skills for leading difficult conversations and building stronger, more equitable relationships across difference.

Sections.title: History of Stdnt Protest at UM
Sections.description:
When Do We Want It? Now! The History of Student Protest at UM

The dramatic and powerful surge of student protest at the University of Michigan in 2023-2024 calling for divestment was part of a national wave of student organizing against the war in Gaza and in support of Palestinian liberation. It was also an extension of a rich history of student activism at U of M. This course explores that history, its connections to the contemporary moment, and the meanings of this legacy for current students. We will examine key movements and moments over the last 60 years in which students protested, issued demands, and called on the university to take action on a range of matters, from racial justice on campus to international wars. In each case, we will explore what the students were fighting for, how the university responded, and what the outcomes were. In some cases this involved changing university policy, other times it meant the creation of programs, cultural spaces, or an academic department–all  as a result of student activism. For example, students in this course will learn about:

  • the original teach-ins and the movement against the war in Vietnam in the 1960s
  • the three Black Action Movements (BAM I, BAM II, and BAM III) of the 1970s and 80s that led to the creation of the Comprehensive Studies Program (CSP), the office of Academic Multicultural Initiatives (OAMI), the Office of Multi-Ethnic Student Affairs (MESA), and the Department of Afroamerican and African Studies (DAAS).
  • the #BBUM (Being Black at U of M) campaign in 2013 and the Black Student Union’s demand for the Trotter Multicultural Center, which opened in 2018
  • the TAHRIR coalition and the Encampment for Gaza in 2024.

Over the course of the semester, students in this course will have the opportunity to critically assess the goals and impacts of student protests across decades, and we will take stock of the ways that student activism has shaped and reshaped the university.

Sections.title: Transnational/Global Asia
Sections.description:
Transnational / Global Asia 

This course begins with a fundamental question: What do we mean by “Asia”? And how has the continent of Asia been historically, and continues to be, entangled with the rest of the world? To explore these questions, we will examine how ideas about Asia circulate in our everyday lives. From the clothes we wear to the wooden dressers that hold them, Asian products and the labor of Asian workers are embedded in our daily routines. From dressing up as "KPop Demon Hunters" for Halloween to dancing to “Like Jennie,” we are surrounded by Asian cultural productions with global reach.

There is no denying that Asia is now global. Yet many scholars argue that Asia always has been. Long before the term “globalization” entered our vocabulary, Asian goods, people, and ideas traveled across vast networks such as the Silk Road and the Indian Ocean world. In this course, we will explore Asia not as a static geographic entity, but as a dynamic set of ideas shaped over time through encounters among peoples, the movement of goods, and ongoing cultural exchange.

Course Requirements:

One in-class midterm exam, one in-class presentation, active in-class participation, a semester long journal assignment, and one final paper

Sections.title: Latinx Freedom Dreams
Sections.description:
Latinx Freedom Dreams

This first-year seminar introduces students to the multiple and varied roles Latinxs have played in U.S. civil rights and racial justice movements, as well as global freedom struggles. It also introduces students to key themes in comparative ethnic studies and solidarity literature. Together we will ask: how have varying Latinx populations imagined alternative visions—dare we say dreams—of social change and liberation? What identities did they mobilize? What demands—political or otherwise—did these dreams encompass? What other ethnic and racial communities did Latinx organize and envision liberation with, and to what success? Students will consider how Latinxs have imagined freedom and liberation as part of the fight for ethnic studies and other student protest movements; civil rights struggles and third world solidarities; farm workers, economic justice, and immigration; and in the struggle against gentrification and police brutality. We will also work together to transform our classroom into a space not only to read and critique how scholars have written about Latinx social movement histories, but also into a space to practice building community at U-M.

Sections.title: Hip Hop Music and Culture
Sections.description:
Hip Hop Music and Culture

This course will examine hip hop music and culture as a way of understanding US society and culture. This course looks at hip hop's relationship to a number of concepts including: race, gender and sexuality, class and religion, as well as questions of politics. Primary course materials will include hip hop music alongside academic writings on hip hop music and culture.

Sections.title: Failure and Play
Sections.description:
Failure and Play

This first year seminar examines narratives of failure, "winning," and play through games and game narratives as well as research articles and book chapters. In an era where perfectionism and anxiety has proliferated, the goal of this class is to get you comfortable with failure and to build a playful and curious approach to your time at U-M and to your life. We'll play video games, create Choose-Your-Own Adventure narratives, play table-top and/or card games, as well as ground ourselves in game studies, the study of storytelling and narrative, the social construction of time and labor, and of course, the process of writing, reading, listening, and speaking.

Course Requirements:

Assessment: To reflect the class's focus on failure, play, and growth, the class will include 1-2 short writing assignments, 2 longer writing assignments (one is a Choose-Your-Own Adventure game with analysis), and a final portfolio where students reflect on their growth (and stagnation) towards the class goals and learning objectives, include revised work that exemplifies their ability to take feedback and improve their writing, and show how they've learned to build a community of support to thrive (and in tough times, survive) during their college career.

Intended Audience:

Who is this class for? This is not a frivolous class, and the study of games is not a simple thing. This class is for people willing to take failure and play seriously and those who want to mix the critical and the creative. While the class will include video games and other forms of gameplay, the class is NOT intended for so-called "gamers" or those with rigid notions of games and play which drive newcomers away. If you've never played a game before, you are welcome. Games used in the class are chosen with newcomers in mind, with more focus on narrative than on quick twitch muscles.

Sections.title: Museums and Social Justice
Sections.description:
Museums and Social Justice

Museums shape how we understand history, culture, and identity—but who decides what stories they tell, and how? This interdisciplinary first-year seminar explores the evolving roles that museums play in perpetuating social inequalities as well as their potential for repairing them. Through readings, discussions, and visits to on- and off-campus museums, students will analyze critically how institutions engage with diverse audiences on issues from representation and repatriation to accessibility and activism. The course also supports students in sharpening key academic skills, including active listening, strategic reading, public speaking, analytical writing, and scholarly research.

Sections.title: Birth Control in America
Sections.description:
Birth Control in America

The history of birth control in the U.S. is both a story of medical advancement and of an emerging social movement asserting women’s rights over their own bodies. In this course, we will look at the history of contraception through the lenses of the courts, legislation, healthcare professionals, public debates, and women’s private lives and communities of care. In this course, we will explore the origin of birth control as a social movement, asking what is the social history of birth control? How did self-regulated forms of contraception (including douching and medicinal herbs) become part of a narrative about women’s control over their own bodies? Through reading personal narratives, health manuals, medical advice, and legislation, as well as visits to archives on campus, we’ll explore the complex history of contraception in America.

To explore these questions, we will examine touchstone moments in the history of birth control in the US, including:

  • Nineteenth-century advocacy of douching as a method of female-controlled contraception;
  • The invention of vulcanized rubber in 1839, which made condoms easier to manufacture and more reliable;
  • The Comstock Act of 1873, which made it illegal to send information about birth control through the mail;
  • Early twentieth-century forced sterilization of women of color and those with disabilities;
  • Margaret Sanger’s establishment of Planned Parenthood in 1916 alongside her belief in eugenics;
  • Condom distribution to soldiers in WWII to prevent the spread of STDs;
  • FDA-approval of the first oral contraceptive (the pill) in 1960; and
  • Debates over Plan B (or the morning after pill) following its approval in 1998.

Course Requirements:

Weekly readings, short writing assignments, a research project based on archival materials, and leading class discussion on a topic of your choice

Intended Audience:

This course is ideal for anyone interested in reading and talking about the personal, social, technical, and legal aspects of birth control in the U.S.

Sections.title: AfroLatinidades Lit,Film,Games
Sections.description:
AfroLatinidades in Literature, Film, and Games

"AfroLatinidades in Literature, Film, and Games" is an introductory-level American Culture class where students will examine AfroLatinx/e characters and representation and as well as how different media (such as memoir, novels, graphic novels, film, and video games) construct "AfroLatinx/e stories." The course will explore AfroLatinidades as a transnational concept, not only a US-based one. While the final reading list is in process, students will read, watch, and play texts like "Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse," "Marvel's Spider-Man: Miles Morales," "American Negra: A Memoir," "Loca," "A Puerto Rican in New York," "Black Mexicans," "Beba," and "Pelo Malo." Students will also examine scholarship in AfroLatinx studies, literary studies, game studies, and media studies. 

Course Requirements:

Assessment: Students will be assessed primarily through 2 in-class blue book exams and a final media analysis project. (As this is a new class, this description is subject to change as I finalize the syllabus and assessments.)

Intended Audience:

Who is this class for? Students who are interested in the study of race and ethnicity, gender and sexuality, and national belonging and identity will be interested in this course, and I welcome students who might not have much background in ethnic studies, but is curious and open to learning. Students in Black studies and Latinx studies will also find this course helpful for delving into the relationship of Blackness to Latinidad and Latinidad to Blackness. The class will appeal to those interested in reading novels and memoirs but also those who enjoy the study of popular culture and new media. Class will be discussion-based, with targeted lectures. Students should be prepared to read 50-100 pages before each class, or watch a film/play a game. Academic scholarship will supplement these readings at times (though will not be assigned for every class period). I am uninterested in students regurgitating AI slop - I want to hear your thoughts and I value your voice.

Sections.title: Race, Religion & Pop Culture
Sections.description:
Race, Religion, and Popular Culture

#RepresentationMatters has become a popular hashtag and saying but why? What is the impact of what we see in the media on how we view others and ourselves? This course explores that question by looking at two stigmatized groups, Black Americans and American Muslims, and how they are represented in US popular culture. We will examine and compare stereotypical representations of these groups on TV and in film and the roles these stereotypes play in shaping what the American public “knows” about Black people and about Muslims. In this course, students are introduced to important concepts of popular culture and the skills to interpret music, film, and television so they learn to look critically at the relationship between race, religion, and popular culture. By the end of the course, students will be able to identify and analyze popular culture’s explicit and implicit uses of race and religion, have a solid knowledge of theories on media and representation and be capable of making their own cultural critique.

Sections.title: CB Learning w/ Older Adults
Sections.description:
Community-Based Ethnography: Intergenerational Learning with Older Adults

In this course, students will explore ethnography by learning with and from senior citizens in the Ann Arbor community through a community-based learning (CBL) project. CBL emphasizes reciprocity, respect, and fostering academic learning while engaging meaningfully in the community and addressing real-world issues.

In the U.S. and many Western countries, the elderly population is increasingly marginalized, facing discrimination, prejudice, and exclusion. Some common and often overlooked health issues among seniors include loneliness, social isolation, and exclusion. Recent studies show that one-quarter of older adults report feeling socially isolated, and approximately one million seniors are considered severely socially isolated.

This course offers an opportunity to meaningfully address the so-called "loneliness epidemic" among seniors by connecting students with local community elders to engage in mutual learning, connection, and enjoyment. At the same time, these relationships will serve as a framework for hands-on learning about ethnography: we will explore ethnographic methods and methodologies, as well as research topics relevant to our research participants in the community, such as subjective well-being, aging in the U.S., and intergenerationality. Students can document their findings and reflections on their experiences either through written forms (e.g., essays), visual representations (e.g., short films/documentaries), or multimedia forms (e.g., photojournalism, infographics).

Course Requirements:

In-class meetings will occur once weekly for 2-3 hours. Course readings from cultural anthropology, cross-cultural studies, sociology, psychology, and philosophy, along with in-class lectures, will provide foundational background knowledge on ethnographic research and related topics. Additionally, students will be paired in groups of two with an elder from the local community and will meet with them weekly, for 2-3 hours, at a standing weekly time that works for everyone’s schedule. Funding will be provided for at-home projects with our community partners (e.g., cooking or crafting), outings (e.g., visits to cafés, museums, and lectures), occasional full group gatherings (at the Residential College and White Lotus Farms), and transportation.

Sections.title: Race,Solidarity&CarceralState
Sections.description:
Race, Solidarity, and the Carceral State

This discussion-based course surveys how U.S. social and racial justice movements have encountered and interacted with the rise and expansion of the carceral state. Using case studies from Black, Arab American, Latinx, and other New Left and progressive movements, together we will ask: what possibilities of resistance are imagined under conditions of repression? And how have these possibilities of resistance and conditions of repression changed over time? Students will consider how imprisonment, surveillance, and political repression have shaped social movements, racial formations, and U.S. politics from the late 1960s to the present, with attention to topics like COINTELPRO & Black freedom movements; Operation Boulder & surveillance of Arab Americans; Reagan-era counterterrorism; prisons & policing; and the militarization of borders. Scholarly readings will be accompanied by the discussion of primary sources, documentaries, podcasts, novels, and social media, transforming our classroom into a space not only to read and critique how scholars have written about histories of repression and resistance, but also into a space to practice building community.

Sections.title: Food in American Culture
Sections.description:
Food in American Culture

This course explores the changing cultural and social value of food in American life through a range of different sources, disciplines, and case studies. We will be guided by how convenience, responsibility, and identity shape our relationship to a dynamic American food industry, while paying attention to how immigration, trauma, and appropriation constitute the industry itself. By doing so, this course seeks to help students connect the food histories, policies, and myths that converge to define American belonging.

Sections.title: Cultures of AI
Sections.description:
Cultures of AI

With the explosive growth of large language models and generative AI, there have been a flurry of debates about what artificial intelligence can and should do. Can it replace writers and artists? Does it actually understand or know things? Should you use it to write your essays for this course? Yet, none of these are questions just about machines, they are questions about us humans too, about our knowledge, hopes, fears, and desires. To answer them assumes we know the difference between intelligence and stupidity, between the natural and the artificial (is the collective knowledge of a university, a government, or a factory—often stored in vast databases and digital documents—wholly natural?). Our discussions of AI, which extend back over more than a century, are as much as anything else, a reflection on how we have come to understand what it means to be a human.


In this course, we will explore and experiment with artificial intelligence (e.g. large language models, machine learning systems, generative AI, etc.) and we will look across the twentieth and twenty-first century at art, literature, film and theory to better understand how we have both dreamed of and recoiled from the possibility of machines automating our very human ways of thinking and making. In doing so, we will hope to understand better both artificial intelligence and our own intelligence.

Sections.title: A Tree Grows in Brooklyn
Sections.description:
Reading the Immigrant City: Community and Identity in A Tree Grows in Brooklyn

This mini-course offers a deep reading of Betty Smith’s A Tree Grows in Brooklyn as a window into immigrant life in early 20th century New York. Through the story of Francie Nolan and her Irish-American family, the course explores how neighborhoods, family networks, and cultural traditions shape experiences of migration and belonging. Students will examine themes of class, ethnicity, gender, and education while considering how novels help us understand the social worlds of immigrant communities. We will also engage with Smith's papers at the Bentley Historical Library. 

This mini-course is held in the first seven weeks of the Fall 2026 Term: 8/31/2026 - 10/16/2026.

Sections.title: Empowering Fam&Comm
Sections.description:
This community-engaged service-learning course explores how research can be conducted with and for communities to promote individual, family, and collective well-being. Grounded in the foundations of community psychology, the course asks a central question: How do we understand social problems in context, and how can research be used as a tool for equity and change?

The course integrates four interconnected forms of learning: (1) direct community-based experience in Detroit, (2) scholarly readings, (3) hands-on research projects, and (4) a weekly seminar. Rather than treating theory and practice as separate worlds, this course intentionally weaves them together. Students will examine how concepts such as prevention, empowerment, systems change, and social justice come alive in real community settings.

The first portion of the semester introduces the core principles of community psychology and frameworks for analyzing social problems at multiple ecological levels. The second portion focuses on research methodologies used to understand and partner with communities. Students will learn and apply methods such as community needs assessments, analysis of census and other population-level data, program evaluation, and survey research. Through lectures, readings, and discussion, we will critically examine when and why particular methods are appropriate and how ethical, culturally responsive research is conducted.

A central component of the course is a sustained partnership with a Detroit-based community organization. Students will engage regularly in applied activities such as tutoring, developing outreach materials, assisting with program evaluation, or conducting community-based research. This experience provides a structured opportunity to observe systems in action, reflect on positionality and power, and contribute meaningful work to community partners.

Work and Evaluation:
Course grades will be based on engagement in the community placement, seminar participation, applied research assignments, written reflections, and a final project or presentation that integrates theory, method, and community experience. Students should expect consistent weekly readings, structured reflection, and collaborative project work. The course requires both intellectual rigor and professional responsibility.

Why Take This Course?
If you are interested in social justice, public policy, education, health, urban communities, nonprofit work, research, or graduate study, this course offers practical and transferable skills. You will learn how to analyze social issues beyond the individual level, interpret real-world data, evaluate community programs, and communicate findings to diverse audiences.

What You Will Gain:
By the end of the course, you will be able to: Apply community psychology principles to real-world social issues; Design and evaluate community-based research projects; Critically assess data about neighborhoods and populations

Course Requirements:

Because this is a community-engaged service-learning course, your grade will reflect both your academic work and your professional engagement with our community partners. Learning in this course happens in classrooms, in neighborhoods, in data, and in dialogue. Your evaluation is designed to honor all of those spaces: Community Engagement, Seminar Participation, Reflective Integration Assignments, Applied Research Project, and Final Integration Reflection

Class Format:

This course is structured as a seminar and community-engaged experience. Learning unfolds across three interconnected spaces: the classroom, the community, and independent research work. 
Weekly Seminar serves as our intellectual anchor. Each week includes discussion of readings, brief lectures on community psychology and research methods, applied exercises, and structured reflection. Early sessions focus on foundational concepts and frameworks for analyzing social problems in context. Later sessions emphasize research design, ethical community engagement, and applied methodological skills. 
Community Placement: Students will complete regular service hours with a Detroit-based community organization. This placement allows you to observe, contribute, and reflect on community systems in action. Community experiences are intentionally aligned with seminar topics so that theory and practice inform one another throughout the semester. 
Applied Research Project (Phased Across the Term): Students will work individually or in groups on a community-relevant research project. Project milestones are scaffolded across the semester to support skill development and feedback. 
Reflection and Integration
Structured reflection assignments are woven throughout the course to help students connect community experience, research methods, and theoretical frameworks. These reflections build toward a final integrative assessment at the end of the semester.

Sections.title: Asian American Lit and Culture
Sections.description:
We will survey in this course the representations of and by Asian American subjects in U.S. culture since the late nineteenth century. Cultural production—literature, drama, film, television, and performance, for example—has historically been the site where tensions among different ethnic and racial groups in the United States are exposed, resolved, exaggerated, or transformed. The cultural representation of such tensions has led, on one hand, to the affirmation of U.S. political and cultural hegemony, and, on the other, to acts of resistance to political and cultural dominance. This course explores the ways in which the cultural and literary production that arises out of the contradictions of U.S. democracy “displace,” in the words of cultural studies scholar Lisa Lowe, “the fiction of reconciliation”—the ways in which the cultural forms of Asian America “disrupt the myth of national identity by revealing its gaps and fissures.”

Texts in the course may include novels, plays, poems, films, television shows, advertisements, blogs, musicals, historical documents, and scholarly articles.

Sections.title: Dancing Women/Dancing Queer
Sections.description:
Dancing Women / Dancing Queer

Every time Beyoncé struts across the stage, punctuating her steps with swings of her hips, she uses her body to make a statement about gender and sexuality, potentially reshaping expectations about how a black, female, American body should and can move. Studying gender and sexuality through dance and performance foregrounds questions about embodiment that run across feminist and queer theory, as well as dance and performance studies. This graduate and upper-level undergraduate seminar will look at representations of gender and sexuality across both concert and social dance spaces and across a variety of genres from ballet to modern dance, the concert stage to the music video, and Broadway to avant-garde solo performance. Although our primary frames of analysis will be gender and sexuality, we will work from the premise that these questions can never be considered separately from questions of race, class, and nationality, among other vectors of identity.
 
The course will include a survey of relevant historical and contemporary literature at the intersection of dance, performance, queer and feminist theory, as well as in-depth analysis of live and archival performances and embodied research (dancing). Prior experience with dance and performance is not required, since a central goal of the course is for everyone—no matter the place from which you begin—to develop vocabulary and strategies for engaging the relationship between gender and sexuality and physical performance. Students will be evaluated on their participation in discussion and in embodied exercises, as well as their successful completion of written and performance-based assignments. In this mix of modes of engagement lies the course’s commitment to feminist methods: we will work together to explore multiple ways of knowing and engaging with the world and one another.
 
Class discussions will invite the following questions (among others): What role have women and queer people—two overlapping, not mutually exclusive categories—played in dance and performance? How are gender and sexuality represented onstage and to what ends? What role do artists’ intentions and processes play in crafting or intervening in these systems of representation? What might constitute a feminist or queer spectatorship in dance and performance? What might constitute a feminist or queer approach to dancemaking and/or performing? What is the world you want to live in and how might performance be a step toward rehearsing for and creating that world?

Sections.title: Indian Law
Sections.description:
Indian Law

This class will do deep dives into three areas: (1) Anishinaabe law, (2) several tribal court cases, and (3) several federal Indian law cases. We will start with an introduction to the Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians (GTB) and its laws, to a legal conflict, then to the adjudication of that conflict in GTB’s courts, and finally to the continued adjudication of that case in federal court all the way to the United States Supreme Court. Along the way, we will learn about Indian tribes, tribal courts, federal and state courts, American Indian tribal law, and federal Indian law. We will turn next to several important tribal court decisions from around the country. Finally, we will turn to federal Indian law cases decided by the US Supreme Court.

Sections.title: Immigrant Justice Lab
Sections.description:
Spend a semester working with law students and other upper-level undergraduate students to support lawyers from the Michigan Immigration Rights Center on asylum cases here in Michigan. Under faculty supervision, students will learn to draft asylum briefs, summarize and translate historical texts, research effective legal arguments, and contribute to developing a national research database for use in asylum cases. Students will also deepen their understanding of immigration law and policy, develop historical and legal research skills, and explore the history of violence and migration through work on real-life asylum cases. This class is ideal for students who are eager to work conscientiously and ethically with others in teams to benefit a non-profit community partner. Instructor permission required.

Please note, our actual work next fall might change depending on the ever-changing landscaping of immigration funding in the current times, but we'll still be doing substantive work. 

Interested students must email the instructor to request permission to enroll.

Sections.title: James Baldwin's Amer to Ours
Sections.description:
Reading, Revolutions, Real(ness): Storytelling and Life Writing from James Baldwin’s America to Ours

In a 1963 interview, the famous Black queer writer, intellectual, and activist James Baldwin (1924-87) proclaimed the power of reading to change lives at home and across the globe. In this seminar, we explore reading as a revolutionary act that helps us understand and interpret reality and its representations as we tell stories about ourselves and others. We will read deeply and passionately Baldwin's select novels, short stories, and essays for how they anticipate narratives on racialized gender, sexuality, and erotic attraction in our own cultural moment. Baldwin’s daring plots often mine his own life and revolve around challenges to politics of respectability as he portrays interracial couples, queer sexual attachments, dissections of class, religiosity, colorism, and family violence. In this upper-level writing course, you will produce a research paper, explore the digital collection at the U-M Library, Chez Baldwin, present your research to your peers, and create a multimedia project for K-12 audiences that will be published online.

Sections.title: Imagining the Arctic
Sections.description:
Imagining the Arctic

The Arctic is often imagined at the literal edge of the map: a cold and marginal place, largely devoid of culture, history, or even life. In reality, the Circumpolar Arctic has been home to a set of diverse and interconnected human cultures for millennia—each with their own rich histories, politics, and cultural traditions. In this course, we will use interdisciplinary methodologies to learn (and unlearn) about the Arctic, with a specific focus on the Iñupiat, Greenlandic Inuit, Yup'ik, Sami, Aleut, Evenki, and other indigenous communities that call the Arctic home.By reading and discussing texts from history, anthropology, literature, and film studies, we will work to build a ‘view from the top,’ in order to better understand how the so-called 'global north’ benefits from the continued systematic exploitation and erasure of the Indigenous peoples who live above 66º N.  In so doing, we’ll develop a circumpolar perspective that reimagines the Arctic not as a frontier, but as a homeland that is continually threatened by colonization, climate change, and resource extraction. 

Please Note: This course is intended for students who already possess a working knowledge of both settler and franchise colonialism, processes of racialization, and interdisciplinary research. However, no prior research or knowledge of the Arctic is required.

Sections.title: Fall & Rise of American Empire
Sections.description:
The Fall and Rise of American Empire

When the Thirteen Colonies successfully revolted against the British (1775-1783), they struck a major blow against the institution of imperialism. Yet today, people within and outside the nation increasingly describe the United States as an imperial power. Did the United States ever have colonies, and do they still exist today? If not, what is the status of American “possessions” such as Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and Puerto Rico? The Republican president Donald Trump has offered to buy the populated island of Greenland from Denmark, but here he is merely following in the footsteps of Democratic president Harry Truman, who made the same offer in 1946. What do the people of Greenland have to say about this? Even earlier in 1898, the Philippines went from being a colony of Spain to being a colony of the United States, after the U.S. bought the archipelago for $20 million. (The Philippines finally gained independence in 1946.) This course gives students a chance to develop their own understanding of a complex history by exploring the origin and various meanings behind the terms “empire/colony,” “postcolonialism,” “settler colonialism,” and “neocolonialism” in the context of American domestic and foreign policies. Students will also examine the various ways the rest of the world has tended to regard the United States since its independence from Great Britain.

Sections.title: HowSocialMovementsBuildAWorld
Sections.description:
Towards Liberation: How Could Radical Social Movements Build a World Without Racism, Capitalism, and Patriarchy?

This is a writing course that approaches liberation from an anti-capitalist, anti-racist, and anti-zionist perspective. What does liberation from oppression and exploitation mean? How can it be achieved, and how might past efforts inform present struggles for liberation? We will explore how radical social movements, past and present, have envisioned liberation and fought for a world without racism, capitalism, and patriarchy. Topics include: strategies for dismantling oppressive systems; the creation of alternative, non-capitalist ways of living; the cultivation of solidarity across struggles; and the problems of co-optation and suppression of radical movements. 

We won’t systematically review the histories of these social movements, but rather use their materials to stimulate our own thinking about liberation. Each week, we will write about one aspect of liberation and give each other constructive feedback, so that we can grow as writers and thinkers.

Sections.title: Queer Arts of Survival
Sections.description:
Queer Arts of Survival

“We’re Here, We’re Queer, Get Used To It!” From riots to dance floors to communities of care, queer people have long been survival artists. This course explores how LGBTQ+ communities have used protest, art, storytelling, technologies, and mutual aid to build worlds in the face of social and political marginalization. Rooted in the long history of queer publishing and community-based archive making, this class will look at historical examples of community care and survival as documented through experimental practices and publishing forms, with a focus on cross-movement and intersectional publications. We will explore local archives and digital collections and materials and investigate how artists have responded in past moments of crisis. 

This course is an advanced writing seminar in which students will develop skills in reading, research and analysis, and communicating narratives to audiences in writing. We will produce a collaborative collection of archival resources as well as individual research projects. Grading in this course will be based on: engaged participation in discussions and writing labs, and a scaffolded research project and presentation.

Sections.title: Politics of Migration & Death
Sections.description:
The Politics of Migration and Death

What does migrant death reveal about contemporary regimes of mobility and labor, state sovereignty and nationalism, violence and the abject, belonging and unbelonging? Drawing on recent and canonical critical ethnographies on migration, this graduate seminar examines how the field of anthropology has grappled with death and dying as political problems. The course asks how migrant death is produced, managed, and rendered meaningful by states, markets, and transnational regimes of governance. How, for instance, do notions of home, homeland, and political belonging shift when migrants encounter death, as explored in Osman Balkan’s "Dying Abroad: The Political Afterlives of Migration in Europe"? How does global capitalism appear differently when migrant workers are positioned at the center of extractive economies rather than at their margins, as Andrea Wright shows in Between "Dreams and Ghosts: Indian Migration and Middle Eastern Oil"? Students will read ethnographies like "Unsettling" (Gilberto Rosas), "The Fragmentary City" (Andrew Gardner) and "Against Innocence" (Miriam Ticktin) to engage questions of bordering, dehumanization, resistance, and alternative political futures.

Course Requirements:

Weekly seminar discussions, in-class presentations, occasional response papers, and a final seminar paper that could potentially feed into a conference paper, dissertation chapter, or a journal article

Sections.title: Intersectional Perspectives
Sections.description: Intersectional feminist perspectives and the liberation ideologies they birthed, apply to all oppressed people groups and orientation identities. Intersectional feminist perspectives actively work to frame and reframe feminism as a larger context in which bodies (Black, Brown, First Nations, Latinx, Indigenous, Asian, and any body within these and other marginalized people groups) own agency and are deserving of political representation and freedom. This course requires previous engagement with intersectional feminist theory and critical race theory as we will collectively work to map and expand these foundational ideologies to existing and emerging issues in digital and algorithmic culture. Together we will question how digital technologies limit or enhance agency; how algorithmic culture influences our perceptions of each other; and how digital media influence popular culture narratives on race, gender, class, sexuality, and other identity categories.
