Sections.title: Food at UM
Sections.description:
Food is an essential part of the University of Michigan student experience. What did UM students eat in the past and where does the food served on campus today come from? This seminar examines changes in the food system that has fed UM students in Ann Arbor over the past 150 years and the ways that food is helping the University become more sustainable. We explore all aspects of the food system from production to waste.

Experiential learning, including historical research with the Bentley Library student scrapbook collection, a visit to the Campus Farm, and a project with student-led sustainable food organizations, is an essential part of this course. Students will have opportunities to learn directly from the people who are working to make the university food system more local, sustainable and accessible.

 

Course Requirements:

In this course, students work in small teams on two mini-research projects and give presentations on their research (50%). Participation (20%) involves short assignments and classroom discussions. Students write two response papers (30%) applying information from the course to broader questions about the food system and sustainability.

Intended Audience:

This course is intended for students in their first year at U-M, who are interested in changes in the food we eat. No background in anthropology or archaeology is needed, only a willingness to be an active learner and a participant observer.

 

Class Format:

This course meets twice a week for discussions of reading, activities, and fieldtrips to locations on campus.

Sections.title: Capitalism and Collective Life
Sections.description:
The University of Michigan Department of Anthropology presents its Fall 2025 Roy A. Rappaport Lecture Series, Bananapocalypse! Un/Making Plantation Capitalism, by Assistant Professor Alyssa Paredes.

Existential crises hang over the producers of the world’s food. Many of these challenges are self-inflicted. In the banana-growing regions of the Southern Philippines, which produce fruit for export to Japanese markets, plantations unleash pesticide drift, food waste, water effluent, and fungal pathogens into the surroundings. The plantocratic elite systematically shirks responsibility for these excesses, using legal contracts, scientific conventions, and standards of trade to frame them as “external” to their supply chains. However, plantation management is regularly proven wrong in its assumption that the things they try to push downstream will not double back to haunt them. Everyday actors on the plantations’ peripheries transform the devices designed to work against them into openings for intervention. Their efforts implore critical scholars of the environment and of global economies to take seriously the possibility that Big Ag’s increasingly frequent failures to reproduce itself are more than just minor inconveniences to business-as-usual. In this series of lectures, I trace the afterlives of the externalities that commodity production obscures, disguises, or otherwise erases from its ambit of accountability. In so doing, I offer an ethnographic model for turning the commodity studies model, inherited from generations of anthropologists, inside-out. 

Join us for all four lectures on the dates below at 3 to 4:30 p.m. in 411 West Hall or virtually on Zoom.

Friday, September 12 - Part One
Elses and Externalities: The Un / Making of Plantation Capitalism

Friday, October 10 - Part Two
Rejects: Food Cosmetic Standards and the Geopolitics of Waste

Friday, November 14  - Part Three
Effluent: Living Downstream of Yourself on the Mindanao River

Friday, December 5 - Part Four
Force Majeure: The See-Through Plantation

 

 

Course Requirements:

The Rappaport lectures are a series of four public lectures on a topic related to the current scholarly research of the instructor delivered over the span of one semester, generally in the Fall term. The course is open to Anthropology graduate students who enroll for one credit and may register for additional independent study credits with the permission of the instructor.  Non-anthropology students require the permission of the instructor. Students who take this course for credit will earn an S or U grade (Satisfactory or Unsatisfactory) based on attendance.

This course is aimed at studying our living and fossil ape relatives in order to understand and reconstruct the biological history of the human species.  Students will receive training in how to carry out research in Biological Anthropology including how to generate and test hypotheses about human and ape evolution, data collection and analysis, and writing. Approaches may include but are not limited to: primatological and paleontological field methods, and/or fossil collections-based research. In 2026, students will be writing mock grant proposals, aimed at convincing funding agencies that research on human evolution remains vital to our current and future well-being.

Intended Audience:

Students interested in evolutionary biology, pre-health studies, primate biology, anthropology, and related fields will receive training relevant to their career goals. The course will pair graduate students with undergraduates, fostering highly collaborative, structured engagement in the scientific method.

Class Format:

The course will take the form of a directed research course and will begin with weekly discussions, laboratory exercises and readings from the primary literature. As the semester progresses, students will develop collaborative project ideas tailored to their interests.

Sections.title: Native Andeans today
Sections.description:
Inka ruins and landscapes draw tourists from around the world, but few of the visitors get to know the modern descendants of the Inkas. This class is an introduction to Native Andeans today: their social practices, ideas about the world, religious practices, and lives. The course will draw on first-person accounts, ethnography, film and music  to introduce modern Quechua-speaking people and their lifeways. We will be reading three ethnographic monographs—book length studies of Native Andean lives in Peru and Bolivia today; view a series of films—both ethnographic and fictional—that introduce lifeways, landscapes, and social-political issues.

The course is organized as a seminar, to give you the opportunity to follow up issues that interest and provoke. Each class meeting is divided into three principal activities:

(1) Introductory lectures, to provide you with background on an essential aspect of Native Andean life;

(2) Films to give you a sense of the diversity--social, linguistic, visual, geographic, and political—that you can encounter in the modern Andean republics. These run the gamut from documentary films to fiction, though the line between the two is a thin one;

(3) Open discussion of the readings, lectures, and films—though since we are a seminar I hope that you feel free to interrupt both of these with your questions, puzzlements, and comments.

This class is as close as you’ll get to experiencing another culture, and another way of life, without leaving Ann Arbor!

Sections.title: The Great Resignation
Sections.description:
American workers — especially in service industries — walked off the job in unprecedented numbers during the Covid-19 pandemic. In this First-Year Seminar, we will try to make sense of the “Great Resignation” by exploring “consumer-oriented” culture from the point of view of employees as well as of customers. We will draw on sociology and cultural anthropology approaches to think through how egalitarianism and hierarchy are performed and negotiated in commercial and professional settings, and the ideologies that distinguish service from servitude. 

Throughout, we will pay attention to how ideas of “customer service” have shifted historically with changes in the economy, in health and dental care systems, and in relation to social inequalities (of class, gender, ethnicity, caste, race and age). We will compare the United States with places that have different orientations to public welfare, to social hierarchies, and to the display of public emotion -- including places such as France, Vietnam, India and Hungary.

The course will also introduce students to ethnographic research methods, as well as to a liberal arts education.

Sections.title: Stranger Danger
Sections.description:
Humans routinely board airplanes and sit quietly, crammed together with strangers, even screaming babies. But what would happen if you traveled with an airplane full of chimpanzees? Chaos, says anthropologist Sarah Hrdy: “Any one of us would be lucky to disembark with all ten fingers and toes still attached, with the baby still breathing and unmaimed.” (2009, 3). Chimpanzees are one of our closest primate relatives, but humans often choose cooperation over conflict when confronting strangers. Why? What accounts for the human capacity to peacefully welcome strangers? How did we develop this ability? How do other primates react to strangers? What evidence in the archaeological record documents ancient human interactions with strangers? What strategies have contemporary humans developed to welcome others? How are native languages connected to questions of homeland sovereignty? How have empires and states dominated, incorporated, or rejected outsiders?


In this course, we will examine practices of hospitality to understand how strangers are incorporated (or not) into societies ranging from bonobo troops to family households to nation-states. We will use a four-field approach that looks to our closest primate relatives, the archaeological record, and ethnographic scholarship of contemporary human communities to better understand the authority and vulnerability of insiders and outsiders, as well as uniquely human capacities for cooperation.

Sections.title: Us vs. Them?
Sections.description: In the past decade, there has been rising concern around the world with a series of issues that appear interrelated: movements that constitute their identities in radical opposition to ethnic, racial, and religious minorities; the rise of hate speech, digital tribalism, and echo-chambers on social media; increasingly stark social divisions around topics like abortion, transgender rights, and policing. Simultaneously, we have seen the resurgence of mass protest movements that take to the streets to express deep-seated grievances. Populism, polarization, and protest seem to have in common that they often imagine a binary world divided between us and them, right and wrong, good and evil. But are they in fact related? And if so, how? Is an “us vs. them” logic always bad, or are antagonisms essential to politics, as some political theorists have claimed? What are alternative ways of imagining politics today? In this class, we will use what anthropology teaches us about how collective identities are formed, and the role of emotions like love, fear, anger, outrage, and suspicion in politics, to explore these questions. For the final assignment, students will work in groups to create a podcast episode that helps a broader audience better understand an issue of their choice.

Sections.title: Ethnographic Explorations
Sections.description:
In this course, students will explore ethnography by learning with and from senior citizens in the Ann Arbor community through a community-based learning (CBL) project. CBL emphasizes reciprocity, respect, and fostering academic learning while engaging meaningfully in the community and addressing real-world issues.

In the U.S. and many Western countries, the elderly population is increasingly marginalized, facing discrimination, prejudice, and exclusion. Some common and often overlooked health issues among seniors include loneliness, social isolation, and exclusion. Recent studies show that one-quarter of older adults report feeling socially isolated, and approximately one million seniors are considered severely socially isolated.

This course offers an opportunity to meaningfully address the so-called "loneliness epidemic" among seniors by connecting students with local community elders to engage in mutual learning, connection, and enjoyment. At the same time, these relationships will serve as a framework for hands-on learning about ethnography: we will explore ethnographic methods and methodologies, as well as research topics relevant to our research participants in the community, such as subjective well-being, aging in the U.S., and intergenerationality. Students can document their findings and reflections on their experiences either through written forms (e.g., essays), visual representations (e.g., short films/documentaries), or multimedia forms (e.g., photojournalism, infographics).

Course Requirements:

In-class meetings will occur once weekly for 2-3 hours. Course readings from cultural anthropology, cross-cultural studies, sociology, psychology, and philosophy, along with in-class lectures, will provide foundational background knowledge on ethnographic research and related topics. Additionally, students will be paired in groups of two with an elder from the local community and will meet with them weekly, for 2-3 hours, at a standing weekly time that works for everyone’s schedule. Funding will be provided for at-home projects with our community partners (e.g., cooking or crafting), outings (e.g., visits to cafés, museums, and lectures), occasional full group gatherings (at the Residential College and White Lotus Farms), and transportation.

Sections.title: Animal-Human Communication
Sections.description: Who do we become in association with other animals? What is the range of ways humans and other critters interact with and interpret each other? How do social and material borders (lab cages, park fences, property lines, performance curtains) affect how we make contacts and decode communications?  When, how, and why do people baby talk with pets and swear at beasts of burden? How are claims about differences among animals, or between humans and animals, projected into claims about differences among humans? How do these phenomena differ over time and across communities? We pursue these questions, surveying scholarship on animal-human communication, with special attention to conditions for interactions — physical materials, biological sensory capacities, social networks, and cultural habits and technologies. In lieu of exams, students gradually build their own observation projects, testing methods for social and linguistic research.

Sections.title: Issues in Race & Ethnicity
Sections.description:
This course examines the cultures and societies of contemporary Latin America, a vast and varied region with more than twenty countries spread over one and a half continents that have developed over more than 500 years of history. We will cultivate an awareness of the particularities of local ways of life while searching for shared themes and histories that in some ways unite the many societies of this vast region.

Topics covered include: race, ethnicity, and national identity; indigenous rights and citizenship; religion and religious change; gender issues; class and economic development; and immigrant communities within Latin America. By the end of this course, you should have a grasp of the various countries and regions that make up Latin America; the most important social divisions within those regions; and the nature of current developments in Latin American societies.

Course Requirements:

As a student, you will be expected to keep up with reading and writing assignments and to participate actively in lectures and discussions. Grades will be based on engagement with the weekly readings, regular attendance and participation in lectures and class discussions, an oral presentation, and two short papers

Intended Audience:

This is an introductory course on the region, with no prerequisites other than a desire to learn new things.

Sections.description: Why do monuments matter? Do monuments matter? Why and when are monuments contested, altered, or taken down? In this course, we will examine the politics of history and public memory by analyzing contested monuments, buildings, landscapes, and places. We will question why and how certain pasts are valorized and memorialized while others are silenced, repressed, and forgotten. To answer these questions, we will explore comparative case studies including the debate over US confederate monuments, the fate of socialist monuments after the fall of the USSR, and ongoing conflict over violent histories and repressed memories of minority communities in Turkey, with a focus on the Armenian Genocide of 1915. Students will engage with anthropological and historical scholarship as well as visual material, memoirs, journalism, and documentaries.

Sections.title: Kinship: Histories & Channels
Sections.description: This course explores the range of kinship systems across the globe by asking how such systems—which link and separate real, particular people—have both channeled and been shaped by historical events and movements. The formation of European aristocracies, the pressures against American matrilineal land tenure, the Soviet purges of class enemies: a broad range of historical processes have deployed, enabled, and broken kinship ties, building roads while displacing relatives, forging trade contracts and occupational dynasties along with marriages. Bringing such questions into the present, students are encouraged to study their own networks as “event descendants.” Against the current hyper-focus on tracing DnA to derive percentages of national origins, students will dig deeper, exploring how and when actual kinship complicates categories and identities, and asking how we have come to claim or to deny current relations to others. Students will build research skills (archival and ethnographic methods) as they design and complete a project of their choosing.

Sections.title: Lang & Society in S. America
Sections.description: First we discover the genre: what did ethnographic documentary film used to be and what is it becoming? We will view, discuss, and reverse engineer classic and innovative ethnographic films, looking carefully at structure and technique. While we do some of this in a traditionally scholarly way, reading and discussing key writings about the films, we put most effort into actively testing techniques for making short ethnographic documentaries. Students explore topics while experimenting with techniques (from interviewing to editing), preparing short weekly assignments to share during class (commentaries, photos, video clips) in order to receive feedback from the group and the instructor as they work towards finishing a project. Students need only a telephone with a video camera, or camera checked out from the campus media center.  Because learning to make doc films involves finding ways to collaborate, be it with film subjects or crew, attendance and participation will be central for credit.

Sections.title: Anthro & Children's Literature
Sections.description: This course brings an anthropological perspective to the understanding of the genre of children’s literature. Our focus will be mainly on picture books, the literature that exists for the youngest children, which typically includes narrative art and visual grammar that incorporates text and illustrations. We will use a multidisciplinary approach to analyze the classics of children’s literature and to consider new trends in picture books that address cultural heritage, gender, race, and social differences as well as children’s hopes and dreams and anxieties. We will examine multicultural and multilingual picture books and address the issue of banned books and the public debates around childhood politics. We will also consider the trends in children’s literature publishing and book awards. We will read books together as a class and discuss them in a seminar format and students will alternate giving presentations on additional readings. For final projects, students will have the opportunity to produce analytical studies of selected picture books or to create their own picture books. Ultimately, the aim is to gain new ways of thinking about the art of storytelling and how anthropological perspectives can enlighten us about the cultural truths being communicated and what they mean to readers. This course will be of interest to students in anthropology, education, psychology, creative writing, and art, and to anyone curious to learn what are the stories that teach children how to be human.

Sections.title: Nonverbal Communication
Sections.description: How do our bodies express, or betray, what we mean when we talk with others? In this introduction to the study of embodied communication, we explore the hidden dimensions of conversational interaction by working closely with video recordings. We look at gesture, gaze, nods, demeanor, and posture; how people manage their bodies in small groups and navigate the built environment. We look at the way small nonverbal behaviors can matter for big social issues like gender politics, everyday racism, socioeconomic class stratification, and religious and cultural difference.

Sections.description:
Ethnography Beyond the Human

Contemporary anthropology is pressing beyond the limits defined by "the study of humans" in several directions. In this seminar we will read a variety of recent ethnographies that go beyond the human, taking on animals, robots, artificial intelligence, climate change, the environment, and the divine We will ask what we find there when we broaden out ethnographic scope. What are the ethical, epistemological, methodological, and political challenges of this kind of work? Considering these questions is also a useful way to reflect more generally on what an ethnography is and what it could be. To that end, we will be reading monographs, not short excerpts or articles. This is therefore also a course in reading and writing, and in how to make clear arguments with complex details. The class is open to students from all disciplines and departments who might be interested in exploring these questions further.

Sections.title: Capitalism and Collective Life
Sections.description:
The University of Michigan Department of Anthropology presents its Fall 2025 Roy A. Rappaport Lecture Series, Bananapocalypse! Un/Making Plantation Capitalism, by Assistant Professor Alyssa Paredes.

Existential crises hang over the producers of the world’s food. Many of these challenges are self-inflicted. In the banana-growing regions of the Southern Philippines, which produce fruit for export to Japanese markets, plantations unleash pesticide drift, food waste, water effluent, and fungal pathogens into the surroundings. The plantocratic elite systematically shirks responsibility for these excesses, using legal contracts, scientific conventions, and standards of trade to frame them as “external” to their supply chains. However, plantation management is regularly proven wrong in its assumption that the things they try to push downstream will not double back to haunt them. Everyday actors on the plantations’ peripheries transform the devices designed to work against them into openings for intervention. Their efforts implore critical scholars of the environment and of global economies to take seriously the possibility that Big Ag’s increasingly frequent failures to reproduce itself are more than just minor inconveniences to business-as-usual. In this series of lectures, I trace the afterlives of the externalities that commodity production obscures, disguises, or otherwise erases from its ambit of accountability. In so doing, I offer an ethnographic model for turning the commodity studies model, inherited from generations of anthropologists, inside-out. 

Join us for all four lectures on the dates below at 3 to 4:30 p.m. in 411 West Hall or virtually on Zoom.

Friday, September 12 - Part One
Elses and Externalities: The Un / Making of Plantation Capitalism

Friday, October 10 - Part Two
Rejects: Food Cosmetic Standards and the Geopolitics of Waste

Friday, November 14  - Part Three
Effluent: Living Downstream of Yourself on the Mindanao River

Friday, December 5 - Part Four
Force Majeure: The See-Through Plantation

 

 

Course Requirements:

The Rappaport lectures are a series of four public lectures on a topic related to the current scholarly research of the instructor delivered over the span of one semester, generally in the Fall term. The course is open to Anthropology graduate students who enroll for one credit and may register for additional independent study credits with the permission of the instructor.  Non-anthropology students require the permission of the instructor. Students who take this course for credit will earn an S or U grade (Satisfactory or Unsatisfactory) based on attendance.

Sections.title: Asian Myths
Sections.description:
This course will explore Asian myths, their incredible variety, commonalities, peculiarities, and universality. We will sample some myths—stories about a moon rabbit, frustrated ghosts, selfless tigers, magical monkeys, water-controlling dragons, evil spirits that spread epidemics, righteous bandit-sorcerers, and so on—in English translation and discuss, in class, scholarly arguments about what to do with myths and other similar forms of storytelling. The goal of this class is to better understand the complexity and beauty of the human condition by looking at the creative ways in which this condition was explored through myths in Asia.

Course Requirements:

Weekly assigned readings, short weekly online writing assignments, and 2 quizzes.

Intended Audience:

Freshmen and sophomores, but everyone is welcome.

Class Format:

Two 90-minute seminars weekly.

Sections.title: Social Media in India & US
Sections.description:
What is the relationship between artistic modernism and political independence? How did the creation of new nation states transform the art institutional landscape across South Asia? What kinds of relationships between form and politics emerged in the wake of significant events like the Partition of India? These are just some of the questions we will explore in this course, as we study artistic practices as well as the institutions and networks of modernism in the Subcontinent following the end of colonial rule. We will critically interrogate the position of the postcolonial artist, and how larger socio-political developments interacted with formal expression and the choice of materials.

The role and development of technologies of production and circulation will be underscored, as will the changing contexts of patronage and exhibition. We will conclude at the turn of the century, evaluating the conditions for the proliferation of 'postmodernist' practices across media, while diagnosing the advent of the so-called "global contemporary." The course will provide both theoretical tools and significant case studies in analyzing relationships between politics and artistic form.

Textbooks/Other Materials: Materials will be available through Canvas. No textbook.

HISTART Distribution Requirements: Asia, Modern and Contemporary

Course Requirements:

Mid-term examination (25%), Paper (25%), Final examination (25%), Attendance and class participation (25%)

Intended Audience:

Undergraduates

Class Format:

Two 80-minute meetings per week

Sections.title: Research: Senior Proj Asian St
Sections.description:
The Junior-Senior colloquium aims to provide students with the first-hand experience in designing, executing, and presenting original research projects in Asian Studies. The course will fall into three parts. The first part will provide students with models of research papers in the various fields associated with Asian Studies. The second part will involve students developing research proposals of their own for critical feedback from the instructor and the students. The third part, students will execute small research projects and produce an original paper approximately 15 pages in length. The drafts of the project will be presented to other members of the class for feedback before being submitted as a final paper for the class. The goal of the class is not only to help students develop skills for original research and teach them how to write humanities essays, but also to expose them to the different paradigms and methodologies associated with the field of Asian Studies.

Class Format:

Two 90-minute meetings weekly

This course teaches advanced speaking, listening, reading, and writing skills in Filipino. These skills will be taught through formal class sessions in which students learn to use new grammatical structures to discuss various topics in Filipino culture and literature. Students will also actively participate in suggesting methods to reach a greater exploration and presentation of knowledge. The class will provide various opportunities to improve fluency in the spoken language. The course involves a significant number of writing assignments and students will be required to submit written works to improve their writing proficiency.

By the end of the term, students will have improved their reading comprehension through expanded vocabularies and will be able to understand and use the words, expressions, and phrases with more confidence. Students will also expand their knowledge of general Philippine culture and history through reading and listening. In speaking, students will be able to narrate and describe concrete topics and interests in past, present, and future tenses. In reading, students will understand both main ideas and notice minor details in selected texts and excerpts of media and other literary materials. In writing, students will develop their own ideas about concrete topics in Filipino. Students will attain oral proficiency equivalent to the advanced low/advanced mid-level of the ACTFL Oral Proficiency Interview.

Course Requirements:

It is required that students use Filipino during class hours and it is recommended outside the classroom to promote further mastery of the language. Grading components include attendance, recitation, and class participation. In-class and take-home readings will also be assigned after every topic. Midterm and final oral assessments will also be components of grading. A creative writing assignment will be required of the students as an overall requirement.

Intended Audience:

This class is intended for students who have successfully completed ASIANLAN 212 with a grade of C- or higher and have fulfilled all the requirements; or those who have taken the language placement exam in Filipino, successfully placing into this level.

Sections.title: Controversies in Indonesia
Sections.description:
This course is a continuation of ASIANLAN 222. This course is to advance students’ communicative skills, including listening, speaking, reading, and writing, through the discussion of reading materials from textbooks and other authentic materials like newspapers, magazines, and audiovisual materials. The reading materials will be focused on socio-cultural, political, technological, medical, and other common issues and problems in Indonesia and around the world. With an emphasis on the analysis of selected texts (fiction and non-fiction), students are required to answer questions related to the texts or write a summary or response on the required readings for each session.

By the end of the semester, students will be able to: read passages from authentic materials like newspapers and magazines; listen and understand extended recordings, of news or movies in the Indonesian language; write responses to the reading and listening materials using advanced grammar and vocabulary; express and support their opinions; compare and contrast the issues discussed in class; make arguments to support their opinion as well as evaluating the materials and topics in depth.

Course Requirements:

The evaluation will be based on attendance and participation in class, weekly news reports, homework, weekly reading logs, and a final paper.

Intended Audience:

This class is intended for students who have passed ASIANLAN 222 with a grade C- or higher or those who have other equivalent Indonesian language training, as proven by the department’s placement test result.

Sections.title: Thai Soft Power
Sections.description:
This course aims to emphasize the Thai language in all communicative realms to give students a better understanding of the Thai language and comparative culture as students learn to use the language in discussions with native speakers. These communicative skills will be utilized through the examination of short and long stories on various topics: Thai daily life, people, traditions, arts, beliefs, and values of different regions and reigns.

By the end of this course students will be able to read academic passages, understand video presentations, predict content, identify main ideas and conclusions, produce written and oral summaries, answer questions about listening passages, and express critical thoughts in Thai. Students will give clear presentations with correct pronunciation to a small group of Thai speakers. Students will also write short and long essays about Thai living, people, traditions, arts, beliefs, values in different regions, and reigns by comparing their knowledge and experience with other cultures.

Course Requirements:

Because mastery of the Thai language depends on practice of it, evaluation will be based on attendance, participation, and homework in which students will practice what we learn in class. There will also be quizzes, two presentation assignments, and a final exam to check for understanding.

Intended Audience:

ASIANLAN 461 is for any student interested in advancing their knowledge of Thai language and culture. Students should have completed ASIANLAN 262 or the equivalent. Students who have not completed ASIANLAN 262, please contact the instructor for a placement test.

Sections.title: Asian American Lit and Culture
Sections.description:
We will survey in this course the representations of and by Asian American subjects in U.S. culture since the late nineteenth century. Cultural production—literature, drama, film, television, and performance, for example—has historically been the site where tensions among different ethnic and racial groups in the United States are exposed, resolved, exaggerated, or transformed. The cultural representation of such tensions has led, on one hand, to the affirmation of U.S. political and cultural hegemony, and, on the other, to acts of resistance to political and cultural dominance. This course explores the ways in which the cultural and literary production that arises out of the contradictions of U.S. democracy “displace,” in the words of cultural studies scholar Lisa Lowe, “the fiction of reconciliation”—the ways in which the cultural forms of Asian America “disrupt the myth of national identity by revealing its gaps and fissures.”

Texts in the course may include novels, plays, poems, films, television shows, advertisements, blogs, musicals, historical documents, and scholarly articles.

Sections.title: Plant World: Floral Fights & F
Sections.description: Despite being rooted in place, plants interact with many organisms in their environment, ranging from mutualists like pollinators and nitrogen-fixing bacteria to antagonists like herbivores and pathogens. In this course we will explore these interactions and how plants have evolved to manage them, as well as applications of plant biotic interactions in agriculture and medicine.

Sections.title: The Human Microbiome
Sections.description: The collection of microbes in and on the human – the microbiome – affects our physical and mental health. This course will focus on how we interact with our microbiome and how we might modify the gut microbiome through diet to influence our mood, responses to medical treatments, and long-term health. A scientific background is not required to excel in this course.

Sections.title: The Bio of Animal Migration
Sections.description: Migratory animals—including species as diverse as birds, butterflies, and whales—accomplish some of the most extraordinary feats of endurance and navigation during their seasonal journeys across the globe. These journeys have profound impacts for ecology, evolution, and conservation. In this course, you will learn how and why migratory animals traverse the Earth each year and how they are impacted by the rapid changes happening to our planet. We will ask questions including ‘how and why do animals migrate?’, ‘how do they navigate?’, and ‘how do we study animal migration?’.Our major goal is to learn about animal migration. Our other goals will be to gain familiarity with reading the primary scientific literature and analyzing data about migration. We will focus largely on birds but will explore animal migration more broadly.

Sections.title: Greek Tragedy Then And Now
Sections.description: This course addresses a wide range of topics from the ancient Greek and Roman cultures. These are studied for their ideas, literary values, and as illustrations of socio-historical and other historical and intellectual developments important for the understanding of the ancient and modern world, their achievements and problems.

Sections.title: Food in Ancient Literature
Sections.description:
Everyone needs to eat. But the study of food is about more than just nutrition and sustenance. What we eat and how in fact reveals a great deal about who we are, and what we consider acceptable or taboo, virtuous or decadent, modest or self-important. In this class, we’ll focus on what the ancient Greeks and Romans said about eating as a way of understanding their relationship to the gods, money and status, and style and identity. We’ll focus on topics including dinner parties, hunger, sacrifices, cannibalism, and compare some modern theory and examples as well.

Course Requirements:

2 papers and a creative project

Intended Audience:

Freshmen

Class Format:

Two meetings per week

Sections.title: Ancient Pharmacy
Sections.description:
A fine line existed between drugs and poisons in the ancient and medieval Mediterranean. For instance, the Hippocratic writers infamously prescribed hellebore, a plant drug that was purported to have therapeutic effects on gynecological and psychological conditions but was toxic at the wrong dosage. This course will investigate where Greco-Roman and medieval pharmacists obtained drugs from the natural world as well as both how and why they used them in their healing practices. Students will gain familiarity with the fascinating and surprisingly global field of pre-modern pharmacy. They will also leave the course with a greater understanding of the ethics of bioprospecting from pre-modern medical sources and the natural world. 

Course Requirements:

A series of scaffold exercises (short analysis paper, annotated bibliography, and rationale) that lead up to the creation of an ancient herbal entry

Intended Audience:

No prior knowledge required

Class Format:

Two meetings per week

Sections.title: Magic & Witchcraft
Sections.description:
Imagine an invisible world of demons and other semi-divine figures that could bend the natural world to your benefit. This course studies the occult – or ‘hidden – in the Greco-Roman Mediterranean to learn how magic operated through the manipulation of unseen forces, whether demons, angels, or other intermediary beings like astral rays. Besides acquiring an understanding of the theories and practices that contributed to ‘magic’, students will survey the often marginalized figures (so-called witches and sorcerers) that were associated with magical practices. Covering a expanse of time that will take us from 5th-century BCE Greece to late-antique Egypt, we will investigate the texts and artifacts related to the making of magic. 

Course Requirements:

Scaffold exercises (short text analysis, annotated bibliography, and rough draft script) leading up to the recreation of an ancient magical ritual 

Intended Audience:

requires no prior knowledge

Class Format:

Two meetings per week, seminar format

Sections.title: Romans in America
Sections.description:
From Capitol Hill to Caesar's Palace; from 'e pluribus unum' to 'sic semper tyrannis'; from the founding of the Republic to the Red Caesar; from 1776 to 2026, ancient Rome has been an ambivalent model for the United States of America, representing both its ideals of liberty and a justification for slavery, a benchmark of civilization and a cautionary tale of moral decadence. On this course, we will explore the ways in which ancient Rome has shaped American national identity, political life, and popular culture over the 250 years from the Declaration of Independence to the present. 

Course Requirements:

In-class participation, short presentations, final research project (no exams)

Intended Audience:

Any interested undergraduate

Class Format:

Two 80-minute meetings per week (mixture of lecture and discussion)

Sections.description:
Ficino, Plato, and the Visual Imagination in Renaissance Italy
Marsilio Ficino (1433-1499) was a Renaissance philosopher, priest, and translator who played a central role in the intellectual life of Florence. Ficino's translations and commentaries on the works of Plato and Plotinus, and the Hermetica were instrumental in reviving Neoplatonist thought in the West and shaping the development of Renaissance humanism. In this course, we will study the connections between Ficino’s theories of the imagination, his work on ancient magic, and the circle of visual artists in his ambit, particularly Sandro Botticelli. We will do a field trip to the Cleveland Museum of Art, where we will study one of the oldest sets of Northern Italian Tarrochi Cards, original engraved etchings. Scholars generally agree that this set of 50 engravings was an educational tool, perhaps devised by a humanist scholar to visually describe a fifteenth-century philosophical model of the cosmos. Students will think about the impact of Classicism on the art, philosophy, and  literature of Fifteenth century Florence. Possibly they will have the opportunity to design their own set of Tarrocchi (or Tarot) Cards, and to study the translations of Ficino from Greek to Latin.

Sections.title: Student Seminar Series
Sections.description:
The Special Topics Seminars (CMB 850) in Fall, Winter and Spring terms consist of student seminars at noon on Mondays. These seminars bring the Program together each week. All CMB students, including candidates, and CMB faculty, participate in and contribute to the student seminars. Precandidates in the CMB Program are required to register for the course. All candidate students are also required to attend (whether or not they enroll for credit). First year students in PIBS can attend CMB 850 seminars and may request an opportunity to present a seminar. The seminar date for each student is indicated on a schedule prepared by the Student Seminar Coordinator at the beginning of each academic year. To accommodate attendance by all CMB faculty while maintaining the personal nature of student-faculty interactions, each CMB faculty member is assigned at least three attendance dates during the academic year.

Precandidate students generally present a critical review of one or two related reports in the current scientific literature dealing with a significant advance in molecular/cellular biology. The presentation should be a critical evaluation of the work, not simply a summary of it. Coordination of paper choices with the topic of each term’s Short Course is scheduled just prior to the Short Course each term. Third year students generally serve as evaluators and chair the discussion session that follows the seminar. More senior candidate students present seminars on their own research. Precandidate students occasionally choose this option.

Students work with a faculty advisor, generally the research mentor, to prepare the talk and practice it formally before the actual presentation. A practice session is scheduled during the week prior to the scheduled seminar and is attended by the mentor, a faculty evaluator, a student evaluator and others invited by the student. At the seminar, discussion and criticism of the research by the audience is encouraged. Student discussants lead off and moderate the discussion, which includes students and faculty. At least one faculty member and a student evaluator discuss the presentation with each student at the end of each session.

Specifics of Seminar Preparation

  1. At the beginning of each fall term, a schedule is set up for student presentations for the academic year. Each student is expected to arrange for a faculty mentor to help prepare for the seminar in the faculty member’s field of interest.
  2. At least four weeks prior to the presentation, each student should begin preparations with the faculty mentor. They should discuss the topic, identify interesting papers, and the student should begin preparing the presentation with advice from the faculty member. In keeping with the broad approaches in CMB training, it is recommended that students select papers from the highest quality journals of broad interest rather than from specialty journals.
  3. Two weeks prior to the seminar, the student should provide the CMB Administrator with the principal references (including pdf or url), relevant secondary references and a paragraph summarizing the topic (as a hard copy and electronically). This is distributed to faculty and students by e-mail a week prior to the presentation.
  4. During the week prior to the seminar, students should schedule a formal practice with the faculty advisor. One of the faculty evaluators for the course, and the student evaluator also attend this practice and provide comments. In this way, the student has an opportunity to implement suggestions for the formal seminar presentation. For convenience, the seminar room is generally reserved on Fridays for rehearsals.
  5. The student presents the seminar to assembled CMB students, faculty and other interested individuals, and answers questions from the floor. Audiovisual equipment is available or requested via the CMB office. An assigned student discussant/evaluator provides a professional introduction to the speaker, prepares questions to lead off discussion during the seminar and serves as moderator during the discussions. The discussant also provides a final evaluation to the presenting student following the seminar.
  6. A faculty member from the Student Seminar Committee and one of the student discussants meet with each student immediately after the presentation to discuss strengths and weaknesses of the seminar. Written critiques from the evaluators are made available to the student and reviewed by the Student Seminar Committee.

Sections.title: Energy and Climate Change
Sections.description:
Energy is an incredibly complex topic by virtue of the inter-linkages of science, technology, public policy, economics, and human behaviors. This course will examine all aspects of energy: supply and demand, technical and social, with a concerted look at the natural place of social science (behavior, pricing, externalities, social norms) in the energy sphere.

Every aspect of present-day society depends on the continuing availability of clean, affordable, flexible, secure, and safe energy resources. Yet nearly 90% of our current energy needs are met by fossil fuels. Our reliance on fossil fuels has led to declining supplies, rising prices, global climate change, and security concerns. The current global energy economy is not sustainable. The technological challenges are formidable; but they cannot be considered solutions without considering the human and social behavioral side of energy demand.

The quest for solutions to "The Energy Problem" is dominated by technology "fixes". The visions of practical technological fixes, whether electricity energy generation, oil exploration and extraction, pollution mitigation, automobile fuel efficiency and alternatives to combustion engines, etc., necessarily build on what we know today and presume that we can achieve in a couple of decades or so, through sufficient R&D, an energy supply-demand balance that fulfills a wide range of incompatible requirements — cheap, environmentally benign, politically secure, unconstrained supply, convenient, and safe. While we expect technology to come to our energy-rescue and support our established patterns of economic growth and energy-intensive lifestyles, we tend to expect very little from the human and social behavioral side of energy use and demand. In some ways the Energy Problem is yet another version of C.P. Snow's Two Cultures — parallel technology and social cultures with little mutual understanding and rare cross-over exchange.

The Complex Systems view would hold that society and Energy technologies have coevolved through the actions of individual agents (inventors, scientists, entrepreneurs, financiers, writers, politicians, kings and queens, dictators, and statesman), learning, adapting, selecting, exchanging information, and interacting through transactions of many kinds. At every stage, the social, economic, and technological systems were tightly coupled. It is not possible to understand Energy Problems without framing them in a systems context.

Course Requirements:

Two midterm exams, a Final Exam, graded homework assignments, and a term project.

Intended Audience:

Freshmen and Sophomores interested in energy and complex systems.

Class Format:

3 hours of lecture per week.

Sections.title: AI & Communication
Sections.description:
As AI technologies become more integrated into our daily lives, they are reshaping not only how different forms of communication are created and consumed, but also how we understand what communication means in relation to consciousness and creativity. From anxieties over plagiarism in academic writing to new modes of creative collaboration in fiction, art and music, from the reinforcement of biases in journalistic reporting to the potential for more inclusive narratives in media, the intersection of AI and communication has become a hot topic in popular media and press coverage on machine-human interaction. Beyond the hype, what do these developments mean for our current communication ecosystem? How can we critically assess the ways AI is being talked about, represented, and integrated into everyday life?

 

This freshman seminar offers historical context and introduces techniques for the critical analysis of contemporary developments in generative AI and large language models. Focusing on a variety of communication genres, we explore debates around how AI is impacting creative writing, journalism, healthcare, political communication, screen acting and script development, visual arts, music, advertising, social media, strategic communication and public relations. Through current case studies, interactive projects collaborating with AI, and classroom discussions, students will examine how AI affects the style, structure, and purpose of communication across different genres. We will address how bias and structural inequality informs these systems and how authenticity figures alongside the potential for misinformation and the implications for creative ownership.

Sections.title: Reclaiming Place in Dgtl World
Sections.description: 'Location, Location, Location' — It’s the mantra of real estate brokers, but how might the phrase apply given the apparent placelessness of the digital world? Over the past century, communication technologies, network connectivity, and other global processes have liberated U.S. culture from national borders and extended America's presence into the lives and imaginations of billions of people. After the September 11th, 2001 attacks on the United States, signs appeared around the world that read: “We are all Americans.” But what does that slogan mean to a student of media and communication and is it even true? This seminar uses historical and contemporary case studies of the expansive power of U.S. media, and responses to that power on the part of individuals and group efforts seeking to (re)claim identity and a sense of place against globalization processes. We will consider some of the surprising outcomes and effects of the incorporation of U.S. culture into non-Western settings to gain an appreciation for the range of responses and strategies to manage identity and place in a digital world in which America often casts the longest shadow.

Sections.title: Self-Pres, Authenticity&SocMed
Sections.description: In today’s hyper-connected world, social media plays a crucial role in shaping our daily lives, influencing how we connect, communicate and present ourselves. As we continue to rely on these technologies, the question of how we navigate constructing identity, impression making, and validating authenticity, becomes important.  This course will examine the relationship between features of communication technology and self-presentation. We will analyze how attributes of technology help to shape our online identity, how technology and self-presentation strategies may impact us both psychologically and socially, and how attributes of technology can also influence how we perceive others. Topics covered in this course may include but are not limited to, online dating, self-disclosure and online communities, and body image.

Sections.title: Reality TV
Sections.description: Few elements of media culture are as loved or as hated as much as reality programs. Rather than debate whether or not reality television is “good” or “bad” for us, you learn the more rigorous approaches that researchers take when they examine and write about reality television. Through screenings, discussions, readings, and projects, this course provides you with opportunities to think about and study how reality programs construct social norms, how they fit into the contemporary media industries, and how they suggest to viewers that there are proper and improper lifestyles. Far more than “trash,” reality television shines a light on the contemporary U.S., suggesting a great deal about who we are as a people and what drives us as a culture.

Sections.title: Brand Storytelling
Sections.description: In this course students will examine how and why organizations use advertising as a discipline to effectively establish, differentiate, and build brands. Students will gain an understanding of the industry, and the specific professions within it, as they learn to apply the specific tools and strategies used to employ best practices in effective and ethical mass communication. Key principles covered in this course include advertising research, strategic planning, audience analysis, media planning, creative ideation technique, creative execution, and new media.

Sections.title: Rep Mgmt for Global Business
Sections.description:
No credit granted to those who have completed COMM 304 - Reputation Management for Global Business

“It takes many good deeds to build a good reputation, and only one bad one to lose it.” Benjamin Franklin.

What do global giants like Amazon, Apple, or personalities, such as Rihanna or Cristiano Ronaldo, have in common? Despite competing in different industries, they share a key trait: the ability to build, promote and protect their most valuable asset — their reputations. Reputational Capital, often overlooked, is responsible for generating over 30 percent of a major firm’s market capitalization and a major enabler of business success. This course will explore the role of Communications and Media in building a positive reputation ecosystem.  From understanding reputational capital to online reputation management, crisis communications and digital content strategy, students will learn, through real-life case studies, the essential communications tools for actively managing reputation as a strategic value-creation discipline. This course will prove particularly beneficial to students in areas such as communications, media, marketing, business & management who want to learn practical skills on how to actively build, promote and protect the reputation of global organizations and brands for long-term success. The instructor will provide relevant reading materials for each key topic, share practical examples derived from over 20 years of experience as a Head of Global Communications for multinational brands and encourage practical application through in-class activities, crisis-simulations, and a final presentation.

Students develop practical communication and leadership skills for running meetings, guiding group processes, and organizing dialogue to achieve goals such as creative exploration, problem-solving, decision-making, and team building.

Sections.title: Sports Documentary Journalism
Sections.description:
In this course, students will learn to produce professional quality sports video documentaries. They will take stories from concept to content, using strong writing, production, and editing techniques, ending up with portfolio quality work that connects sports to larger issues in society. Students will begin the course by studying award-winning long-form sports broadcast journalism and documentary films, deconstructing content, writing, production, and editing techniques. Students will then learn and perform the art of pitching, researching, writing, and producing their own long-form sports broadcasts that go beyond games, wins, and losses. Then, in groups, students will create original sports documentaries. Students will perform extensive interviews, capture video and sound, and create stories that connect sports to the world around it. By the end of the course, students will have written and produced a 10 minute or longer, sports documentary that meets professional standards and builds their professional portfolio.

Students will develop a conceptual and practical understanding of the most useful tools that filmmakers use in non-fiction filmmaking. This will be achieved through lectures, discussions, screenings and practical exercises that focus on technique and content. Students will study and strengthen their interview skills, shooting, writing and editing and understand the subtle distinctions between long-form journalism and filmmaking.

TEXTS/SCREENINGS:

There will be limited assigned reading. All readings will be available digitally and this will include several formal write-ups from HBO Real Sports producers. Please make sure all readings are completed before class in order to participate in class discussions. Students will also be assigned weekly screenings of documentary films, docu-series and pieces that aired on Real Sports.

GUEST SPEAKERS:

We have scheduled award-winning documentary filmmakers, TV-sports journalists, editors and writers.

Sections.title: Entertainment Media & Society
Sections.description: Entertainment media is a cornerstone of contemporary life, yet its role in society is often called into question as frivolous—and its devotees derided as unproductive. This course considers how entertainment media might instead work to shape our communities, cultures, discourses, ideologies, and participation in civic and social life. Students will consume and engage with various forms of entertainment media, from film and television to gaming, podcasts, and online video. The course will focus on both the production and reception of entertainment media, with attention to the historical development of these industries as social, cultural, and political-economic forces.

Sections.title: Hist of Doc Photog & Photojour
Sections.description:
Powerful photographs often evoke an emotional response in the viewer. Documentary photography and photojournalism have played crucial roles in shaping worldviews and collective memory. 

This class will focus on documentary photography and photojournalism from the mid 20th century to today. We will view and discuss a wide range of diverse photographs from well known photographers as well as those who are often overlooked. Understanding historical and regional context will be an important part of the course. We will explore the evolution of aesthetics and ethical standards as well as the changing media landscape over time. Students will also regularly view photographs from current news events from various parts of the world.

Sections.title: Photo & Video for Social Media
Sections.description:
Compelling photographs and short-form videos have the power to evoke emotions and communicate stories. This class will develop a solid photo and short-form video foundation so students can better communicate visually with their audience.

Experiential classes and practical assignments will explore creative uses of photography and video through documentary, sports action, portraiture, and landscape genres. Specifically, we will study how to utilize composition, quality of light, color, moment, movement, and gesture to produce meaningful imagery. Students will shoot photographs and short videos on subjects they care about and want to explore with an eye towards creating original content with intention and personal style.

A background in photography or video is not necessary. The course will be engaging and interactive. We will view diverse photography and short videos related to social issues, art, and advertising for inspiration and to investigate how to develop ideas and create powerful images. Students will regularly share their work for class discussions and critiques. A sample of photographers and filmmakers we will view include: Lauren Greenfield, Moises Saman, Fazal Sheikh, Sara Terry, Mary Ellen Mark, Martin Bell, and Olexandr Glyadyelov.

Sections.title: Intersectional Perspectives
Sections.description: Intersectional feminist perspectives and the liberation ideologies they birthed, apply to all oppressed people groups and orientation identities. Intersectional feminist perspectives actively work to frame and reframe feminism as a larger context in which bodies (Black, Brown, First Nations, Latinx, Indigenous, Asian, and any body within these and other marginalized people groups) own agency and are deserving of political representation and freedom. This course requires previous engagement with intersectional feminist theory and critical race theory as we will collectively work to map and expand these foundational ideologies to existing and emerging issues in digital and algorithmic culture. Together we will question how digital technologies limit or enhance agency; how algorithmic culture influences our perceptions of each other; and how digital media influence popular culture narratives on race, gender, class, sexuality, and other identity categories.

Sections.title: Great Performances at Michigan
Sections.description:
In this writing-intensive course, performances in music, theater, film, dance and related arts will offer us not just entertainment but also provocations to feeling and thought. We will respond to those provocations by shaping thought and feeling into carefully crafted writing that communicates our thought to others. We will attend a series of events presented by local performing arts organizations. We will think about differences between mediated and “live” performances and attend to practices of attentive listening, looking, and participation as audience members. Details about featured performances will be announced in August.

Course Requirements:

Attendance at all required performances; regular attendance at both lecture and section meetings; timely completion of all writing assignments; regular participation in discussion sections; active involvement in peer writing workshops. To meet the LSA First-Year Writing Requirement, students will write a series of short response papers (2-3 pages) and develop two longer papers in multiple drafts: an argumentative essay and a final research project. No mid-term, no final exam.

Intended Audience:

Designed for first and second-year students, this course is open to undergraduates in all departments and programs in LSA, including the Honors Program and the Residential College, as well as other schools across campus, including Music, Theater and Dance, Art & Design, Engineering, etc. No performance experience required!

Class Format:

Lectures are designed to prepare for the featured performances, and will often include visits from guest speakers and performing artists. Discussion sections will allow students to respond to performances through writing and discussion, and work on their writing  in peer writing workshops.

Sections.title: Jews in the Modern World

Sections.title: SocMed in India & US
Sections.description: Festivals define the popular image of contemporary South Asia in the West as much as they shape everyday life of the region. This course is aimed at a comparative exploration of South Asia through its festivals, as conceived in Progressive era fictions, Indian Dalit poetry, women’s account of rituals, art cinema of the 1960s, as well as recent archival debates in the formation of South Asian popular culture. Curated by global tourism, diasporic mobility and majoritarian state formation, the stereotypical image of South Asia as a land of festivals reveals as much as it hides. As spaces of collective participation, shared joy and tradition bound identification, South Asian festivals are dynamic fields of emotions and attachments, aspirations and mobilities, and hierarchies and control. Building on the performance theorist Diana Taylor’s creative mobilization of the tension between the archive and the repertoire1, i.e. the relatively fixed and legitimate official record and the changeable, fragmentary, less visible everyday repertoire of memory, spectatorship and participation, this course foregrounds the literary, cinematic and creative accounts of festivals that fall off official records and dominant visuality of South Asia.

Sections.title: Mideast in Metro Detroit
Sections.description:
You flee your home when the Ottoman Empire begins to crumble, crossing the Atlantic Ocean on a great steamship when you get your chance. Against all odds, you eventually put down new roots in Detroit, Michigan. At first, your life is relatively constricted: you stick to a few neighborhoods, hanging out mostly in coffeehouses, speaking your mother tongue, and smoking until the small hours of the morning with your compatriots. Sometimes, you even sleep in these places, where you also get your mail. But as time passes, your community grows, and so does its infrastructure. Some are drawn by the allure of work at the Ford factory; others by the growing Armenian, Arab, Turkish, Greek, Sephardic, Assyrian, and other communities that have already been established here. Your community, also, must change as it expands. And here is a great irony: Although you are quite different from these other Middle Eastern communities, and sometimes have fraught and conflicted relationships with them, you still share much in common from your Ottoman past that cannot always be shed, either. So: where do you go from here?

This course takes an in-depth look at disparate peoples who left the Ottoman Empire for very different reasons, and eventually came to call Detroit their home, in roughly the first half of the twentieth century. Based on the Public Humanities project “The Middle East in Metro Detroit,” it brings multiple local histories together to tell different stories about the lives and afterlives of formerly Ottoman subjects in the Motor City. Over the semester, we will gain a solid understanding of the collapse of the Ottoman Empire and of early twentieth-century American history in Michigan. Students will also learn how to piece together different archival sources–from newspaper clippings to song recordings, from memoirs to letters and short films–to tell their own stories about this complex period in creative ways. Finally, the course will have a conversational dimension, with special invited guests, from the descendants of these communities, who still live and work in Detroit today.

Course Requirements:

Regular attendance and participation in class discussions, reading/watching class material, timely submission of assignments through Canvas.

Intended Audience:

Undergraduate students interested in any or all questions pertaining to the future, including, but not limited to: ecology; labor, racial, or gender politics; sociology; architecture, etc.

Class Format:

Close readings and viewing of class material will provide students with new vocabulary and ideas that they can apply in class discussions.

If you would like to register but have accessibility concerns, please reach out and we can discuss possibilities for accommodations.

Sections.title: Rights & Races
Sections.description:
The course explores the long history through which the concept of race is articulated, which means the history of European racism. And it must do this while at the same time studying the origin of the modern notion of rights, beginning with John Locke and the idea of natural rights (to life and liberty). These two stories dovetail, since the ideal of rights proposed as indelible, equal and universal is announced just as, thanks to colonialism and the rise of the modern European nation State, the world is divided into colonizer and native, citizen and subject. This story will emphasize various concepts of race as they play out in the Eighteenth and Nineteenth centuries.
Slavery and genocide are the two greatest degradations of colonial rule. Slavery is a way of dehumanizing a people while keeping them alive as a mere labor force. Slavery brings a people to the brink of disappearing as persons and is therefore close to genocide. Nationalist driven racism finds it final and ugly conclusion in genocide, first in South West Africa (1904-8) as a response to native resistance. Thereafter in the Armenian and Nazi atrocities. The enormity of these crimes in turn lead to the birth of new moral concepts--those of genocide and of crimes against humanity-adequate to their horror, and to a new world order of international law and humanitarianism. This at the end of the Second World War (1945). The course then turns to this new world order, in various of its aspects. These include the expansion of kind and character of human rights, including group rights and substantive rights such as the rights to health, work, housing, customary practice, linguistic sustainability and the like. Second, a fundamentally new form of justice which is confessional and forgiving rather than retributive. We explore restorative justice, relying on the example of the South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Third, the response to genocide. Here we turn to Canada and Australia and their attempts to breed out the Aboriginal from the indigenous person through the forced extraction of indigenous children and their reeducation as European menials. And fourth, the issue of global humanitarian organizations, most centrally the United Nations and the World Court, and the problem of humanitarian intervention. Here the example will be the Rwandan genocide of 1994.
We will rely a broad swath of writings, from philosophical debates to history, cultural criticism, journalism, and literature.

Course Requirements:

Course assignments will consist of short papers. There will be no exams.

Sections.title: Translating Lit Workshop
Sections.description:
How to work with AI and other technologies without sounding robotic? What makes the work of accomplished human translators Google Translate aims to emulate “the gold standard”? This course provides an opportunity for you to take your skills in reading a foreign language to the next level by learning to translate literary texts into English. In the process you will learn to think critically about the unique contributions human translators are able to make. The readings and writing assignments work together to introduce you to the history and theory of the practice of translation, extending a language-based approach to translation into a literary framework that emphasizes the process of reading and re-writing texts. While you are expected to write critical responses to these literary texts, periodically you will also be asked to engage with the readings through short creative exercises focusing on key issues in translation studies, and to experiment with using UM GPT.

All types of assignments demand a regular commitment to drafting, editing and revising. These critical and creative writing assignments are designed to build on one another, enabling students to become more attentive readers, to produce increasingly articulate responses to the translated texts, which in turn inform your own translation strategies. These will form the basis for the midterm paper reflecting on your views of translation, and will help you as you formulate your approach. For the final project, students will be expected to translate 8-12 pages of literature of their choosing from the language of their expertise, prefaced with an accompanying 5-8 page introduction that situates your practice in terms of the history of translation in English.

Sections.title: Comparative Marxism
Sections.description:
This course familiarizes students with the complex and multifaceted tradition of Marxist 
theory and practice while also tracing Marxism’s role in some of today’s most vibrant
political movements. Our comparative approach considers classical texts like The Communist
Manifesto and State and Revolution alongside lesser known but no less important works by Latin
American and Caribbean writers and intellectuals. Instead of working toward a single
definition of Marxism, we explore the history of heterodox experimentation with the
tradition’s most basic categories, always mindful of the continuities and discontinuities
between different “Marxisms.” This necessarily interdisciplinary course incorporates readings
and discussions that span philosophy, literature, history, and politics. Special focus is
directed at Marxist analyses that attend to (and also sometimes fail to attend to) the
interpenetration of class, race, and gender.

Sections.title: Canon Translation
Sections.description:
"I have always imagined that Paradise will be a kind of library" - Jorge Luis Borges

To gain firsthand experience in translation editing and literary publishing, join the Canon Translation Journal team and build our "kind of library" together!

As the director and senior editor of an award-winning independent French literary press publishing works in translation, I have been a key player in the thriving literary translation publishing scene for over a decade, publishing books from over 20 different languages from all over Asia, leading translation workshops and advising other translation publishers. This course will guide students through the practice of editing translated work, from initial draft to publication in the Canon Translation Journal. 

Canon is an online translation magazine housed in the University of Michigan's Comparative Literature department. It publishes original undergraduate student translations of any type from classic, modern and contemporary fiction: short-stories, poetry, creative non-fiction, essays and songs out of any language. It is Canon's goal to acknowledge the many cultures and languages represented both here at the University of Michigan and in the world at large through translation.

The course will give a practical understanding of translation and teach students about literary translation editing (writing with clarity and purpose, revision and editing, copyediting, proofreading) as well as publishing processes (acceptance and rejection, project management, design, rights acquisition, marketing and promotion). The class will provide opportunities for students to fill multiple roles over all aspects of publication. 

Students will have the opportunity to translate and publish their own translation in Canon while gaining valuable experience as a first-time published literary translator. All levels of language proficiency are welcome.

Students will also have the option to solicit other students' works, so reading proficiency in other languages, while welcome, is not required. 

Canon is a great opportunity to become more experienced in the growing field of translation and to gain hands-on experience for those interested in the literary world!

Course Requirements:

Grades are based on attendance and proactive participation in editorial meetings, timely completion of assignments, content contribution through commissioning other students’ works or submission of your own translation.

Assignments will reflect the multiple roles on an editorial production team, including submissions reports and reviews, writing and editing, marketing and promotion. 

  • Attendance: 25%
  • Editorial participation: 25%
  • Assignments: 30%
  • Translation and/or commissions project: 20%

Intended Audience:

This class is open to undergraduate students across all disciplines; reading proficiency in other languages, while welcome, is not required. 

Class Format:

During each class, we will explore one aspect of literary translation and literary publishing in a short seminar. The lecture will be followed by an editorial meeting where every student will take turns reporting on how the work is progressing. All editorial decisions will be discussed and made collectively. This studio-class will provide opportunities for students to fill multiple roles. 


Time will be devoted individually to each student for guidance and support through their projects and assignments in the third part of the class.
