Sections.title: Lit Studies For/Against Lit
Sections.description:
The course will introduce students to the relations between Comparative Literature
(Complit) and literature during the near century of the discipline. These relationships have been
celebratory, incisive, philosophical, but also iconoclastic and antagonistic. One can learn from all of
them.
The history begins with the origin of Complit in Germany and France in the late 19th and
early 20th centuries where the study of literature was part of a broad pan-European focus on the
idea and ideal of progressive European culture. Symbolized by a belief in the deepening of the novel
over time in range of expression and relation to truth about the world, this was the moment of
intense scholarship across European languages and literatures. It was transposed to America
thanks to World War II.
The next moment in the history of Comparative Literature was prompted by iconoclasm
generated through the emancipatory movements of the 1960s: anti-imperialism, anti-colonialism,
feminism, black liberation and the like. Scholars steeped in political critiques of European power
and authority relied on close reading of literary texts to generate critiques of both earlier literary
approaches and textual ideologies of power, usually implicit. A more general goal was to implode
the idea of the “the canon”: a set of exemplary texts which framed judgments of superior and
inferior in Eurocentric ways.
Next, we will turn to the way the 1980s and 1990s opened up a dialogue between the global
north and south as decolonization and globalization brought that vast and neglected part of the
world (the global south) into conversation with writings from Europe and America. This was the
moment when the concept of “World Literature” was born.
Also included will be the problem of language, both with respect to what Deleuze and
Guattari call “minor languages”. And the question of writing in one’s own tongue.
The final two classes will allow for student presentations, first those working on their
honor’s theses, then by others in the class. All will workshop their final assignments.

Course Requirements:

One paper of 2000 words or more due at the end of class.

Intended Audience:

Comp Lit Majors, Complit Honors Students and advanced undergraduates

Sections.title: What is Philology?
Sections.description:
Philology is the foundational discipline atop which modern literary studies have been built. It is an old science, with roots in textual criticism, literary criticism, linguistics, and history. We can also trace the influence of philology on the larger political manifestations of modernity, such as colonialism, imperialism, nationalism, and modern race and ethnicity. 

This course will offer students a survey of the development and history of philology, its impact on literary studies, and recent reassessments of philology from the lens of postcolonial studies, race and ethnicity, comparative literature, classical reception, and border studies.

Course Requirements:

This course will sample academic monographs from a range of fields and require significant reading. 

Intended Audience:

This course is intended to be helpful to graduate students of literature and is designed to equip you with a history of your discipline, a sense of the roots from which modern literary study has grown up. You will leave the course with a stronger sense of the shortcomings and potentials of philology, whose tools and methods remain crucial even today.

Class Format:

Seminar-style discussion and symposium-style snacks and food-sharing.

First Year Seminar in Digital Studies

Sections.title: Digital Memory
Sections.description:
This FYS introduces students to a wide variety of topics and issues in Digital Studies in a seminar format, building a foundation in the humanities and humanistic social sciences. This course uses the lens of digital pasts, archives, death, and memory to ground conversations. We will engage with how the unique properties of digital technologies affect our everyday lives and deaths, exploring objects ranging from computer storage to video games to memory-enhancing brain chips and AI clones that purport to let an individual live forever.

This course is designed to teach students how to read critically at the collegiate level, how to draw out canonical arguments in scholarly texts about digital technologies, and how to use them to build your own.

Course Requirements:

This course requires regular lecture attendance, participation in in-class discussions, some group
work, and timely completion of assignments. Students are expected to read regularly. Assessment
includes reading annotations, a series of discussion-based seminars, short (open note, untimed)
quizzes, and a final small group class-facilitation.

Intended Audience:

This class is accessible to all first-year undergraduate students and requires no technical background.
Students interested in the arts, humanities, and humanistic social sciences who are interested in the
study of digital archives, social justice, design, and computer history are especially encouraged to take
this course.

results.title: Writing with Digital and Social Media

Sections.title: Activism in Online Spaces
Sections.description:
The revolution may not be televised, but it may end up on TikTok. This three credit hour class will introduce students to the tools of online advocacy and provide opportunities to experiment with designing their own advocacy campaigns through content creation in a highly production-oriented environment.

This class invites students of all experience levels with digital media and content creation to make and experiment alongside each other as we encounter how writing mediates capacities for change and connection online. Students in this class will explore online communities and their impacts, develop research skills to help generate knowledge about online advocacy and interpret analytics of impacts of advocacy-related content, and develop advocacy and community-building projects of their own throughout the semester.

Together, we will understand how platforms structure the kinds of engagement and content we can more readily produce, engage questions of online safety and surveillance, and explore tactics for adapting to ever-shifting social landscapes online with rhetorical awareness.

Sections.title: Writing the Wild: A Workshop
Sections.description:
Calling all hikers, paddlers, rock-climbers, and surfers—not to mention foragers, botanists, trail riders and anglers. Writing the Wild is a multi-modal creative composition course designed to help students interrogate their passion for the outdoors among like-minded peers. 

Over the course of the semester, students will hone their respective crafts of writing, photography, and podcasting by analyzing published work, conversing with preeminent members of the outdoor media, and workshopping their own evolving projects. The paths students follow in their individual endeavors will by the end of the semester converge to help unpack our big, collective driving question: “Why do wild experiences matter?”

results.title: Writing with Digital and Social Media Mini Course

Sections.title: The Rhetoric of Online Cute
Sections.description:
Cats wearing knitted hats, shiny-eyed dogs looking for their furever homes, polymer clay mushrooms, toddlers acting like adults, fuzzy stop-motion creatures cooking tiny foods, baby animals that may or may not exist IRL, Barbies who swear, and long Furby…what does it all MEAN? What makes any of these online phenomena "just cute," and what makes them cursed? What makes cute content innocuous, and what makes it manipulative? And what kind of cute makes you feel a little gross for liking it? What IS that gross feeling all about, anyway? If you've ever wondered about any such question, and if you want to practice harnessing the rhetorical power of cuteness for your own purposes, take this class! 

In this class, we will read and write and make with a skeptical eye toward the familiar idea of cuteness as silly or benign. Cuteness is everywhere online, deployed with all sorts of complicated rhetorical aims. In other words: plenty of people are betting on the power of cute content to do more than just warm hearts. We'll spend time in and outside of class critiquing cute content, reading affective and rhetorical theories of cuteness, making our own cute content, and writing about it all. 

 

Course Requirements:

Expect weekly readings and informal, in-class writing assignments, one creative project with a written analysis due at the end of class, and a project proposal due at the midpoint of class. Regular attendance and participation during class sessions comprises a non-trivial portion of your grade. 

 

Intended Audience:

This class is open to any student with a genuine desire to investigate, experiment, and reflect on their own relationship with cuteness.

Sections.title: Rhetoric Online Advice Column
Sections.description: When people anonymously seek guidance from an advice columnist, or a forum like reddit’s r/AmITheAsshole, they are often seeking solace, sympathy, practical suggestions, and, whether they like it or not, moral judgment. A peek at the pleas for help on daily columns like Dear Prudence, Ask a Manager, and Carolyn Hax reveals resonant cultural crises of our times, just as newspaper columns like Dear Abby and Victorian conduct guides did in years past. In this mini-course, we will explore how advice columns reveal fascinating implications about the norms of etiquette, relationships, self-perception, and how we “should” go about something. In other words, we will explore ideological and rhetorical nuances of “online advice.” Assignments will move between analysis and more creative prompts. Analyses will dissect the rhetorical strategies and social norms in real advice columns. The creative prompts include imagining fictional characters’ dilemmas and crafting emotionally charged queries in the voice of a specific columnist, and writing satirical “anti-advice” that subverts conventional wisdom.

Sections.title: Activism in Online Spaces
Sections.description:
In this course, students analyze and apply rhetorical principles in their writing with digital media. A variety of topics and innovations in pedagogy are hallmarks of this course. Why pay attention to multimedia in a writing course? As members of a media-saturated culture, we know that print text is only one form of "writing" and communication, and sometimes it is not the most effective choice. Because all of us make sense of texts and issues in a variety of ways, this course will ask students to utilize multimodal (visual, aural, kinetic, etc.) forms of communication and become more informed and critical consumers of digital media writing themselves.

Course Requirements:

Regular attendance, class participation, online discussion, participation in drafting and peer review, and some form of self-reflective writing.

Intended Audience:

Undergraduates who want to learn to make multi-media more effective rhetorically. Digital Studies Minors.

Class Format:

Pedagogical approaches will vary according to the instructor or topic, but may include laboratory sessions, multimedia presentations, electronic and in-class workshops and demonstrations, full-class and small-group discussions, and gallery presentations.

Sections.title: Netflix Edit:Rhet Edge of Real
Sections.description:
This mini-course examines “the Netflix edit” not simply as a storytelling style, but as a contextual rhetorical practice that shows how digital platforms shape our sense of reality. Focusing on Netflix reality television (e.g., Love Is Blind, Perfect Match, and The Ultimatum: Queer Love), the course analyzes how editing constructs narrative through cuts, pacing, music, sequencing, and strategic pauses between batch releases.

Students will explore how these editorial choices do more than produce “heroes” and “villains”: they guide audience emotion, invite speculation, and shape online discourse as episodes circulate across social media. The course asks what it means to literally edit reality in the streaming era, examining how narrative control, platform design, and viewer participation work together to produce meaning.

In addition to analyzing editing and release strategies as persuasive rhetorical choices, students will study fan commentary and online engagement to understand how meaning emerges through collective interpretation. The course emphasizes writing and composing within these digital genres, attending to their specific conventions, rhetorical moves, and timeliness. 

Students will be expected to have an active Netflix account to watch selected episodes in preparation for class.

Sections.title: Wrtg Games Across Modalities
Sections.description:
Video games, board games, table top games, sports, and more all involve the mediation of playful activities through writing game design choices. In this course, students will engage with questions of how we compose play, but also how we can compose playfully. 

Students will design games or sports of their own making across a wide array of modalities, playtest and workshop their creations, and seek to be playful but intentional designers and writers.

This class is not a coding or animation class. As such, this class offers opportunities for both people who are looking to grow their digital development or game design experience and those who are looking to experiment with these modes of composing for the first time.

Sections.title: Science/Tech/Racial Capitalism
Sections.description:
Workers (and people generally) are not treated equally under capitalism. Capitalism feeds on racial hierarchies. Racial capitalism refers to this fact about how capitalism works. Capitalism exploits differences among peoples – along the lines of race, gender, sexuality, religion, reproductive or physical abilities – to suppress solidarity and create hierarchies of human worth. It produces highly unequal and racist societies.


In this seminar, we will critically examine the roles that science and technology play in sustaining racial capitalism. We will explore how scientific work enables the differentiation of people into groups for the purposes of profit and accumulation of land. Our perspective will be anti-capitalist, anti-imperialist, and anti-zionist.


We will draw examples from several scientific fields, including biology and psychology, but pay special attention to the roles that statistics and computation play in creating hierarchies of worth. We will examine how scientific theories and practices fit into the agendas of the state and institutions such as universities, prisons, and hospitals.


Throughout the course, we will also look for alternatives to the racial capitalist way of doing things and to dominant scientific practices.


Note: Students who have previously taken DIGITAL 158: Science, Technology, and Racial Capitalism are not permitted to enroll in this section of DIGITAL 258. Additionally, students who have taken this course under a Meet Together department (i.e. American Culture) are not permitted to take this course

Intended Audience:

*NOTE: Students who have previously taken DIGITAL 158: Science, Technology, and Racial Capitalism are not permitted to enroll in this section of DIGITAL 258. Additionally, students who have taken this course under a Meet Together department (i.e. American Culture) are not permitted to take this course. If a student is found to have double-registered for this course ,they will be administratively dropped.

Sections.title: Digital Media Culture
Sections.description:
Is it Gif as in “Jif” or “Gif” (with a soft G)? How Social is social media? What does it mean to “hate watch” a television show of movie? Together, across 7 weeks, we will explore these questions and more, as we encounter the history and culture of digital media. We will discuss various important technological innovations from the Kodak Eastman Camera to the development of VR chat bots, but this is not a course that charts the linear development of technology alone. Rather we are interested in the why as well as the when. That is, why do various communities use digital media in the way they do, and to what ends?

This course is grounded in a media studies cultural production approach, and so, together, we will learn about media, but also politics, power, and how media and technology shape our everyday life.

Course Requirements:

The course is a short 7 week mini-course. It requires participation in virtual class meetings and lectures, and timely completion of reading assignments/screenins which will be posted to Canvas. Students will write a series of blog posts to Canvas, and in lieu of a mid-term, report on a media object of their choice. There will be a final research or event proposal of 8-10 pages. No mid-term, no final exam.

Intended Audience:

The course is ideal for students interested in digital culture, media history, and production. As well, students interested in alternative media of various kinds. No prior knowledge of these topics is required!

Sections.title: Intro to Digital Art
Sections.description:
This studio course provides an intensive introduction to key software tools, techniques and fundamental concepts supporting digital media arts production. As students are introduced to the various fields in the digital arts, they will learn and apply the fundamentals of digital media arts production with software applications (Adobe Creative Suite and open source software), web-based coding techniques (html, css, javascript), as well as study the principals of design and digital production that translate across multiple forms of media production. In this way, students will learn to work with various digital media production software and design concepts that are employable across an array of digital-based media arts. We will first cover the basic foundations of software for digital image production and editing with photoshop. We will then move on to sound production and editing, and lastly we will work with basic animation with After Effects.

Throughout the course we will cover the basic foundations of techniques for digital design and digital web production, with basic web coding. Lastly, throughout the course, we will also work with and gain an understanding of foundational principles of digital media design that can be applied widely to many forms of digital media art. Viewing/interacting with contemporary digital media art works and web-based art projects will also allow us to critically analyze the relations between media producers, viewers, and media culture. We will explore a broad repertoire of media possibilities, and perform critical analysis of works that we view and our own works during in-class critique sessions.

Class Format:

In Person

Sections.title: Sustainable Board Game Design
Sections.description:
The last two decades have seen an absolute explosion in both interest in and production of hobbyist board games. In this course, we will explore how the design of modern board games differs from the classic family games with which many of us grew up (Monopoly, Risk, etc.), as well as the role that technical writing performs in facilitating this unique form of play. In small design groups, students will create their own unique board game prototype, perform playtesting data collection and analysis as part of an iterative design process, and learn about recent trends in making board game manufacturing a more sustainable practice.

Course Requirements:

This is a project-based course that requires students to produce work both independently and as part of a small design team of approximately 4 students. In the first unit, students will create an accessibility teardown (4-6 pages) of a modern board game to assess potential design flaws that make the game unintentionally inaccessible to players. In the second unit, students will be working in small design teams to produce a prototype for a new board game (physical components such as cards/board/3D-printed game pieces, printed rulebook, etc.: Varying length). All projects include a preliminary design plan and a reflective post-mortem.

No mid-term, no final exam.

Intended Audience:

This course is accessible to all undergraduate students at all levels, including both those minoring in Digital Studies as well as those who simply have an abiding interest in game design and digital marketing. We welcome all students, whether you spend entire weekends playing Twilight Imperium or haven’t touched a board game since that one time you played Uno with your family

Sections.title: Peer to Peer
Sections.description:
Peer-to-Peer Networks

In an increasingly platform-driven internet, who (and where) are our peers? From a strictly technical perspective, “peer-to-peer networks” use distributed nodes help to share the burden of information exchange. While this model served as an underlying force for the initial design
of the internet and its attendant technologies, now a small group of websites and platforms (often serving corporate interests) dominate the landscape. This shift, typified by appeals to convenience, equitable access, and building a worldwide “town hall” internet, has ended up privileging some networks, while leaving other (smaller, simpler, stranger) networks behind.

In this class, we examine what forms the peer-to-peer network has taken over time, and work to uncover its component parts in technical, computational, and networked infrastructures. We trace the history of the internet through its alternatives, work to imagine “other networks” that re-emphasize peer connection, foregrounding the peer as a community of equals, friends, neighbors, and citizens. We examine their facilitating systems ranging from Instagram followers to gossip systems to alt-newsletters to Snap maps.

Along the way, we’ll examine how such systems design co-construct communities, power, politics, social strata, and more.

**Please Note: This section does NOT meet the ULWR**

Course Requirements:

To foreground its community-driven subject, this course requires regular lecture attendance, participation in in-class discussions, some group work, and timely completion of assignments. Coursework includes reading annotations, a series of discussion-based seminars, short (open note, untimed) quizzes, and a final small group class-facilitation.

Intended Audience:

This class is accessible to all undergraduate students and requires no technical background. Students in the arts, humanities, and humanistic social sciences who are interested in the study of digital communities, community organizing, computer history, and internet history are especially encouraged to enroll.

Sections.title: Networked Disability Cultures
Sections.description:
What is disability culture online? Who gets to produce it? How does it get produced? What are its impacts across culture and technology? Across 7 weeks, this course presents a survey of disability culture online, exposing students to a variety of topics that animate disability culture online, including but not limited to healthcare infrastructure and hacktivism, sexual access activism and media art, disability tech dongles, and mutual aid.  Alongside these topics, we will explore a breadth of theoretical scholarship, and media.

Course Requirements:

The course is a short 7 week mini-course. It requires participation in virtual class meetings and lectures, and timely completion of reading assignments which will be posted to Canvas, Students will write a series of blog posts to Canvas, and in lieu of a mid-term, report on a digital disability community or media object of their choice. There will be a final research or event proposal of 8-10 pages. No mid-term, no final exam.

Intended Audience:

The course is ideal for students interested in digital activism, culture, disability, healthcare, and disability studies. No prior knowledge of these topics is required!

Sections.title: Criticl Making & Cultural Prod
Sections.description:
None of us are passive consumers of culture or technology. Indeed, each of us create online—we produce data for others, as well as unique forms of sociality. In tnis course through scholars like Nick Couldry, Renate Lorenz, and Sean Lee among others, we will ask the questions:

What is “Critical” Making? 

Who makes Culture?

What is the relationship between art, culture, and technology?

This course is interdisciplinary, and draws on Design Theory, Cultural Theory, and Science and Technology Studies to answer these questions. Students will also have numerous opportunities to make digital objects of their own, applying theory to practice across audio, video, and new media.

Course Requirements:

The course is a short 7 week mini-course. It requires  participation in virtual class meetings and lectures, and timely completion of reading assignments which will be posted to Canvas, Students will write a series of audio posts to Canvas, and in lieu of a mid-term, student will undertake a small, multimodal essay, hosted on a class Wiki, taking up topics from the first three weeks. There will be a final research proposal of 8-10 pages. No mid-term, no final exam.

Intended Audience:

Students interested in digital culture, activism, and a humanistic approach to the study of technology may be particularly interested, but all are welcome!

Sections.title: Virtual Reality
Sections.description:
This studio production course introduces students to the technical and conceptual foundations of Virtual Reality and immersive media production. We will examine VR within the framework of creative media arts and 3D animation, paying particular attention to the fundamentals of immersive world-building using the Unity3D engine. Throughout the course, we will explore the possibilities of the medium by doing short weekly VR exercises. Alongside our production work, we will critically examine an array of VR/immersive works by artists, filmmakers, and critical game designers in order to gain an overview of the historical landscape of the field. Students will develop competency in the technical, conceptual and artistic foundations for more advanced work in virtual reality and immersive media production.

Course Requirements:

Students will complete weekly production exercises, reading responses, a midterm project, and a final project.

Intended Audience:

This course is appropriate for students with a background or familiarity with the conventions of filmmaking, but who are interested in expanding their practice to include immersive storytelling, 3D animation, and VR. Previous knowledge of VR or 3D animation/graphics is not required. This course is appropriate for beginners.

Sections.title: Dig Aesthet: Pwr, Form, Politi
Sections.description:
This course will introduce students to the most recent discussions around creative expression and production of digital content. We will study “classical” aesthetic concepts, their further development in new media aesthetics, and their critique and revisions in feminist, anti-racist and decolonial scholarship. Our examples and case studies will focus on contemporary global digital cultural products. The course outcomes will involve a midterm research paper, a presentation and a choice between a project and the second paper.

Class Format:

In Person

Sections.title: History of the User
Sections.description:
There are many terms that describe how one engages with media: Spectator. Viewer. Consumer. Fan. Maker. Player. Gamer. Producer. Influencer. Creator. Author. Reader. Writer. There are fewer that describe how one engages with computers: Operator. Coder. Administrator. User.


Throughout the 20th century, media studies and popular culture scholars worked to understand positions like the film spectator, television viewer, fan, and consumer. This seminar seeks to think through how a new modality has emerged since the rise of personal computing in the 1980s: the user. We will explore the history of how people became users of computers, software, platforms, and more. In uncovering the history of the user we shall understand what users have in common with spectators, viewers, fans, and consumers while also exploring how digital modalities invite other forms of participation, collaboration, and acquiescence. Students in this course will gain an understanding of how the history of digital technologies and their industries have encouraged their consumption and use and how the history of computer users is also a history of unanticipated, unexpected and, occasionally, anti-consumerist approaches to tech. We will read and learn how to think about the user across multiple fields, including media studies, digital studies, and the history of technology.

Sections.title: Intersectional Perspectives
Sections.description: Intersectional feminist perspectives and the liberation ideologies they birthed, apply to all oppressed people groups and orientation identities. Intersectional feminist perspectives actively work to frame and reframe feminism as a larger context in which bodies (Black, Brown, First Nations, Latinx, Indigenous, Asian, and any body within these and other marginalized people groups) own agency and are deserving of political representation and freedom. This course requires previous engagement with intersectional feminist theory and critical race theory as we will collectively work to map and expand these foundational ideologies to existing and emerging issues in digital and algorithmic culture. Together we will question how digital technologies limit or enhance agency; how algorithmic culture influences our perceptions of each other; and how digital media influence popular culture narratives on race, gender, class, sexuality, and other identity categories.

Sections.title: Course-based Authentic Researc
Sections.description:
This is a class-based undergraduate research experience, or CURE course. In this course, students will conduct primary research on never-before-studied fossils, with each student responsible for their own fossil samples and data collection on those specimens. Towards the end of the semester, we will combine the class’s data to answer larger-scale questions.
In Fall 2025, we will be studying marine mollusk fossils (fossil seashells) from the US East Coast, dating to the past ~3 million years to reconstruct how ocean temperatures have changed over that time period. In addition to learning techniques of paleontology, isotope geochemistry, and paleoclimate, students will learn transferable skills such as making plots of data, basic statistics, testing hypotheses, and reading literature that can be employed in any future research endeavor. This course can be a gateway into research in the Earth department or elsewhere.

Course Requirements:

Attendance is required. This class is in-person, with a high emphasis on attendance and participation. Grade will be based on participation/attendance, weekly lab assignments, and a final written report/presentation.

Intended Audience:

EARTH majors and minors, or anyone curious about research in the natural sciences

Class Format:

Two 50-min lectures and one 2-hour lab per week. Lectures will cover basic research skills, fundamentals of the techniques we will use, and how these techniques are used in research across the Earth department. The lab time will be spent doing hands-on activities, collecting and interpreting new data.

Sections.title: Economics of Personal Finance
Sections.description:
“Personal Finance” refers to the financial management of an individual’s or household’s income and wealth, usually in the context of multiple goals. We’ll consider issues around the topics of money management, usually with banking services, education, investment, risk management, retirement, taxes, and estate planning.

Class Format:

This is a one-credit C/NC participation-driven workshop.

Sections.title: Economics at Work
Sections.description:
"Economics at Work" is an alumni speaker series. All students are welcome and able to register. Invited speakers will tell their story; including their career path, an explanation of what they actually do, and insight into how their economics major has defined and plays a role in their career path. In this way, students will get a perspective on the inspirational career paths of alumni (their personal “stories”) and substantive real-life examples of the role economics has played in alumni careers.

Course Requirements:

Evaluation of students is based on the submission of regular writing assignments, and in-person attendance. Successfully completing the writing assignments depends on your active participation in the course at the designated time. [Students who will regularly be unable to attend the Friday session should not enroll in this course. This includes students with University sanctioned absences.]

Intended Audience:

Economics at Work is intended for students who are interested in learning about a variety of career opportunities for economics majors. Freshmen and sophomores may use this class to explore whether an economics major best suits their interests and goals. Juniors and seniors who are economics majors will benefit from the information and networking opportunities.

Class Format:

This course is a speaker series. Each session will feature an alumna or alumnus from the Department of Economics. Each session begins at 1pm, contains a presentation, and question and answer segment. This portion will end at roughly 2pm. From 2pm to 2:30pm student will have an opportunity to speak directly with the featured speaker. (Please note that speakers have the option of being in-person or online via Zoom. Students should be prepared for the possibility that a session's mode of presentation may change on short notice.)

Sections.title: Economics of Crises
Sections.description:
The course covers basic theories of crises. Specifically, the course attempts to build students’ understanding of the origins of crises and basic propagation mechanisms. The course covers theories that address crises that stem from the real side of the economy as well as theories that address crises that originate in the financial sector. Primarily, the course focuses on theories that account for the occurrence of crises from within the system and on theories that explain propagation and amplification mechanisms of otherwise weak external shocks. The course is mostly theory-oriented supported with a real-life narrative.

Course Requirements:

In Person Exams

Class Format:

In Person Lecture. Lectures taped and made available for later viewing.

Sections.title: Monetary and Fiscal Policy
Sections.description:
The course focuses on the analysis of monetary and fiscal policy, often referred to collectively as “stabilization policy.” Topics include the history of various monetary regimes, monetary policy rules, the evolution of neutral interest rates, unconventional monetary policy, risks associated with excessive government debt accumulation, and exchange rate management. The emphasis will be on applying the theories studied in Econ 402 rather than introducing new ones. 

Intended Audience:

It is recommended, although not required, that students take Econometrics (Econ 251 or Econ 452) before this course.

Sections.title: Analysis of Modern Labor Mkts
Sections.description:
Traditional Labor Economics studies the role of human work in the process of production. Human work is allocated to firms and occupations in a labor market, in which individuals supply work and firms demand work.

In Topics in Labor Economics we advance our knowledge of labor markets by studying a number of phenomena that make a worker. Specifically, we study four major events in the lifecycle of workers: Education (the decision of initial human capital which is valuable both in the marriage and the labor markets), Marriage Market (where individuals decide on their marital status and meet their spouse), The Family (where individuals make their labor supply and fertility decisions jointly with their spouse), and Labor Market (where individuals get income for their households and develop their careers). We will build up towards a unified framework to study how all those events interact to explain gender inequality in labor market outcomes. To this end, we combine models from economic theory with rigorous empirical methods.

The class graded assignments will assess students mastery of economic models as well as data and regression analysis skills.

Sections.title: Topics Long-Term Econ Develop
Sections.description: This is a one-semester course on conducting research in long-term economic development. Modern economic growth---the sustained rise in living standards seen in many countries in the 20th and some in the 19th Century---is a phenomenon that defines our era. We study this phenomenon by comparing economies at different levels of development today and by comparing the historical growth of economies. Over the semester, students will identify specific questions, formulate hypotheses, find suitable data, and implement empirical tests. The class will be a collaborative environment in which students develop their writing projects and support their peers doing the same. The end result will be an original and high-quality paper that can serve as the basis for an honors thesis.

Sections.title: Econ of Developing Countries
Sections.description: This course surveys what we do and don't know about economic growth and poverty alleviation in developing countries. We will cover the following topics in detail; the definition of development; the theory of economic growth; human capital (education and health); technology and innovation; economic policy; economic shocks; institutions; geography; and social conflict, violence, and war. In addition, we will discuss program evaluation (with a focus on educational interventions) and sustainable development (with a focus on microfinance). The course also includes two in-class debates related to the paper assignments.

Sections.title: C++ Section
Sections.description:
Fundamental concepts and skills of programming in a high-level language. Flow of control: selection, iteration, subroutines. Data structures: strings, arrays, lists. Algorithms using selection and iteration (decision making, finding maxima/minima, searching, sorting, simulation, etc.). Good program design, structure and style are emphasized. Testing and debugging.

This course (website: eecs183.org) is an introductory course to computer science and programming. Students will learn the basics of computing, as well as problem-solving and algorithmic thinking. Languages include C++ and Python.

Learning takes repetition, and approaching the topic from different angles. EECS 183 provides the repetition and the different approaches through multiple tools integrated into the course. We use: zyBooks is an online animated interactive textbook. ZyBooks have minimal text, and instead consist of question sets, animations, interactive tools, and auto-graded homework, so students can learn by doing. CodeLab is an online program for learning and practicing computer programming. It provides you with hundreds of very short exercises with immediate feedback. Problem Roulette is an online tool where you can practice multiple choice exam questions from several years of past exams.

Students will complete projects and create programs that are practical to life outside of class. At the semester’s end, students will work on a real-world final project. You will be working as part of a team. Course Requirements: No data submitted


Intended Audience:

Suitable for both prospective computer science majors in LSA and non-majors. No prior programming experience required.

Class Format:

Lectures are conducted in-person. Lecture attendance is required IN YOUR ENROLLED LECTURE SECTION. Labs are in-person and attendance is required IN YOUR ENROLLED LAB SECTION. There is a significant workload with this course. Students say they spend at least 10 hours every week outside of lecture on this course.

Course Home Page:
Go to eecs183.org to find the current syllabus, schedule, and assignments for the course.

Sections.title: Rhetoric and Rights
Sections.description:
Many people spoke for – and against – women's right to vote in the United States. These speeches are terrific opportunities to understand how activists argue for an absolutely fundamental civil right. They also show us how even progressive activists sometimes rely on conservative ideas in their paths to social change. Let’s look together at the slippery boundaries between binaries such as inclusion and exclusion, progressive and conservative, and also seemingly self-evident identities like “woman,” “white,” “healthy,” and “middle-class.” Sure, these speeches led to the 19th Amendment. What else did these speeches do, and undo? We’ll connect to contemporary U.S. politics, and lots more in our every-day-worlds.

Course Requirements:

This course is a gameful course, which means students can select from a menu of assignments, try different activities, and collect points as they move through the semester. Some options include writing traditional essays and journal entries, designing and completing multimedia projects, presenting posters, attending and reflecting on relevant campus events, leading and/or recording discussions, and introducing additional materials into our course.

Intended Audience:

No background knowledge is required for this introductory course. Any first-year student is welcome.

Sections.title: Totalitarianism and Literature
Sections.description:
In authoritarian states, leaders tell you what you can and cannot do. In totalitarian regimes, they tell you what you can and cannot think. Some of the world’s greatest twentieth-century novels were keen analyses of totalitarianism as it had been developed by both the Right and the Left, and three of these fictional masterpieces are at the center of our seminar: Aldous Huxley’s Brave New World (1932), Arthur Koestler’s Darkness at Noon (1941), and George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949). These novels will be read in dialogue with two important nonfiction books from the same period including C.S. Lewis’s The Abolition of Man (1944) and Eric Hoffer’s The True Believer (1951). All five works share concerns over matters such as free speech, propaganda, surveillance, bureaucracy, social engineering, and the rise of “experts” and “masses.” But these books are even more interested in the precarious condition of the individual human being who was made in the image of God but remains subject to powers exercised by other people. Is freedom possible? Do rights exist? Does truth matter? Can one’s life have meaning? Finally, why does totalitarianism seem to keep coming back?

Work will include papers, exams, contributing to class discussions, and oral presentations.

Sections.title: You?re Majoring in WHAT?!?
Sections.description:
Why English?  Given the pressing problems we face today, your family members and friends—and perhaps you, too—may wonder about the value of taking courses in the field of English.  In this First-Year Seminar, we’ll address this question head-on through our readings, discussions, activities, and interactions with class visitors.  Questions such as the following will guide our conversations:

  • How might the humanities help us to address the many political, social, and environmental challenges we currently face?
  • If the world is on fire, why should we care about beautiful language, our imaginations, or creative forms of expression such as poetry, fiction, and creative nonfiction?
  • What can humans working within the field of English do that even the most sophisticated forms of Generative AI cannot do?
  • How does English overlap with fields such as law, medicine, history, computer science, art and visual culture, biology, psychology, anthropology, sociology, philosophy, and environmental studies?

Throughout the semester, we’ll explore the kinds of thinking, reading, and writing that take center stage in the study of English, and we’ll discuss what the field can teach us about race, gender and sexuality, class, disability, nationality, and religion.  We’ll also consider how studying English can help us to understand global histories, current events, shifts in language use, and trends in popular culture.

By participating in weekly reading and writing activities, assembling a course portfolio, and creating a public-facing project, you’ll develop a deep, hands-on understanding of the many reasons one might choose to take courses—and perhaps even declare a major or minor—in the field of English.  I hope to see you there!

Sections.title: Reading Shakespeare
Sections.description:
This course introduces students to key literary and critical terms, as well as some methods by which texts can be analyzed and interpreted, all through the works of William Shakespeare. The goal of this course, then, is not simply to introduce students to Shakespeare but to equip them with analytical tools they can then employ in any number of different humanities courses. Beginning with Shakespeare's Sonnets, students will learn how to identify and interpret what constitutes a metaphor, a simile, synecdoche, metonymy, irony, and so on. We will also cover how to scan lines and connect the rhythm of a poem to its thematic content. Following our study of the Sonnets, we will read several of Shakespeare's plays from different points in his career, including an early play (Romeo and Juliet), a midcareer play (Othello), and a late play (The Tempest). In studying these works, we will think through how Shakespeare paces his narratives, develops his characters, and draws upon poetic strategies to make the language of his dramas engaging, poignant, and also funny. We will watch clips from recent filmic adaptations of these plays to appreciate how Shakespearean language is performed. Students should emerge from this course confident in their ability to decipher and interpret challenging texts.

Course Requirements:

Assignments will include two short papers (3-5 pages) and one longer essay (4-6 pages). There will be no midterm or final exam. PDFs of all assigned readings will be made available on our Canvas site. Group exercises will be employed so that students can help one another learn to master difficult skills such as how to scan poetry.

results.title: Introduction to English Language and Literature Studies

Sections.title: Reading for Life
Sections.description: This course introduces students to the study of English language and literature through lecture and discussion. Courses explore a broad range of topics across historical periods, genres, and themes.

Sections.title: The Hustle
Sections.description:
In this course, we will consider the role of “the hustle” in American literature and culture, paying special attention to ethnicity, race, and the art of fiction. 


Quite often, we think of “hustling” as an admirable trait: it’s about drive, diligence, and dynamism—being a go-getter, working hard, or playing with alertness and energy. But just as frequently, “hustling” carries negative connotations—of luring unsuspecting victims, of defrauding and deceiving others for money or similar rewards. How, then, does the praiseworthy “hustle” of initiative and enterprise intersect with concepts of “upward mobility” and “the model minority”? How, too, do the illegal or unsavory acts of swindling and con artistry intersect with systemic racism, inequality of opportunity, and the mechanisms of American capitalism? And why do we use the same term to describe both gumption and duplicity?

As we think through “fictions of con artistry and upward mobility,” we will work to understand how novels, short stories, films, and TV shows (especially those by and about African Americans, Asian Americans, Latinx Americans, and Native Americans) have dramatized and questioned illicit schemes and social advancement. Yet we also will investigate how the concepts of “con artistry” and “upward mobility” are themselves fictions—social and semantic constructions whose meanings and implications shift over time.

Among other topics, we will address: racial and ethnic “passing” and “identity theft”; the distinctive functions of the trickster and the conjurer in Black, Indigenous, and Asian diasporic literary histories; the genre of the heist narrative; the politics of reconnaissance and espionage; shadow economies and the black market; the stereotyping of certain groups as “frauds” and “cheats”; and cultural differences in conceptions of ethics and criminality.

Course assignments will include regular reading responses, two short essays, and a final research project.

Novels we will read include Oscar “Zeta” Acosta’s Autobiography of a Brown Buffalo, Sherman Alexie’s Indian Killer, Nella Larsen’s Passing, Chang-rae Lee’s Native Speaker, Han Ong’s Fixer Chao, and Mark Twain’s Pudd’nhead Wilson. We also will watch a few films (The Godfather, Goodfellas, and Out of Sight), as well as episodes of The Sopranos and Breaking Bad.

Sections.title: Women Write the World
Sections.description: Sometimes sweet, sometimes spooky, often fierce, and always artful, the women writers of this course work to imaginatively right and repair wrongs in the world – be it interpersonal or geopolitical wrong, private pain or cultural devastation. We will read a variety of novels, short fiction, and memoirs by women writers from (and writing about) Bangladesh, Britain, India, Japan, Nigeria, and Zimbabwe, and that range in content from family, friendship, school, love and romance to colonialism, war, and political oppression. We will study fiction genres and styles such as bildungsroman, romance, speculative fiction, magical realism, and modern “literary” realism, and take time to learn and practice basic terms and techniques of both literary study and feminist literary criticism. While a few of our writers are diasporic (living abroad, emigrated) and writing for an international audience, others are based in their home country and thinking about local audiences, and so we will also think about the stakes of reading English-language novels from around the world.

Sections.title: Intro to Disability Studies
Sections.description:
This lecture course introduces methods and topics in the interdisciplinary field of Disability Studies, a broad area of inquiry that foregrounds transportable concepts and practices that matter across university departments. Students will engage with written texts that range from memoir to literary fiction to history to academic argument, as well as with visual texts including film and video, visual art, and social media. While the course will explore the history of disability, disability rights, and disability justice in the U.S., we continuously foreground disability studies as an historically-contingent method of analysis that helps us understand the ways nonnormative bodies and minds have been constituted by different groups and for different purposes.

We can also learn to recognize disabled people’s power to reshape those practices and purposes both in the past and in possible “crip” futures. Through our work together, we can begin to develop an understanding of how our fields constitute disability and how disability studies can inflect those fields.

Sections.title: Writing a Self
Sections.description:
In this literature and creative writing course, we’ll read a wide range of literatures (mostly essays, though also poems, memoir excerpts, and hybrid texts) that make their own attempts at autobiography — that is, telling the story of what it means to be a person in the world. 

As we read, we’ll keep an eye on how writing a story of oneself also necessarily involves writing the story of a moment, a country, a history, and a society; how writing autobiographically is bolstered by being present to and for our surrounds. In both our reading and our writing, we will stay curious about this term — “autobiography” — as it manifests in 21st century literature. 

This class is ideal for creative writers who are eager to write their way into their own true-to-life experiences while reading, analyzing, and inhabiting the craft of published autobiographical literary essays. We will take on, in equal parts, both literature study and experiments in personal writing, with written assignments falling on both sides of this line, and occasionally blurring it. Expect to write analytically, descriptively, personally, and curiously.

Sections.title: Science in Science Fiction
Sections.description:
How do science and science fiction help to shape our ideas about who we are, the function of our bodies, our relation to the nonhuman, our place to the universe, and our engagements with the environment? To what extent are works of science fiction anchored in real science, and what are the implications of their divergences from the scientifically possible? How are the imaginative leaps that scientists make in their investigations echoed in—and often extended by--the imaginative leaps of science fiction? This course will give students the opportunity to explore these questions in an interdisciplinary context.


Since its emergence, science fiction has encouraged us to imagine possible futures toward which technological innovation might lead. The genre, initially given shape by Romantic critiques of Enlightenment thinking, has helped us to explore the imaginative possibilities enabled by science and the ethical implications of new technologies. This course shares the attitudes of exploration and critique embodied by its double subject matter.


Readings include Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, Andy Weir's The Martian, as well as short stories by Ted Chiang, Isaac Asimov, NK Jemisin, Ursula Le Guin, Liu Cixin, Vandana Singh, WEB Du Bois, Arthur C. Clarke, Ray Bradbury, and Nnedi Okorafor. 

Course Requirements:

Requirements: Canvas discussions, in-class collaborative work, short reflection essays and science assignments, and a take-home final.

Sections.title: Popular Horror
Sections.description:
This course is the sister to my upper-level course ENG318 Classic Horror. In that course, we study (as you’d expect) the horror classics—Dracula, Frankenstein, Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, among others more dated and recent, all texts that count as “literature,” and as evidence that “literature” can make for great horror. But many horror stories—ones that are pretty great, too—don’t fit traditional ideas about what counts as literature, and that’s why I also have this course. ENG266 Popular Horror focuses on horror that some people might call mass-market, unsophisticated, or lowbrow. The stories we study exist in many forms; there will be a few traditional literary genres like novels and short stories, but also films, comics, podcasts, and creepypasta. All the texts in this course are fantastic horror stories, and more than that, can tell us a lot about what our culture fears and values.

This class will show that these popular stories do warrant serious thought and can stand up to scholarly scrutiny. You don’t need to be an English major to do well in this course, but it will ask you to develop your skills of narrative analysis. These skills are honed not by memorizing dates or learning terms but through reading carefully (or viewing or listening carefully, for non-written stories), discussion, and writing—and these three are, in simplest terms, the components of this course.

Sections.title: Wonderlands
Sections.description:
This course will explore and examine works of contemporary literary fiction (mostly novels) that intersect with the unreal, the uncanny, and the strange. In particular, we’ll explore the way these works create their own logic (and wonder!) through these elements, and how they contribute to our overall experience and understanding of the work. Not for purposes normally associated with the genres like horror and suspense, say, which employ them for page-turning reasons. Instead, we’ll ask: what is it about the strange, uncanny, or unreal that says something about the real? And how do these elements dramatize something about the human experience that’s difficult (or different) to articulate?

These are timely questions, I believe, both because of the way the pandemic has reshaped our relationship with the strange and surreal and because of the way technology (both in wondrous and terrifying ways) has asked us to begin questioning reality, personhood, and lived experience, as well as what it means to be alive today—quite literally, in some of these novels. And as a literature-focused course, we’ll not only discuss these larger issues, but also examine the ways these stories are being told, how these narrative strategies contribute to the overall project of the book, and the way hybridization across genres is reshaping the larger cultural conversation around contemporary literature itself.

After all, until recently, what was known as “literary” fiction was often positioned in opposition to (or distinct from) what might be categorized as “genre” fiction. Yet those lines have begun to blur. In 2007, Cormac McCarthy’s post-apocalyptic novel The Road won the Pulitzer Prize, and in 2014, Emily St. John Mandel’s dystopian pandemic novel, Station Eleven, was a finalist for the National Book Award. So where is the genre debate today? And how might styles of storytelling that were once marginalized speak to larger concerns of contemporary society? In fact, how might they even be ideally suited to speak to the experience of our times? And do so in a global way, since these novels and stories range from writers around the world.

Short readings will include essays and stories from such writers as ‘Pemi Aguda, Charles Baxter, Laura van den Berg, Kelly Link, Karen Russell, Charles Yu, and others. Primary texts will include such novels as:

 • The Memory Police, by Yoko Agawa

• The Book-Censor’s Library, by Bothayna Al-Essa 

• Orbital, by Samantha Harvey

• The Employees, by Olga Ravn

• Annihilation, by Jeff VanderMeer

Please note: Completing the first-year writing requirement is a prerequisite for this course. Also, though we will be doing a fair amount of writing, this class does NOT fulfill the Upper-Level Writing Requirement (ULWR).

 

Course Requirements:

Students will be expected to participate regularly in discussion, as well as to complete several short writing assignments and a longer essay. There will also be a journaling component, which will include note-taking, reflection, and annotation. Finally, it should be noted that our primary readings will be novels. As such, this is a reading-heavy course.

Sections.title: How to be a Hippie
Sections.description:
“The Sixties” is more than a decade—it is the afterimage of a dream. For those who believed in that dream, not just the global political order but human nature itself was evolving into a new age of peace, love, and freedom for all, and at revolutionary speed. The discovery that human nature can be re-engineered into something more adventurous, creative, peaceful, and powerful than ever before permanently transformed the imaginations of countless Americans, especially young Americans. The so-called “hippies” became a major figure of this new counterculture, exciting to some and frightening to others, flowering especially at certain locations (Haight-Ashbury in San Francisco, Greenwich Village in New York City) and at touchstone events (the Human Be-In, the Woodstock Festival), celebrating both the telltale pleasures of new youth culture (“sex, drugs, and rock n roll”) while circulating new ideas from widely read philosophers, essayists, political thinkers, and poets.

This course invites students to evaluate this remarkable movement of self-reinvention by confronting its major intellectual and artistic achievements. Rather than a history of the counterculture, we will take a trip into the phenomenon’s philosophical underpinnings, its values and its visions for the future, while situating its major practices within the worldviews that justified them. The seminar is interdisciplinary in the range of genres we’ll encounter, from avant-garde theatre to popular film to rock music to novels to poetry to ‘new journalism’ to philosophical and psychoanalytical treatises. Topics will include the sexual revolution, psychedelics and psychiatry, rock and roll, Eastern spirituality, communalism, anarchism, Marxism, Black nationalism, and more.

Engaged and open-hearted discussion is required. Assignments will include discussion questions posted to Canvas before each class, two interpretive essays of course texts, and a longer final project that may be creative.

Sections.title: RacialPassingin20thC AmLit
Sections.description:
This course focuses on the literature of racial passing and the complex motivations that led some African Americans to cross the color line in the early 20th century. These performances challenge our essentialist notions of racial identity and highlight some of the extraordinary ways in which African Americans negotiated the social, economic, legal, and cultural boundaries of American life at the turn of the century.

Readings include novels and short stories by Charles Chesnutt, Jessie Fauset, Sinclair Lewis, Fannie Hurst, and Nella Larsen. Coursework includes informal writing and two short essays.

Sections.title: Virtual Realities, Real Worlds
Sections.description:
What happens when we put on a virtual reality headset and enter an imagined or recreated world? Embodied digital technologies are reshaping entertainment, the way we produce knowledge, and ideas about technology itself—but they also reshape lived experience and identity in the actual social world. Whether you’re an avid gamer or completely new to embodied media or headsets, this mini-course is designed for shared exploration of VR experiences and their promise of unprecedented immersion in unfamiliar worlds, far-away spaces, and the lives of others and strangers. Ranging across gaming, art and installation projects, documentary and socially conscious work, we’ll explore the power of VR, centering its claims to promote understanding and empathy. We’ll focus on projects that aim to put us “inside” real-time or historical experiences of social inequality, displacement, climate distress, and rapid or unprecedented change.

As we trial different modes of VR world-building, we’ll draw for critical context on readings in the history of digital technologies, attention to narrative strategies borrowed from literature, film, and other media, and conversations with VR makers and developers about their work. Our materials will include such VR titles as Randall Okita’s The Book of Distance (2020), Roger Ross Williams’ Traveling While Black (2019), MIT docu/base’s This Is Climate Change (2018), and John Hull’s Notes on Blindness (2019). Subject to availability, we will also trial popular gaming experiences (e.g., Half-Life: Alyx, The Last of Us).

Together we’ll ask how—and whether—VR helps us know or connect imaginatively with lives beyond our own. Our work will be split between a conventional classroom approach and VR lab activity, so we can develop collaborative strategies for exploring VR and multi-media texts, accounting for the experience, and responding critically to it. Please note: no previous experience with VR, gaming, or digital platforms is necessary—just interest, curiosity, and willingness to experiment. Student interests in VR production, visual culture, design, critical media studies, racial and social equity, genre fiction, cognitive studies, gender and sexuality studies, psychology, marketing, and any other angle of approach are welcome. Class requirements: strong engagement and contribution to both discussion and lab; weekly short responses; and a final project of each student’s choice. These projects may incorporate elements of VR production, from narrative development or storyboarding to digital drafting, for those so inclined.

Sections.title: Exploring Virtual Reality
Sections.description:
What does it take, before and beyond coding or software skills, to design a virtual world and make it fully present? to create an immersive experience that feels powerfully real? This one-credit mini-course is designed for students of all majors and interests to explore world-making and storytelling in immersive digital (virtual reality) environments. No technical skills or experience with VR are required--we'll focus on the conceptual work of understanding what makes immersive VR experiences compelling, narratively rich, and satisfying. To do that, we'll attend to questions of genre (e.g., action-adventure, quest, documentary), perspective and point-of-view, and graphic style, to consider how choices about the look, feel, and story elements of a VR experience shape its impact and users' experience. Together, in a VR lab/classroom, we'll trial a range of environments across games, educational titles, simulations, and digital art, to explore the potential of VR to transport us beyond our everyday world--and perhaps even help us understand it differently. The course will emphasize our work together in class, both in VR headsets (provided) and in discussion.

Requirements are simple: regular attendance and robust engagement; and the project of conceptualizing a VR experience on paper, in storyboarding, or perhaps (for those inclined) via 360 video or game engine. Student interests in narrative, gaming, VR production, visual culture, design, media studies, genre fiction, cognitive studies, psychology, equity and justice work, marketing, and any other angle of approach are welcome! We will center safe and supportive use of VR equipment, along with shared attention to what makes VR environments look, feel, and land the way they do.

Sections.title: Wright, Hurston, Faulkner
Sections.description:
There’s a tradition in the United States of assuming that the two words “southern” and “modern” do not belong together. According to this tradition, migrants became modern once they left the “feudal” or “backward” South and went north to encounter urban, industrial, fast-paced and future-facing modernity. But was this version of the nation’s cultural geography accurate? What about major US authors who hailed from the South and who made critical innovations in American fiction during the modernist period? In this mini-course we will read one book each by early to mid-20th-century southern writers Zora Neale Hurston, Richard Wright, and William Faulkner to understand how they perceived their region, its growth out of slavery and monoculture crops, and its place within the rest of the nation. We will also set their writing within the context of the northern imagining of “Dixie” in these decades. How did these authors use story-telling techniques that were both part of a southern vernacular but also on the cutting edge of modern representation? How did these artists mix distinctly southern cultural forms, like the spiritual, with recent continental intellectual practices like psychoanalysis, anthropology, and surrealism? 

Course Requirements:

You will do a short writing assignment for each novel or short story collection.

Sections.title: American Civil Rights Rhetoric
Sections.description: This course takes a rhetorical approach to examining American civil rights rhetoric across the 19th and 20th centuries. We will examine the arguments, appeals, and strategies that form a foundational American rhetorical tradition that privileges freedom, equality, and human dignity. Although civil rights rhetoric was embedded in the national consciousness through 1960s struggles for racial justice, its legacy was already firmly established from America's earliest days and most heated debates. In this course we will begin by examining the rhetorical strategies of some of the earliest forms of American activism and consider how this rhetorical legacy is apparent in the American Civil Rights Movement and new generations of activism. The course concludes with an in-depth study of a student-selected social movement.

Sections.title: Queer of Color Lit and Culture
Sections.description:
What meanings do the terms “queer” and “of color” carry? How do different literary and artistic genres represent the experiences of (racial, sexual, gender, or other social) minorities? What relationships can we trace between textual legibility (how a work of art can, or asks to, be interpreted) and cultural legibility (how an individual or community can, or asks to, be identified)? In this course, we will explore these questions as we read, watch, and evaluate artistic works that transport us across the globe—from Parisian bars to the Rio Grande Valley to Philippine jungles to Oklahoman indigenous communities.

In our travels across space, time, and genre, we will consider the benefits—as well as the limitations—of understanding the term “queer” not simply as a reference to LGBT identities but, more expansively, as a signifier of opposition to any number of sociopolitical norms. Similarly, we will contemplate what can be gained (or lost) by taking comparative and intersectional approaches to the study of race, gender, sexuality, class, ability, and nation. How useful is it, for instance, to understand subjects as “of color” rather than “black” or “Asian”? What do we learn when we shift our focus from, say, “Latinos” or “the gay community” to “trans Afro-Latinas in the U.S.”?

Writing assignments will include regular reading responses, two short essays, and a final research project (that you will draft, review with your classmates, and then revise) related to the major themes of the course.

Required Books:
James Baldwin, Giovanni's Room (1956)
Gloria Anzaldúa, Borderlands/La Frontera: The New Mestiza (1987)
Jessica Hagedorn, Dogeaters (1990)
Craig S. Womack, Drowning in Fire (2001)
Ocean Vuong, On Earth We're Briefly Gorgeous (2019)

Sections.title: Theatre of US Women's Lib
Sections.description:
Modern women’s liberation in the United States emerged from the fire of New Left and Black Power in the 1960s-70s, and the theatre provided one of the movement’s most vigorous weapons. This seminar will explore theatre and performance works created alongside or in response to radical and cultural (sometimes collectively called “second-wave”) feminism in the US. Whether through “street theatre” protests, performance art, devised theatre, or more recognizable dramatic forms, feminists regularly turned the theatre into a weapon for smashing patriarchy and building sisterhood. Examining their theatrical accomplishments, we will ask such questions as: How did the theatre change to accommodate the insights of women’s liberation? What effect did phrases like “the personal is political,” “identity politics,” “consciousness raising,” and “patriarchy” have on the way theatre was made? What makes a feminist play—and how does the answer change depending on what feminist principles one is upholding? How did radical feminists represent class, race, sexuality, and solidarity on their stages? How do playwrights from later decades remember the early flourishing of women’s liberation, and how differently does it look in memory rather than in practice?


Our readings will be representative feminist theatre works alongside feminist political manifestoes and social and literary analyses, as well as samples of the feminist theatre criticism that emerged in their wake. Playwrights may include Martha Boesing, Alice Childress, María Irene Fornés, Ntozake Shange, Split Britches, Karen Finley, Robbie McAuley, Wendy Wasserstein, and Eve Ensler. 

Course Requirements:

No prior experience with feminist texts or with theatre and performance is necessary. Engaged and open-hearted discussion is required. Assignments will include discussion questions posted before class, interpretive essays of course texts, and a longer final project that may be creative.

Sections.title: Neuroqueer
Sections.description:
This lecture course provides a general overview over a significant set of disability studies’ concerns in a humanities framework. Topics covered in this course will likely include language and identity, aesthetics, cultural production, race and disability, body studies and sexuality, issues of in/interdependency, histories of institutionalization. Disability studies understands disability not only as a medical, biological or public health issue but as a social phenomenon, historically shaped by (and itself shaping) concepts of humanity, individuality, beauty, knowledge and the social contract. In disability studies, disability is cultural: a category invoked in the ordering of the world and of arrangements of power; a way of understanding human difference in relation to gender, class, race and ethnicity; a minority cultural identification which builds on lived experience.

Course Requirements:

Requirements will vary with instructor but typically include a combination of the following: 8-10 page paper plus short writing assignments throughout the term; quizzes testing comprehension of key texts and concepts; midterm exam with identification and short answer questions, final exam with identification, short answer, and essay questions; group presentation; and participation.

Intended Audience:

Sophomores-Seniors

Class Format:
