Sections.title: RacialPassingAm.History&Lit
Sections.description:
In this course, we will explore the fascinating history and literature of black-to-white racial passing in the United States.

“Passing” refers to the act—sometimes temporary, sometimes ongoing—of secretly crossing the color line, typically to gain material or social advantages or to escape the constraints of racism. The term emerged in the early nineteenth century to describe how light-skinned fugitive slaves strategically presented themselves as white in order to pass for free. Later, after the abolition of slavery and especially during legal segregation, passing came to encompass a wider network of scenarios: people passed to get into whites-only establishments and institutions, evade discrimination in education and employment, pursue socially forbidden romances, and avoid the daily indignities of second-class citizenship.

Although passing was statistically rare, as most people are not racially ambiguous, it exerted a powerful influence on American culture. From the late nineteenth to mid-twentieth century, the subject became a source of outsized intrigue and anxiety for white and black Americans alike. Across novels, autobiographical accounts, court cases, and films, the experience and scandal of passing captivated popular audiences.

Reading a diverse sampling of these texts alongside key literary and historical scholarship, we will deepen and complicate our understandings of American racial and literary history, and reflect on what passing reveals about the construction, recognition, and enforcement of racial categories. Our guiding questions will include the following: Under what kinds of historical circumstances and social pressures have people decided to pass? How is racial passing like and unlike other forms of social mobility and disguise? Why is there so much literary fiction about passing and how should we understand its relationship to real social conditions? How do passing novels stage and work through a range of abstract ideas and ideals, including freedom, alienation, loss, nature, authenticity, and morality? Do the history and practice of racial passing remain relevant today?

Students should expect to read 150-200 pages per week. Assignments will likely include regular entries in a reading journal, several skills-based written homework assignments, a midterm exam, and a final group presentation.

Sections.title: What Diff Can a Story Make?
Sections.description:
Sure, pop culture is fun. It’s great to watch an Academy Award winner, read a best seller. But stories that sell shape our values and beliefs, change how we act and what we do – often in powerful ways. Given the power of what’s popular, we better understand how that power works. Let’s read some best-selling books, watch a few Academy Award-winning movies, and see what we can figure out.

We’ll use as our arenas for inquiry some of the most significant civil rights movements in our lifetimes as we read and watch popular books and movies. Our primary aim will be to figure out, in fairly concrete ways, how stories shape people’s beliefs about people and the worlds in which we live. Best-selling books likely will include March and Firekeeper’s Daughter, and movies likely will include award-winning movies Hidden Figures and The King’s Speech.

This course is a gameful course, which means students can select from a menu of assignments, try different activities, and collect points as they move through the semester. Some options include writing traditional essays and journal entries, designing and completing multimedia projects, attending and reflecting on relevant campus events, leading and/or recording discussions, and introducing additional materials into our course. 

No background knowledge is required for this course. Everyone is welcome regardless of major, including people with backgrounds in history, politics, or activism as well as people just taking this course to fill a requirement. 

 

 

Class Format:

Lecture and discussion.

Sections.title: Banned Books
Sections.description:
For as long as free-thinking authors have felt moved to write, anxious authorities have stemmed the flow of unwelcome ideas from their pens. In this course, we will read a selection of well-known works from the past three centuries that have, at some point, been burned, banned, or censored by political or religious enforcers. We will explore the histories, purposes, and implications of various forms of censorship and of the arguments offered against it, and we will consider forbidden works from the perspectives of those who have felt both inspired and challenged by the ideas they express.

The class will be conducted as a seminar with an emphasis on in-depth discussion of the readings, and will offer a menu of assignment options enabling students to tailor the course to their own learning goals.

Sections.title: Abolition Literature
Sections.description: This course studies the effect of scientific, economic, political, or cultural change upon literature, with particular reference to the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Some of the topics which may be offered include science and poetry, or politics and the modern novel; or the focus may be on a particular theme (e.g., urbanization and the theme of alienation in modern literature).

Sections.title: Wilderness Narratives
Sections.description:
This course will consider American fiction that explores the “wilderness”—wilderness as a physical space and wilderness as a shifting cultural notion. These are tales of high adventure and danger, earth-creation and apocalypse, bewilderment and sublime beauty, ecological loss and spiritual restoration. Inevitably, part of what we’ll be thinking about is how depictions of wild spaces reflect back on the cultures and moments that produce them. And part of what we’ll be thinking about is why fiction, as a literary mode, is uniquely well adapted to surveying, inhabiting, and cultivating the terrain that we’ve told ourselves is unsurveyed and uninhabited and uncultivated. We’ll take pleasure in beautiful language. And we’ll try to articulate something of our personal response to the wildness we ourselves encounter in the world.

Students will read a good deal (mostly short fiction), write a few essays and maybe a story, and spend a bit of time outside.

Sections.title: Oceanic Visual Cultures
Sections.description:
This course introduces students to visual culture—films, art, performance—from and about the islands in the Pacific Ocean known as Oceania. Images of the islands have found their way into western imaginations through the earliest accounts of explorers, missionaries, and writers, many of whom claimed to depict, in Melville's famous words, “the unvarnished truth.” Ironically, these images also produced the vivid and often inaccurate and sometimes demeaning images of the primitive, the savage, the exotic that are part of the imperial and colonial imaginary. We will explore both early images created by explorers and others as well as contemporary films that engage the contradictory claims of truth and the production of fantasy. How do indigenous filmmakers and visual artists engage with these contradictions? We will also be engaging some of the written texts that inspired these visual forms.

 

Course Requirements:

Requirements: Journals, quizzes, reading questions, midterm paper, and final paper.

Intended Audience:

This course is accessible to undergraduates across all departments and programs.

Sections.title: Nature Poetry
Sections.description:
In this class, we’ll dedicate ourselves to the project of reading poems about the natural world—mostly poems by American writers published within the last 100 years or so (with an emphasis on the late 20th century), though any meaningful study of nature poetry has to spend at least some time thinking historically, to get a sense of how ideas about nature have evolved, and how poetry has changed in order to capture and explore those ideas. We’ll spend a lot of time with one anthology in particular, Camille Dungy’s Black Nature: Four Centuries of African American Nature Poetry, and we’ll read one or two complete volumes, including Louise Glück’s much beloved Pulitzer Prize-winning The Wild Iris. The rest of our reading will come mostly from poems reprinted online by some of our most important poets whose work makes a project out of exploring the natural world through poetry: Robert Frost, Emily Dickinson, Mary Oliver, Gary Snyder, Galway Kinnell, Elizabeth Bishop, E.E. Cummings, Ruth Stone, Maxine Kumin, Wallace Stevens…


I’m a firm believer in learning-by-doing; no one ever learned how to ride a bike simply by having someone explain to them how it works. So the bulk of our class time together will be devoted to creating space for you to practice the work of reading and interpretation—on your own through in-class writing, and collaboratively in small-group and all-class discussions. In addition to short, weekly writing exercises, you’ll submit a Midterm and a Final Portfolio of work, made up mostly of analytical writing in response to the reading you’ve done over the course of the term–though you’ll also have an opportunity to try writing your own nature poems. (Again, learning-by-doing is key here–I suspect you’ll find that taking on the role of poet yourself will help you think in new ways about the poems you’re reading as you take on your own experiments in the genre of nature poetry.)

Sections.title: Longform Storytelling&Podcast
Sections.description:
What makes a podcast good? In this class, we will listen to and evaluate a selection of storytelling podcasts. We will explore the resources for podcasting available to us through the university and look to our classroom community to cultivate recording and editing expertise. Though many of us will be amateurs in this medium, we will identify the tools and strategies that make podcasts possible and emulate those strategies.

Students will be required to write reviews on Canvas, give a presentation contextualizing the podcast for the week, offering a “skill share” to the class, and prompting us to do an activity based on that skill. After each unit, students will propose and create a podcast emulating some element of that unit’s theme.

Sections.title: Lovers&FightersEarlyEnglishLit
Sections.description:
This course will explore English literature from its beginnings in the late 600s up to and including William Shakespeare. We’ll read a lot of texts you’ve probably heard of and maybe not had a chance to study yet--like Beowulf, The Canterbury Tales, Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, The Faerie Queene, and Dr. Faustus. But also, we’ll dig into less-known texts like the first book we know to have been written in English by a woman and the speeches of Elizabeth I. As the course title suggests, we’ll spend time thinking about evolving representations of love--romantic and otherwise--and depictions of warriors. Both change a lot in English literature between the 600s and the 1600s; we’ll track and investigate those changes and, as we do, learn a lot about the historical and cultural contexts that shaped the earliest stories in English.

Course work includes short low-stakes writing assignments, a couple exams, and four 1200 word papers. Participation will be a requirement.

results.title: Southern Natures: The Making and Unmaking of Races and Environments in the US South

Sections.title: ThePlaysofWmShakespeare
Sections.description:
This is a course on the plays of William Shakespeare and the culture from which they emerged. Our primary focus will be on learning how to read Shakespeare and how to situate his work in the fascinating context of early modern London and England. The plays we will read include the following: Much Ado About Nothing, Henry the Fifth, Twelfth Night, Othello, King Lear, Macbeth, and The Tempest.

Students will learn about the divine rights of kings, philosophical skepticism, and the Protestant Reformation. They will also encounter how Shakespeare and his contemporaries approached social problems such as income inequality and poverty, and how early modern thinkers theorized race and sexuality. In that Shakespeare returns to these and other topics again and again, we will chart how his thinking evolves and shifts. We will also repeatedly reflect on the institution of marriage as it was understood in this period, the bonds that were thought to constitute friendship and family, and the broader questions of what it means to think historically and nationalistically as a writer. Throughout the semester, we will watch scenes from some of the many cinematic adaptations of Shakespeare's work.

Course Requirements:

Two papers will be assigned, as well as a final project that will ask students to engage with Shakespeare's works in ways that interest them. PDFs of all assigned readings will be made available on our Canvas site. There is no midterm in this course; neither is there a final exam.

results.title: Readings in African American and Black Literatures

Sections.title: Arab American Literature
Sections.description:
Arab-Americans have been a presence in the United States for more than a century.  An active, diffuse, and heterogeneous group, Arab Americans have maintained a low profile even as their cultures of origins have received a great deal of negative media coverage for decades. Shaped by Middle East politics as well as American foreign and domestic policies, Arab American history and culture are still in the process of documentation and analysis.  Scholars have suggested that Arab Americans have moved from exilic, to assimilationist, to ethically conscious forms of identity, with these forms sometimes operating concurrently.  These experiences of identity formation are best articulated in  the  small, and growing, body of Arab American literature that has grown in variety and esthetic range in the past few decades.

The course will begin with earliest Arab American writings at the beginning of the 20th century and concludes with works published only a few years ago. Words studied will include, but are not limited to, Moustafa Bayoumi's How Does It Feel to be a Problem? Sahar Mustafa, The Beauty of Your Face, Hayan Charara, Something Sinister, and from Beyond Memory: Anthology of Arab American Non-Fiction.

Sections.title: Asian American Lit and Culture
Sections.description:
We will survey in this course the representations of and by Asian American subjects in U.S. culture since the late nineteenth century. Cultural production—literature, drama, film, television, and performance, for example—has historically been the site where tensions among different ethnic and racial groups in the United States are exposed, resolved, exaggerated, or transformed. The cultural representation of such tensions has led, on one hand, to the affirmation of U.S. political and cultural hegemony, and, on the other, to acts of resistance to political and cultural dominance. This course explores the ways in which the cultural and literary production that arises out of the contradictions of U.S. democracy “displace,” in the words of cultural studies scholar Lisa Lowe, “the fiction of reconciliation”—the ways in which the cultural forms of Asian America “disrupt the myth of national identity by revealing its gaps and fissures.”

Texts in the course may include novels, plays, poems, films, television shows, advertisements, blogs, musicals, historical documents, and scholarly articles.

Sections.title: Jewish in America: 1945-Pres
Sections.description: The course considers a range of topics in the study of Jewish literature. It raises questions concerning the canon of texts studied, the cultural construction of Jewish literature, race and ethnicity.

Sections.title: Africa?s Nwst Nbl Prze Wnner
Sections.description: In this course we will study some of the novels, short stories and essays of Africa’s newest Nobel Prize in Literature winner, Abdulrazak Gurnah (Nobel Prize 2021). Our discussions will center on close readings of his writings as well as on the larger social and literary contexts in which they emerge. Among the topics to be discussed will be the politics of language in African literary production, the social power of literature, the representation of history in literary texts, the question of imported genres, the role of the writer in presenting a critique of colonial and postcolonial society, the experience of migration and the predicament of ethnic and sexual minorities. Texts studied will include Memory of Departure, Admiring Silence, Gravel Heart and Theft.

Sections.title: Islam in Graphic Novels
Sections.description:
This course uses rhetoric as a lens for understanding constructions of disability and accessibility across disciplines. Our analysis will call us to question deeply held beliefs about what it means to be “normal.” Our texts will include academic scholarship from the field of Disability Studies, personal narratives, podcasts, blogs, and videos—much of which is authored by people with disabilities and people with other marginalized identities. These texts may include Sitting Pretty by Rebekah Taussig, Criptiques by Caitlin Wood, The Country of the Blind by Andrew Leland, and Disability Visibility by Alice Wong, We will use what we learn from Disability Studies to analyze how disability and accessibility are rhetorically constructed in our own fields and disciplines of interest. like medicine, technology, design, architecture, environmental studies etc., as well as in intersection with other identity experiences like gender, race, sexuality, ethnicity, and class.

Your workload will include frequent drafting, deep revision, reflection on your growth, and regularly exchanging feedback with peers and the professor. The assignment sequence will ask you to use writing to investigate constructions of disability and accessibility in various modes. Your research will combine analysis of personal accounts, public policy, media, and research writing. We will begin by using critical personal narratives to interrogate norms and then we will research problems related to disability and accessibility using various sources of information, and finally we will translate the findings of our research for public audiences. You will be encouraged to choose a line of inquiry that excites you and engages an area of your interest. Previous students have researched the intersections of disability/accessibility and environmental justice, gender politics, hip hop culture, web design, medical education, democratic participation, Native American history, athletics, and more! Whether you study STEM, social sciences, or humanities, this course will teach you how to use rhetoric as a lens for challenging norms and creating new ones.

No prior knowledge/experience with disability/accessibility required—simply a sense of wonder.

Sections.title: Food and Culture
Sections.description:
The theme of the course revolves around food, which we will explore from literary, cultural, and historical perspectives. “Tell me what kind of food you eat, and I will tell you what kind of man you are,” is an oft-quoted declaration by Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin (1755-1826), the famous French epicure. While this interdisciplinary course does not guarantee grand revelations about “what kind of [person] you are,” we will explore how food—its production, consumption, history, culture, pathways—so powerfully influences our sense of personal, ethnic, communal, familial, physiological, gendered, racial, sexual, and other cultural identities.

Class time will be devoted to discussions of the texts and topics, and there will be a variety of writing exercises, including a personal essay, a food blog, and a short research paper.

Sections.title: Stories of Place
Sections.description:
How do places take on meaning in the public imagination? How do the stories attached to places shape the experiences of those who inhabit or visit them? What are the stakes in ongoing debates about what kinds of stories concerned with particular places should -- and should not -- be told?

We will explore such questions, and many others, through a wide-ranging investigation of the role of narrative in our understanding of place. We will read works from non-fiction genres including literary journalism, travel writing, and ethnography, that have contributed to the imaginative construction of story-saturated places across the US and beyond. We'll give special attention to writerly efforts at re-storying places central to the experience of historically marginalized groups.

This course will appeal to students in any field who are curious about the work of language in the world, and it will be of special interest to students considering career pathways in journalism, museums, public history, and the Arts, Culture, and Tourism sector more broadly.

Most assigned readings will be available as PDF files. Students can choose their own pathway through the course by selecting from among a wide variety of writing and other project options.

Sections.title: Eco Imaginations
Sections.description:
In this course, you will engage eco-imaginations in experimental and mainstream film and video, with a focus on material that combines ecological awareness with fantastical elements: from blockbusters like Mad Max: Fury Road and the Godzilla franchise to experimental shorts like the Kenyan Afrofuturist Pumzi. You will deepen your close reading skills and engage experimental approaches to film, video, and writing. In about half of our classes, you will make your own short videos using your phones and you will critique them in our class group. You will also be introduced to virtual reality creation – at least one of these sessions will take place on North Campus. No technical experience necessary.

We will look at the curation of festivals and sharing platforms that offer new relations to the worlds that surround us. We will have multiple ‘Into the Field’ sessions, visiting with museums, galleries, urban and natural spaces. This is a blended course, which means that some days, we will meet online to review videos we’re making in class – a task that is much easier on individual screens. You will know exactly which days we’ll meet online. You are welcome to use the classroom on these days if you do not have a private space. Please note: this is NOT a hybrid course: physical presence is necessary.

Assessment:

  • Occasional quizzes: pass/fail 
  • responses on Canvas (due by 9am on due day): pass/fail
  • mid-term take-home exam (literature review and research): 20%
  • group presentation where you share with the class one film and a short (3 min) sequence form it, and discuss it as an Eco-Imagination film (20%)
  • Final Project (either creative or critical, collaborations welcome, creative approaches should come with a 3 page commentary): 30%
  • Wellness Exercise: pass/fail
  • Participation, including creating and sharing videos in the media + film festivals: 30%

Additional for Graduate Students: Pedagogy exercise and reflection: pass/fail

ALL components of the assessment scheme need to be completed in order to receive a grade in this course.

There are no required course texts - all shorter readings will be provided on your LMS.

Sections.title: Chasing the Utopian Turtletop
Sections.description:
PLEASE NOTE: This class if for students who have completed English 324: Creative Writing: Poetry (enforced prerequisite).

At the end of 1955, Marianne Moore submitted her 43rd and final proposal to the Ford Motor Company, which had asked her help in arriving at a name for its new series of cars. Her magnificent, un-Edsel-like idea: Utopian Turtletop. (Moore had written earlier that she felt “complimented to be recruited in this high matter,” and that she would confer with her brother, who would “bring ardor and imagination to bear on the quest.”) After Moore’s final proposal, Ford sent her a floral arrangement of roses, white pine, and spiral eucalyptus. The accompanying card read, “TO OUR FAVORITE TURTLETOPPER.”

Now it’s seventy-one years later, but the stakes remain the same. My hope is that we’ll spend the semester chasing down the thing within ourselves that makes us distinctive as writers. It’s difficult to imagine a poet other than Moore coming up with Utopian Turtletop—or, for that matter, Mongoose Civique and The Intelligent Bullet, two of Moore’s other proposals. By 1955, Moore had spent four decades cultivating her sense of sound and imagery; we’ll have only three months. But that should be enough time to get us started (or further along) on what really, for writers, is a lifelong quest—a quest that requires dedication, curiosity, and, not least, ardor and imagination. In his introduction to Moore’s Selected Poems (1935), T. S. Eliot wrote, “Miss Moore is, I believe, one of those few who have done the language some service in my lifetime.” Perhaps that should be our aim: not acclaim, not the settling of accounts, but doing the language some service. Texts will include several recently published poetry and essay collections and a course packet.

We’ll treat this workshop as a workshop, by which I mean we’ll try out different tools, different methods, for advancing our craft. We’ll memorize and recite poems; we’ll imitate the works of others; we’ll practice (like a carpenter with her sander, an artist with his sketchpad, a clarinetist with her scales). We’ll usually write two pieces a week: one springing from a prompt, one from someplace else. (The muse? The pineal gland?) And we’ll prioritize, in our discussions, process over finished product. (Paul Valéry: “A work is never completed except by some accident such as weariness, satisfaction, the need to deliver, or death: for, in relation to who or what is making it, it can only be one stage in a series of inner transformations.”)

 

Class Format:

Workshop and discussion.

Sections.title: PersonalImpersonalConfessional
Sections.description:
Why did so much of the best-known poetry written in the United States in the mid-twentieth century advertise itself as being more “personal” than what came before it? Why did queer poets and poets of color more often refuse than embrace that trend? And what makes a poem “personal,” or impersonal, anyway? How does a written poem make us believe it is a person, one who “speaks” authentically, intimately, immediately, either to or for its readers? What did poets like Sylvia Plath or Robert Lowell or Anne Sexton mean by calling their work “confessional,” and how has confessionalism evolved since the 1950s when the term first emerged? How do the performances of self these poets experimented with compare to and predict our own highly self-conscious social media performances of who we are (or want to be) and how we feel?


These are some of the questions we’ll explore as we read the great poetic experiments with and against “the personal” in the decades immediately after World War II: Allen Ginsberg’s Howl, Frank O’Hara’s Lunch Poems, Sylvia Plath’s Ariel, Robert Lowell’s Life Studies, Amiri Baraka’s Preface to a Twenty Volume Suicide Note. We explore the historical and aesthetic backgrounds that make this late 1950s and early 1960s era in poetry make sense, including looking at poets who explicitly resisted the allure and market for self-revelation: Elizabeth Bishop, Robert Hayden, Gwendolyn Brooks, among others. We read contemporary works of literary theory that help us think about these concerns, such as “What is an Author,” by Michael Foucault, and “The Death of the Author,” by Roland Barthes. The course provides lots of opportunities to hone reading and writing skills, to encounter interesting poetry, and learn about cultural history in the U.S. It will involve and often feature discussions about how aspects of race/ racism, ethnicity, gender, class, and aesthetics intersect in the period and its culture.
Students will buy several poetry collections. PDFs will also be provided for some of the readings.



Course Requirements:

The course requires active participation in lectures / discussion and keeping pace with the weekly reading. Students write a series of low-stakes papers responding to and asking questions about the reading (2 pages) and develop a longer literary and cultural analysis paper through multiple drafts. There will be a take-home, timed final exam and students will work on a group presentation.

Intended Audience:

This course is intended for sophomores, juniors, and seniors. You should enjoy careful reading and thinking about writing and culture. While perhaps most appropriate to those with especial interest in close reading and writing about texts, it is suitable for all students in LSA, the Honors Program, the Residential College, as well as students in music, theater, dance, art and design, architecture, engineering, etc. We will work on our literacy in reading poems together: varying levels of experience reading poems is a-okay.

Sections.title: Journeys Abroad
Sections.description:
What do we learn about others and ourselves when we go abroad? What do we gain and what do we leave behind? This course explores how authors in English have described the journey to strange new places from the age of exploration to the industrial revolution to the era of modern alienation. We will discover how travel writing shaped literature’s role in modern society – first as a tool of imperial expansion, but then as a bridge between vastly different spheres and as a cultivator of new ways of seeing and being in the world.

Required texts will include novels and travelogues by Aphra Behn, Richard Henry Dana Jr., Herman Melville, James Baldwin, and George Orwell, as well as a few of the earliest descriptions of Michigan by European migrants.

Course requirements include two written assignments (including the option of writing your own travel narrative), discussion questions, two reading comprehension exams, and participation.

Sections.title: James Joyce
Sections.description:
This is a course for students who desire to be part of an intensely focused group of readers that will work its way through what has repeatedly been called the greatest novel of the past century: James Joyce’s Ulysses. As I trust we will all discover, Ulysses is a book that is best read in such a group. It is extremely difficult but also very much worth the effort that it demands of its readers. And though Ulysses will constitute the central object of our study, this course will challenge and reward you with an exploration of a great deal of Joyce's prose, including Dubliners, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, and selected poetry and essays as well. At the end of the term we will make a brief excursion into Finnegans Wake. We will spend some time studying the interpretive history that frames Joyce's prose.

Course requirements will include three essays (two short papers and a final, substantial essay on Ulysses. The course will conclude with the option of an unforgettable final exam. Class participation is crucial: this is a lecture / discussion course. In Finnegans Wake Joyce describes “that ideal reader suffering from an ideal insomnia.” These are books worth losing sleep over and giving up sleep for.

 

Required texts for the Course:

The U.K. Editions (available through the US Amazon site, though make sure you’re getting the OUP edition—as copyrights expire and indiscriminate reprinting becomes common, Amazon seems bent on sending you to other editions instead!); links to the Oxford Press site provided below)

  • James Joyce, Dubliners (Oxford World Classics, 2008)  ISBN 0199536430
  • James Joyce, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (Oxford World Classics, 2008)  ISBN 0199536449
  • James Joyce, Ulysses (Oxford World Classics, 2008)  ISBN 0199535671 (the second edition recently came out and it’s got slightly enlarged notes and a longer introduction; the page numbers for the novel remain the same; if you’re getting a new copy, get the 2nd ed.; if you already have the 1st ed. of this text, that’ll be just fine). And if you’d like to have larger margins, better paper, and the same pagination, the Dover Press facsimile is perfect. You’d need also to get the Oxford World Classics edition for its notes, but the actual experience of reading in the Dover may be more pleasant (particularly if, like me, your eyes aren’t what they used to be)

Sections.title: Sex,Gndr,&Rlgn in CntrbryTales
Sections.description:
Canterbury Tales has something for every literary taste. Some tales are bawdy and contain jokes about sexuality; other tales praise virginity. The tales offer tongue-in-cheek treatments of gender roles, portrayals of gender ambiguity, and descriptions of gender reversals. Some tales are highly irreligious, while others appear serious works of Christian devotion, and still others leave us wondering about the values associated with Chaucer's religion. Reading through the tales, students will learn about class structure, fashion, music, and material culture in Chaucer's time. The Tales' language is a little more difficult than modern English, but the works are also wonderfully lively and fun.

Class meetings will involve discussion of Chaucer's text and the culture surrounding it, as well as some role playing and informal attempts at dramatic reading.

Sections.title: Dbt Wrtng Pblshng First Book
Sections.description:
In this MFA-level craft course, we will examine notable fiction debuts from the past fifteen years, including indie hits, overlooked gems, and blockbuster bestsellers. How do unknown writers make the perilous journey from first draft to final, from submission to bookstore shelf?

Are the concerns of a debut distinct from a writer’s later work, even beyond the specific demands each project makes of its author? What defines "failure” and “success," and how might those definitions change depending on whom—publisher, editor, writer, Goodreads reviewer—

we ask? How do we account for the fact that, very often, a first book is not a first attempt? Is “debut” simply a marketing term, or does it hold deeper significance? And why are readers and publishers so obsessed with them?

We’ll consider questions of craft and artistic vision alongside each book’s publication story and eventual reception. Guest speakers may include authors, agents, editors, and publicists. We’ll dissect elements of fiction like POV, plot, and character, while developing a concrete, practical knowledge base about the many paths to publication and how to build a literary career without compromising one's art.

Sections.title: Prosody and Poetic Form
Sections.description:
This course blends workshop-style instruction with an in-depth exploration of prosody and both established and evolving poetic forms. We will study a wide range of formal verse samples and read essays by contemporary poets to deepen our collective understanding of poetic form. Students will experiment with meter and rhyme schemes, including blank verse and terza rima, while also composing sonnets, villanelles, sestinas, and other fixed forms. We will also delve into syllabic, accentual, and quantitative meters. Through a series of writing exercises, readings, and discussions, students will become more familiar with prosody and enhance their technical awareness of poetic structures while exploring the vast possibilities of the poetic line.

Sections.title: Intersectional Perspectives
Sections.description: Intersectional feminist perspectives and the liberation ideologies they birthed, apply to all oppressed people groups and orientation identities. Intersectional feminist perspectives actively work to frame and reframe feminism as a larger context in which bodies (Black, Brown, First Nations, Latinx, Indigenous, Asian, and any body within these and other marginalized people groups) own agency and are deserving of political representation and freedom. This course requires previous engagement with intersectional feminist theory and critical race theory as we will collectively work to map and expand these foundational ideologies to existing and emerging issues in digital and algorithmic culture. Together we will question how digital technologies limit or enhance agency; how algorithmic culture influences our perceptions of each other; and how digital media influence popular culture narratives on race, gender, class, sexuality, and other identity categories.

Sections.title: Animating Archives
Sections.description:
The subject of this seminar is archival method in literary studies. It asks a basic question: how do literary scholars effectively use and build arguments from archival sources, such as letters, institutional materials, state documents, sound archives, ecologies, original manuscripts, newspapers, objects, maps, ephemera, syllabi, records of publishing, and other artifacts. Over the course of the semester, students will both study and practice the art of doing interesting things with archival materials. Readings will be drawn from respected work in our discipline that has animated archives in inventive and interesting ways. We will ask what kinds of archival methods seem to be most valued across the many sub-disciplines of English studies. We will also consider how recent shifts in our discipline’s center of gravity––the turn to post-critical and “surface reading,” affect new formalism, and ecologies, for instance––are changing how archives are used or even what counts as an archive. Can archival materials and methods offer more than “context”? And are there specific ways that literary scholars use archival material that distinguishes them from scholars in other disciplines such as history?

Sections.title: Chapter Writing Workshop

This two-credit, weekly in-person workshop is open to PhD students in English Language and Literature, English and Women’s and Gender Studies, and the Joint Program in English and Education. Students at all stages of dissertation writing are warmly welcome. The workshop will be a collaborative, interdisciplinary space for cultivating effective and sustainable writing habits, discussing and developing works in progress, and trouble-shooting a range of strategic and logistical challenges as they arise. By the end of the term, you will have drafted a substantial portion of a dissertation chapter and developed useful skills and habits for drafting subsequent chapters.

results.Advisory Prerequisites: Enrollment restricted to first-year students, including those with sophomore standing.

Sections.title: Water Wonderland: Issues in GL
Sections.description:
In this course, students will gain a background in the physical and cultural geography of the Great Lake basin and explore water issues in the watershed pertaining to topics such as pollution, climate change, ecosystem services, human water usage, and local and basin-level water resource policies. Emphasis will be placed on systems-based thinking as it pertains to the characteristics and functioning of water features (e.g., lakes, streams, wetlands, aquifers) within the basin.

Digital storytelling describes the practice of using digital tools to tell a ‘story’ in an engaging and compelling format. A story map is a digital storytelling tool that combines maps with multimedia content (e.g., images, video, text) to convey geographic information as a narrative. Students will employ elements of cartographic design, spatial analysis, and data visualization within story maps as a means for creating interactive science stories about Great Lakes water issues. Students will explore multiple story map formats and their utility in the effective communication of science to scientists, the public, and policymakers. Prior experience with web maps or story maps is not required. A laptop or tablet with an internet browser is required for multiple class meetings.

Sections.title: Ecol&Religion for Anthropocene
Sections.description:
W.B. Yeats asserted in his poem The Second Coming that "[t]hings fall apart; the centre cannot hold . . .", which seems to aptly describe our current times. We live in an age of geological history referred to as the Anthropocene in
recognition of the overwhelming impact of human society on the natural world. Our climate, landscapes, and biota are being reshaped by powerful forces, some of them of human origination.

This course will examine current trends in human impacts on the earth’s ecology and help students envision likely future conditions which will affect their lives. The course will give depth to this inquiry by exploring ecology at multiple levels.

Students will be required to connect immediately and locally by keeping a nature journal. The course will avail itself of the best scientific information regarding the status and likely future of the biosphere. The seminar will also explore various ways
of conceptualizing the world, especially as these have been envisioned through religions and spirituality, whether traditional, contemporary, or indigenous. Students enrolling in this seminar will have varying backgrounds of knowledge and
experience in relation to ecology, science, and religion / spirituality. This course welcomes:

  • Students with religious commitments in traditional faith communities;
  • Students who identify themselves as agnostics, atheists, secular humanists, skeptics, or ‘undecideds’;
  • Students who have formulated their own system of values and related belief systems and practices.


This seminar’s opportunity for the participatory inquiry will require enrolled students to engage in respectful dialogue along with acceptance of people with backgrounds and present commitments and beliefs that are different from their own.

Intended Audience:

First year students

Class Format:

 

Instruction Mode: The class meets twice a week in person.

Sections.title: Env History of North America
Sections.description: Environmental History of North America welcomes you to learn about the bonds between the people and places of this continent. This course does not assume that you have any background in environmental studies or history. We will explore the relationships among landscapes, humans, and other forms of life from prehistory to the present. We will ask how people’s connections to their environments changed from the period of Indigenous settlement, to European colonization, to the expansion of industrial states. What is “natural”? What is “sustainable”? How have people modified their surroundings, and how have environments shaped societies?

Sections.title: MI: People & Place, Climate
Sections.description:
Preparing for a future in the face of a changing climate is a grand challenge for humanity. This challenge can only be seriously addressed by taking a multidisciplinary perspective. In this course, we will bring together 15,000 years of Michigan's geological, biological, and human history with contemporary climate science, and use it all as inspiration for a multi-disciplinary imagining of our region's future. Along the way, we will consider carefully how we can learn about the world as it was in the past, expand our appreciation for how the past informs the present, and explore how our actions in the present influence the future. You can’t prepare for the future without knowing the lessons from the past. In this class, we’ll do both.
We will learn together about these topics, from texts in many forms and from the landscapes and environments that surround us at the University of Michigan. We will read short extracts from authors who encountered Michigan’s environment and people in the past, those who shaped their evolution through the 19th and 20th century, and those who are anticipating our collective future. Students in this course will have substantial freedom to focus their work for the class on areas that interest them. Together we will be able to explore much more about this topic than any one of us could ever do alone.

Sections.title: Organizing for Social Change
Sections.description: This seminar will engage with ideas and perspectives around how people organize for social change and innovation. This course is designed to introduce students to different ways individuals and groups drive efforts to address social and environmental challenges. Throughout the course, students will have the opportunity to explore the roles and interplay of various change agents including social entrepreneurs who tackle social issues with innovative business ventures, intrapreneurs who work within existing organizations to drive transformation from the inside, and the collectives and leaders who create social movements. Class sessions will be interactive and discussion-based to encourage critical and thoughtful dialogue around social change work in and through organizations. By delving into different approaches to social change and innovation, students will equip themselves to become more informed advocates and leaders in their workplaces and communities.

Sections.title: Energy Sol for Changing Planet
Sections.description:
Everything we do relies on energy. Our current energy system has plenty of flaws, but also makes everything in our lives possible, from being able to get a cup of coffee in the morning to setting the alarms on our phones before bed. If we wish to stabilize our climate and reduce strain on our ecosystems, we need to significantly redesign our energy system. Throughout this course, we will analyze the benefits and tradeoffs of the technical and non-technical options available, helping to envision our energy future. This course will help develop a foundational understanding of how our energy system works, as well as the environmental, social, and economic implications of future energy solutions.

Course Goals and Learning Objectives 

This course has three main goals, each with specific learning objectives. 
Goal #1: Become proficient with basic energy science and technology concepts. To achieve this goal, students will be able to:
• Comfortably perform power and energy calculations, including unit conversions and calculations of total energy, costs, and greenhouse gas emissions
• Describe the basic processes associated with energy use and production, including how energy resources are transformed into electricity and transportation services

Goal #2: Interpret energy and environment data discussed in popular and news media, differentiating what is important and the differences between fact and opinion. To achieve this goal, students will be able to:
• Use quantitative reasoning to estimate overall magnitude of a proposed solution (e.g. Is installing a MW of solar a big deal?  What about reducing 10 tons of CO2?)
• Document processes of estimation/calculation
• Examine arguments and data to determine flaws in logic or calculation errors; identify when something doesn’t seem correct and should be double checked
• Factcheck a resource
• Differentiate between fact and an expressed opinion  

Goal #3: Critically evaluate specific technologies/solutions for the energy transition. To achieve this goal, students will be able to:
• Compare and contrast different solutions using a range of criteria (environmental, economic, social)
• Make concrete decisions on paths forward, while understanding and acknowledging the tradeoffs and limitations of different solutions.   

Course Requirements:

There will be regular homework assignments that include a mixture of quantitative and qualitative exercises, as well as two in-class exams, and a final group project.

Intended Audience:

Any student who is interested in energy science and the environment.

Class Format:

Lecture plus discussion

Sections.title: Climate Solutions from Nature
Sections.description:
As global change transforms our planet, many people are seeking solutions to slow its progress. This course introduces and explores nature-based solutions (NBS), the methods for meeting climate challenges that emerge from natural processes, such as growing forests and restoring coastal ecosystems. We will read influential works that highlight NBS’ potential for climate mitigation and discuss the possible outcomes of offset trading. We will also examine current projects that aim to sequester carbon, support biodiversity, and foster people’s livelihoods, considering their environmental and social impacts and learning from their successes and failures. My goal is to provide you with an understanding of the ways that widely applied climate solutions from nature might unfold and help you build the skills to evaluate these approaches, discerning those that have real potential to address global change from those that make false promises.

Course Requirements:

The course grade is based on assignments drawn from the reading, case studies, a project, and one or more exams. Group work will be an integral part of most lectures, and therefore, attendance is required. Students will complete a project that investigates and evaluates a real-world climate solution.

Intended Audience:

Previous college-level coursework in environmental science and/or biology is recommended (e.g. ENVIRON 110 and/or BIO 171). Willingness to engage with a variety of sources and materials across natural and social science disciplines is encouraged.

Class Format:

1.5 hrs twice per week, combined lecture/discussion

Sections.title: Intro to Environ Humanities
Sections.description:
In the face of the very real climate challenges facing our planet, why read literature, make art, watch film, or study history to learn more about the environment? This course is built on the premise that, far from being a distraction from (or simply a form of pleasure amidst) environmental degradation, such practices can, in fact, enable us to be more attentive, imaginative, ethical, and effective environmental stewards. More specifically, we’ll consider the habits of attention that various written, artistic, and conceptual modes demand — and consider how engaging carefully with work in these genres can help us think of environmental crisis anew.

Along the way, we will find ourselves asking questions like the following: How might turning to the humanities not only offer us new answers to the questions that various environmental challenges pose, but also alter the terms in which we define such questions and challenges themselves? How can the seeming indirectness of literature (its tendency, say, to speak in symbol or metaphor) help us rethink our belief that successful activism is necessarily “direct”? How might the pace and scale of literary and historical narrative help attune us to environmental problems that unfold slowly, beneath notice, or at a geological rate? How can the “human” focus of the “humanities” give us the language with which to articulate the strange intimacies between human bodies, nonhuman others, and the material environments that surround (and constitute) us all? How can insights from various fields in the humanities help us to understand the relationship between environmental activism and various social justice projects — or, more fundamentally, to understand the way in which our relationship to the environment is so often already itself gendered and racialized?

Course Requirements:

Op-Ed: 20% 

Creative Midterm Exam: 15%

Final Project: 25%  

Final Exam: 20%

Class Participation 20%

 

Intended Audience:

Take this class if you’re a student of the humanities who wants to better understand the connection between what you do in your home discipline and the work involved in environmental problem-solving and activism. Take this class if you’re an environmental activist (and/or PitE major or minor) who is unsure what role the activities you do in the “rest” of your life might have to do with your political and ethical commitments. Take this class if you’re skeptical that the humanities and environmental studies might, in fact, have anything to say to one another.

Sections.title: Mapping Rivers in China
Sections.description:
Rivers and landscapes reflect the goals, anxieties, and capabilities of the humans who interact with them. Maps allow us to understand and analyze these relationships. To practice analyzing how rivers and Chinese society have shaped each other, this course begins with the present day and works backward toward the 19th century.

This unusual perspective will help us to see the world as it is, and ask how it got this way. Beginning with today’s massive and controversial Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze River, we will look at hydro-engineering projects in the People’s Republic of China since 1949. We will trace the roots of these schemes to the state-building efforts of the Nationalist government in the early 20th century, which arose from water control in China’s last dynasty, the Qing. In addition to scholarly readings and translated texts, we will use ArcGIS mapping software to ask and attempt to answer questions about the interactions between humans and hydrology. How has the relationship between the Chinese state and rivers changed during the last two centuries? Have rivers and people ever been able to coexist? How?

Sections.title: Water in Ancient Mediterranean
Sections.description: Why study the history of water? Since water is essential to biological life, it is the most universal natural resource and therefore of paramount importance to all human societies in all periods of history. Yet owing to the environmental, cultural, social, institutional, and technological diversity of human societies, water’s universality manifests itself in innumerable ways across space and time. This course addresses such complex and diverse human-water relationships in the ancient Mediterranean world between the 3rd century BC and the 7h century AD). Covering both a vast geographical space and a full millennium of human history, we will study a great variety of human interactions with water during Mediterranean antiquity and explore how, in remaking their watery landscapes, ancient societies remade themselves.

Sections.title: Community Organizing: EJ
Sections.description: Community organizing is the process of building collective power, usually (but not always) in proximate geographic locations by uniting people to identify shared problems, develop local leadership, and take direct action to influence decision-makers for changes in policies and/or practices. This course will focus on grassroots empowerment and the transformation of collective grievances (and joys!) into strategic, organized campaigns that improve community conditions.While community organizing can have many origins and goals, this course will focus on community organizing for environmental justice in the United States (US). It locates the beginning of the environmental injustice in European colonization of Turtle Island/Abya Yala since 1492, and so will draw from historical as well as contemporary examples of community organizing. Incorporating insights from Social Movement Ecology, this course will also feature a variety of experiments in regenerative relationality, efforts to build a world where environmental justice is integral and central.

Sections.title: Climate Action: Your Role
Sections.description: Climate change is a collective crisis that calls us, as individuals, to act with intention and strategy. Yet many of us are left asking, “What is my role?” In this highly participatory course, students examine climate emotions, justice, and community-based responses while mapping existing solutions at local, national, and global scales. Through readings, discussion, reflective writing, and field-based engagement, participants identify their strengths and values, explore social change roles, and consider how to engage in climate action in ways that align with their skills and interests. The course emphasizes care, collaboration, and purposeful pathways toward a more just and sustainable collective future.

Sections.title: Nature & Well-Being
Sections.description:
How can we intentionally partner with nature to support our resilience to personal and environmental challenges? This seminar moves beyond the basic benefits of nature contact to focus on applied psychology and facilitation. Students will develop the skills to function as practitioners, mastering nature-based interventions for personal resilience and learning to facilitate these activities for others in future professional settings (sustainability, healthcare, education, social work, etc.).

As this course emphasizes experiential learning, our meetings take place primarily outdoors. A backup indoor space for inclement weather is provided.

Sections.title: Climate Change & Human Health
Sections.description:
This course introduces students to the social and environmental factors that determine how climate change affects human health. We will examine the physical drivers of climate change, the exposure pathways through which it impacts health, and the social, behavioral, and environmental contexts that influence vulnerability to climate change-related health effects. The course also introduces the concept of social and structural determinants of health and examines why climate-related health impacts are distributed unequally across populations in the United States and globally. We will discuss the health benefits of climate solutions such as climate mitigation, adaptation, and resilience efforts. Students will analyze real-world climate and health events through assignments designed to develop practical skills in problem solving, evidence-based analysis, analytical writing, and oral communication. 

Intended Audience:

This course is intended for first- and second-year students.

results.title: Energy and Climate Change: Technology, Markets, and Policy

Sections.title: Energy and Climate Change
Sections.description:
Energy is an incredibly complex topic by virtue of the inter-linkages of science, technology, public policy, economics, and human behaviors. This course will examine all aspects of energy: supply and demand, technical and social, with a concerted look at the natural place of social science (behavior, pricing, externalities, social norms) in the energy sphere.

Every aspect of present-day society depends on the continuing availability of clean, affordable, flexible, secure, and safe energy resources. Yet nearly 90% of our current energy needs are met by fossil fuels. Our reliance on fossil fuels has led to declining supplies, rising prices, global climate change, and security concerns. The current global energy economy is not sustainable. The technological challenges are formidable; but they cannot be considered solutions without considering the human and social behavioral side of energy demand.

The quest for solutions to "The Energy Problem" is dominated by technology "fixes". The visions of practical technological fixes, whether electricity energy generation, oil exploration and extraction, pollution mitigation, automobile fuel efficiency and alternatives to combustion engines, etc., necessarily build on what we know today and presume that we can achieve in a couple of decades or so, through sufficient R&D, an energy supply-demand balance that fulfills a wide range of incompatible requirements — cheap, environmentally benign, politically secure, unconstrained supply, convenient, and safe. While we expect technology to come to our energy-rescue and support our established patterns of economic growth and energy-intensive lifestyles, we tend to expect very little from the human and social behavioral side of energy use and demand. In some ways the Energy Problem is yet another version of C.P. Snow's Two Cultures — parallel technology and social cultures with little mutual understanding and rare cross-over exchange.

The Complex Systems view would hold that society and Energy technologies have coevolved through the actions of individual agents (inventors, scientists, entrepreneurs, financiers, writers, politicians, kings and queens, dictators, and statesman), learning, adapting, selecting, exchanging information, and interacting through transactions of many kinds. At every stage, the social, economic, and technological systems were tightly coupled. It is not possible to understand Energy Problems without framing them in a systems context.

Course Requirements:

Two midterm exams, a Final Exam, graded homework assignments, and a term project.

Intended Audience:

Freshmen and Sophomores interested in energy and complex systems.

Class Format:

3 hours of lecture per week.

Sections.title: Assessing Sustnability Culture
Sections.description: This course explores the concept of sustainability culture and the use of social science research methods to assess cultural change. It focuses generally on the concept and as well efforts to develop a culture of sustainability on the campus of the University of Michigan (U-M). This includes U-M’s Sustainability Cultural Indicators Program (SCIP) designed to monitor progress in fostering a culture of sustainability on campus. SCIP, launched in 2012 administers surveys among representative samples of students, staff and faculty, measuring sustainability attitudes, awareness and behaviors as well as beliefs and views on climate change. Through lectures, discussion, guest lectures, and a team-based research project this course will provide students with hands-on opportunity to learn how to evaluate sustainability initiatives and programs as well as address innovative research questions that can help catalyze further cultural change. Drawing on relevant theories of individual behavior, organizational, and cultural change students will engage in team-based activities to develop research questions and hypotheses, analyze survey data to test hypotheses, interpret results, and present results in a scientific paper and oral presentation. Students will also be asked to discuss implications of their research findings for U-M’s sustainability policies and initiatives.

Sections.title: Climate Politics: Devel World
Sections.description:
In 2019, the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) released a report clearly stating the dire consequences of hundreds of years of accumulated carbon emissions and calling for urgent action to avert climate chaos, including a rapid drawdown of the extraction and burning of hydrocarbon energy and its replacement with renewable, no-carbon sources such as wind and solar. The report laid bare the distributional implications, and economic and ethical responsibilities, for causing, suffering from, and adapting to climate change. Low and middle-income countries have never been the world's largest polluters, but as we contemplate the twin imperatives of raising the standard of living of billions of the world's citizens outside of high-income countries and creating resilient societies, they will be central actors in how we confront climate change.

This class will provide students with a framework on how to think about the political and economic implications of climate change in low and middle-income countries. We will engage with how academics, policymakers, and fiction and non-fiction writers have thought about the political problems and solutions to climate change in low and middle-income countries. Together, we will think through ways out of this crisis that are attuned to the agency and demands of citizens and states in low and middle-income countries.

Sections.title: Political Ecology of AI
Sections.description: In this class, we will use a political ecology framework to understand and analyze the global environmental impacts of AI and data centers, the regional geographies of land use change and economic tradeoffs, and the local contexts of AI development and resistance. We will bring these concepts home to examine how communities, municipalities, universities, and businesses are engaging with data center development and AI technology in southern Michigan. Students will develop the conceptual understanding, analytical tools, and applied skills to understand the complexities of AI and actively contribute to evolving conversations and action in Ann Arbor and the region.

Sections.title: Local Food Policy
Sections.description: In recent decades, local governments have drawn growing attention for their potential to influence how communities grow, eat, and sustain themselves — yet few have fully integrated food systems across the many policy tools at their disposal. Despite the rise of food policy councils and expanded interest in local food, food access, and sustainability, both practitioners and advocates often lack a clear understanding of how local governments actually operate and what levers can produce change. This course examines how food systems interact with local governance — from food production and processing to retail, waste, and public health — and explores the opportunities and limits of municipal, county, and regional action in shaping more equitable and resilient systems. Students will investigate how local governments relate to state and federal policy; analyze their structures, authorities, and decision-making processes; and learn to design policy approaches using both legislative and administrative strategies. While centered in U.S. contexts, we will draw comparative examples from abroad to illustrate alternative models of local food governance. Through applied projects, students will assess existing food system policies and plans, engage with data and case studies, and develop actionable proposals for local government partners. Students will leave with practical tools to navigate — and influence — the complex intersections of governance, community action, and food systems change.

Sections.title: Environ Governance African Dev
Sections.description: Environmental sustainability and economic development are two of the most pressing issues of our time. Nowhere is the imperative for both clearer than in Africa. In this course, we will explore the institutional structures that mediate human interactions with the environment in Africa, and consider how different approaches to natural resource extraction and use have shaped economic and ecological outcomes across the continent throughout history. Emphasis will be placed on both nonrenewable resources (e.g. extractive industries, from colonial exploitation to national development programs to multinational corporate operations) and renewable resources (e.g. forests and biodiversity, from community-managed commons to market-based conservation to protected areas managed by foreign NGOs). Moreover, we will examine the varied strategies individuals, communities, states, corporations, and organizations have used in seeking to gain and maintain control over resources for purposes of subsistence, profit, conservation, and/or development. In doing so, we will consult literature in political ecology, environmental history, and development studies, as well as popular media and policy documents.

Sections.title: Planet Earth
Sections.description: How does one visualize ecological crisis on a global scale? Is it possible to “see” climate change, microplastic pollution, or mass extinction? How can we reconcile human vision with planetary scale and deep geological time? In this class, we will explore artistic and scientific responses to the problem of visualizing the planet and its ecology, beginning with the German inventors of the science of ecology (Alexander von Humboldt, Jakob von Uexküll, Ernst Haeckel). From this foundation, we will explore a range of visual approaches to ecology and the planet throughout the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, from the Earth visualized as a fragile “Blue Marble,” to mid-twentieth century land art, geoengineering, and contemporary examples of climate art that draw on and reinvent the long history of ecological visions of the planet. Our central focus will be the relationship between vision, knowledge, and political responses to planetary ecology and its crises. As a final project for this class, you will create your own visual representation of an ecological entity or problem, either as a work of art (with an artist’s statement) or as a piece of science communication.

Sections.title: Talking w/Animals:Child &Other
Sections.description: This mini-course investigates the roles that animals have historically played in children’s literature, illustration, and film. Why do stories for the young frequently employ animal life to explore human suffering and existence of souls? How do images and ideas about the child and the beast conflate in our myths? As people grow up distanced from farm and wildlife, how do other species animate what it means to be child and adult? This mini-course studies the aesthetic, generic, and rhetorical uses of animals in visual and verbal media. It pairs theoretical perspectives and other traditions of animal figuration--from ancient fables and 18th c. models for English-speaking children to contemporary children’s literature and films. Guest speakers and experiential learning enhance our study as we ask amid climate changes: what animal scenarios speak to the next generation?

Sections.title: Wilderness Narratives
Sections.description:
This course will consider American fiction that explores the “wilderness”—wilderness as a physical space and wilderness as a shifting cultural notion. These are tales of high adventure and danger, earth-creation and apocalypse, bewilderment and sublime beauty, ecological loss and spiritual restoration. Inevitably, part of what we’ll be thinking about is how depictions of wild spaces reflect back on the cultures and moments that produce them. And part of what we’ll be thinking about is why fiction, as a literary mode, is uniquely well adapted to surveying, inhabiting, and cultivating the terrain that we’ve told ourselves is unsurveyed and uninhabited and uncultivated. We’ll take pleasure in beautiful language. And we’ll try to articulate something of our personal response to the wildness we ourselves encounter in the world.

Students will read a good deal (mostly short fiction), write a few essays and maybe a story, and spend a bit of time outside.

Sections.title: Intro Environmental Politics
Sections.description:
This course introduces students to global environmental politics, justice and development. This course will explore environmental issues around the world and the relatedness of nature to politics, development and culture. We will address historically unique social form that presents special challenges to our understanding of environmental politics, gender, race and culture by looking at case studies from around the world. Among the questions that we will examine are the following: How have local and global histories, memories, practices, values, gender, race and identities that derive from our understanding of politics intersect with nature? Are there environmental issues that are also issues of race, class and gender? For example, are there particular forms of knowledge and subjectivity that intersect or interact with race and gender difference, or ideas about civilization and primitivity that could be seen as distinctive instruments of environmental rule?

Sections.title: Found of Sust Food Systems
Sections.description:
This course will offer a unique opportunity for students to gain interdisciplinary knowledge of food systems and to integrate theory and practice through experiential learning and dialogue-based inquiry both on campus and in the community. Interdisciplinary research and education require bridging worldviews and recognizing the values implicit in different disciplinary and theoretical perspectives. This course will incorporate multiple perspectives, from local to global levels, as well as an understanding of how those perspectives are underpinned by different epistemologies and value systems. That is, this course directly engages with values, exploring how they shape food systems. Benefitting from collaborative interdisciplinary instruction that draws on the expertise of three professors from three different departments, students will develop competencies and cognitive skills in the area of food system sustainability including critical and systems thinking, creativity, and analytical ability.

Intended Audience:

Junior and Senior standing

Sections.title: Org: People, Power, and Change
Sections.description:
Do you want to learn how to make lasting changes on a larger scale than one person can normally achieve? Organizers do that by identifying, recruiting, and developing leadership; nurturing community around that leadership; and building power from the resources of that community. In this course, you learn how to do this kind of organizing in your workplace and your community. You will form leadership teams of 3 to 5 classmates based on common values, identify the constituency with which your team will work, develop a campaign strategy to make a change that constituents think is important, try to implement that strategy. Organizing is a craft: you learn by doing and you get better with practice. You will learn five core leadership practices: building public relationships, turning values into motivation through public narrative, turning resources into power by strategizing, turning intentions into effective action, and structuring organization to develop leadership, engage constituents, and achieve goals. You will also learn to coach others and to receive coaching in organizing practices.

 

Course Requirements:

Course Assessment: Grades derive mainly from nine reflection papers, a mid-term report, an organizing team presentation to the class, and a final reflection assessing what you have learned from the team formation, strategy development and campaign implementation processes. Grades do not depend on whether or not your team’s campaign “succeeds” within the short time-frame of a single term; you will learn a great deal whether or not you achieve a success of this sort

Sections.title: Holy Sh!t: Why Poop Matters
Sections.description:
Human excreta is generally considered waste, but this is a modern idea. Since time immemorial people have had to deal with urine and feces, and did so in different ways. You can learn a lot about a society based on how they deal (or don't) with their crap--literally and metaphorically. And what does poop have to do with religion? What you learn in this course may surprise you. The class format is mainly lecture and discussion that delves into, and builds on, the readings. Some classes will feature videos, guest speakers, or other interactive components.

This course will examine a wide range of aspects of human life, death (and even afterlife) through the lens of an under-discussed phenomenon--human excreta. It will explore these themes on individual, communal, and international levels, giving attention to excreta's centrality to both intimate daily routines and the global sanitation crisis (a key aspect of environmental justice, water usage, and climate change concerns).
 
It will begin by focusing on excreta from a religious ritual angle, elucidating how toileting practices, linguistics, and spaces relate concepts of sacred, pollution, danger, indispensability, health, discard, and group belonging. Then it will continue by examining the way these concepts manifest through excreta infrastructure systems in oppressive (e.g. racist, settler-colonial) and/or liberatory ways (e.g. regenerative economics, human rights). Throughout the semester, students will get to examine their worldviews, experiences, and practices, and meet advocates breaking the poo taboo...learning how innovators in the field of ecological sanitation help humans deal with their crap, literally and metaphorically.

Sections.title: Env Protest in Art & Media
Sections.description:
In 2017, Cristina Mittermeier released footage of a starving polar bear with the National Geographic in an effort to draw attention to global warming’s tangible effects. Yet within a year, National Geographic issued a public apology in light of the controversy. Critics pointed out that bears could look emaciated this time of year under normal climate circumstances or it might be suffering an unknown illness that may not be climate related. So how do we ethically and factually depict climate change and the impacts of industrialization on the environment?

 

These are some of the questions that we will be exploring in ENVIRON 464. This class will discuss the presentism and impact that images of the environment and environmental issues and protests can have on drawing awareness, misrepresenting, or generating eco-anxiety. We will also discuss why photos and art become targets for environmental protests in cases of “eco-vandalism.” The class will ask: In what ways do images play a role in shaping our understanding and relationship or cultivate a responsibility to the environment? How can we use historical images to understand changes in the environment? What can capturing the environment do? And how can it be problematic? As such, we will examine a range of media and images from Anna Atkins’ cyanotypes and seventeenth century woodcuts to contemporary photos, such as the Just Stop Oil protests.

Sections.title: Local Environmental Journalism
Sections.description:
Students in this new course will collaborate with Interlochen Public Radio and other news organizations to monitor local government meetings in northern Michigan, gaining practical experience with environmental news that impacts community life and helps democracy function. Topics addressed might include data centers, algal blooms, erosion, roads, weeds, development, parks, and flooding. One goal of the course: to help
journalists build the case for reforming Michigan’s Open Meeting Act to require public meetings to require recordings.

Sections.title: Music trends France 50s-now
Sections.description:
In this course students will explore French and francophone songs and how major movements throughout the years shaped the current music scenery in France.  While listening to a variety of artists and analyzing the text and music influences, we will address topics such as the representation of women, political and cultural symbols, inclusion and diversity.

Students will analyze music and lyrics, read texts from the Internet, watch videos, and listen to songs in-class and outside of class.

Course evaluation will include in-class presentations, written reflections, longer compositions, quizzes/written assessments, a final individual speaking evaluation, and a final assessment.

In this course, we will cover the same language structures as students of other FRENCH 232 sections, and use the same textbook, Séquences, for grammar explanations and reference.

Sections.title: Vive la revolution
Sections.description:
In this course students will explore and analyze the history of revolts and revolutions and resistance in France and the francophone world. Students will examine a mix of films, literature, art, music, and historical documents to consider causes and results of revolt and resistance, as well as the dissonance of a colonial power that was itself formed by revolt. Students will also evaluate how revolts and revolutions have been depicted in media and literature.

Course evaluation will include an in-class presentation, unit exams, written reflections, quizzes, a final individual speaking evaluation and a final exam.

In this course, we will cover the same language structures as students of other FRENCH 232 sections, and use the same textbook, Séquences, for grammar explanations and reference.
