Sections.title: Everyday Life in the Sov Union
Sections.description:
After the October Revolution and the founding of the Soviet Union, Soviet leaders claimed to be forging new civilization. According to official ideology, the “new Soviet person” was to be an active builder of communism, dedicated to collective life and raised in a spirit of state patriotism. At the center of Soviet society was the state, which sought to provide its citizens with a complete and coherent “Soviet” experience from the cradle to the grave. This experience is the focus of this first-year seminar. Weekly meetings walk us through everyday life in the Soviet Union, starting with childbirth and early childhood and ending with retirement, death, and funerals. Our weekly readings include a mix of primary and secondary sources. Along the way, you'll also be guided through the historical research process, including an independent project utilizing Soviet Life, an English-language magazine produced by the Soviet Union for American audiences between 1956 and 1991. All readings are in English, no prior knowledge expected.

Sections.title: Stories from Deep Time
Sections.description:
What happens to our understanding of the present when we think about history on geologic rather than generational time scales? This course explores the history of “deep time” in science, culture, and politics. We will debate when human history begins; explore controversies over the scientific discovery of “lost worlds” three centuries ago; analyze what is at stake in passionate arguments over the roles of humans and climate in the extinction of megafauna 10,000 years ago; uncover the legacy of religious creation stories in secular natural history; and compare how scientists and science fiction authors use data from deep time to imagine future worlds.

As a first-year seminar, the course is designed to prepare you for academic success at the University of Michigan. We will read a wide range of texts from scientific articles to policy memos to fantasy in order to develop strategies for reading particular genres. We will also practice writing in a range of genres. Every week we will set aside time explicitly to address challenges of university life, the development of effective study habits, university and community resources, and other issues that students propose.

Sections.title: Commodore Perry Meets Shogun
Sections.description:
By the time the four battleships, exhaling black smoke, sailed into the Uraga Bay in 1853, Japan’s third shogunate and its vassal samurai had been ruling and enjoying undisturbed “total peace” for two and a half centuries. True, other Westerners had been showing up around Japan’s waters recently, but this visit, led by Navy Commander Matthew Perry, seemed more determined than others to impress Japan with a greater purpose. The samurai had seen the raw power of the industrial West only a decade before when the profit hungry Great Britain devastated Qing China to force the sale of opium. What to do? This course explores the momentous encounter of two forces--the rising imperialist nation, the United States, and the proud warrior regime that had barred all Christian countries from its soil centuries before. This is a story of palpable “threat and anxiety at first sight” that generated remarkable adjustments on the part of the vulnerable but also impacted the aggressor. We examine this dramatic and transformative time in the long history of Japan by focusing on the lives and beliefs of the samurai and the intent and conduct of the United States. We experience this moment through feature films, documentary films, American newspaper entries, and scholarly articles as well as contemporary prints kept at the Clements Archive.

Course Requirements:

Evaluation will be based on in-class short writing exercises, discussions, presentations, occasional quizzes, and at-home writings. 

Intended Audience:

Sections.title: Journeys & Stories
Sections.description:
Different kinds of travellers have long set out, returned home, and told of their adventures. Their experiences and storytelling range across time and space, but other kinds of journey and telling require little or no physical mobility, happening mostly in the mind and in the living of life. Our course will especially explore history-making, memory and recollection, and different kinds of participant-teller. Readings and other stimuli will be drawn from several settings and genres, not least histories, memoirs, novels, stories, satire, films and television series, picture books and graphic novels, music, and threatre. Students will be encouraged to consider the development of their own selves, perspectives, and curiosities as dynamic journeys and stories.

Our small seminar is discussion-centered, and reading- and writing-intensive. It features: a series of short writing assignments and creative research opportunities, oral presentations; commentary on peers' writing; and a collaborative performance emerging from our themes and course of study.

Sections.title: Music, Protest, and Politics
Sections.description:
Focused on the 20th century United States, this course considers the historical relationship among music, protest, and politics. Our explorations will cut across many musical traditions, from jazz to country to blues to Plena to disco to hip hop to folk to punk to Tejano to many others. We’ll hear and consider music from a wide range of artists, including Gladys Bentley, Lydia Mendoza, Woody Guthrie, Bob Dylan, Nina Simone, Marvin Gaye, Willie Dunn, Bruce Springsteen, and Public Enemy. We’ll ground our explorations in the context of various social, political, and cultural movements and contexts, from the Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s to deindustrialization in the 1970s, from mobilizations for migrant and workers’ rights to struggles for civil rights and Black Power to battles over gay rights and women’s rights. We’ll define ‘protest’ broadly to examine music related directly to activism and politics as well as music that protests by centering joy, pride, and community.

Sections.title: Uses & Abuses of Fame-US Hist
Sections.description:
Today, we describe "celebrity" as something all-consuming—an inescapable feature of modern life. One can become famous via Tik Tok, YouTube, and Spotify, as well as through the “older” media of theater, photography, newspapers, radio, television, and film. In recent years, we’ve seen the emergence of celebrity cats, criminals, chefs, video gamers, and porn stars, as well as “celebrity Presidents” from both parties. More and more, we are all participants in this voracious cycle—from the selfies on our smartphones to our serial posting online. But how did we get here? How did this increasingly global "culture of celebrity” first take shape--and how has it evolved over time? Relatedly, how has the experience of becoming famous differed for women, people of color, and sexual minorities? What broader effects (both positive and destructive) has this process unleashed on our increasingly fragile democracy? 

As a starting point, we will investigate the history of fame itself: from pre-modern warriors, kings, and saints to the early architects of the modern star system. Along the way, we will look at key watersheds in this history: Phillis Wheatley, P.T. Barnum, Frederick Douglass, and Sarah Bernhardt; FDR, Shirley Temple, Paul Robeson, and the Beatles; Muhammad Ali, Beyonce, Donald Trump, Taylor Swift, and Bad Bunny. We will also push beyond the glamorous surfaces to examine celebrity's inner workings: from the first theatrical syndicates, Hollywood studios, and fan magazines to radio, TV, social media, and algorithmic motors. Above all, we will try to provide you with deeper contexts and critical distance on this phenomenon. By the end of the term, you will possess the historical tools necessary to explain celebrity as something complicated, powerful, increasingly inescapable, and surprisingly enduring--a form of public life about as old as the United States itself. 

Course Requirements:

Quizzes, weekly study questions, midterm, final project

Intended Audience:

Freshmen

Class Format:

Seminar

The US media portrays Vladimir Putin in dramatic terms as an enigma, an evil genius, or the incarnation of timeless Russian tyranny. Sections.title: Palestine in the World
Sections.description:
Palestine in the World seeks to analyze how Palestine became a major touchstone for anticolonial forces around the globe. It interprets Palestine’s role as a point of symbolism, debate, and activity at various critical junctures, including but not limited to: the competing visions of the British & the Comintern during the Mandate era, U.S. and Soviet maneuvering during partition, the Bandung Conference, the Tricontinental, the Cultural Revolution in China, the rise of Black Power and the left in Latin America, the PLO’s connections across Africa, and the neoliberal era after the mid-1970s. The course will end by analyzing the role of Palestine in the post-Cold War world, including the changing attitudes in the West and the role of regional power blocs in envisioning Palestine. In short, this course would not only deal heavily with Palestine and Palestinian primary sources, but also with how the world interpreted and understood Palestine over time.

Sections.title: Uganda in the 1970s
Sections.description:
Idi Amin was one of history’s most charismatic dictators. As president of Uganda between 1971 and 1979 he earned an international reputation as ‘The Butcher of Uganda’, and as many as 300,000 Ugandans are said to have perished under his brutal rule. In any catalogue of dictators of the 20th century, Amin is near the top, alongside Hitler, Pol Pot, and Stalin. 

Within Uganda, though, Amin was regarded by many as a hero: a pioneering nationalist who played a key role in re-engineering the country’s economy and expanding its international role. In this introductory course we’ll study how Amin’s regime generated support, created consensus, and unified Ugandans around the president’s program. Our focus will be on the media—radio, television, and print—by which the Amin government set the tempo of public life. We’ll explore the ‘Economic War’, by which the Amin regime expelled Indians and Pakistanis and replaced them with black businessmen. We’ll study Amin’s foreign engagements, his efforts to bring anti-imperialism home to Uganda. We’ll look at the gender politics of the Amin government. And we’ll examine the Amin government’s efforts to regulate and control religious life.

We’ll be working with a wide range of historical materials that the Amin government generated. We’ll look at the thousands of pictures made by Idi Amin’s personal photographers. We’ll listen to radio addresses made by President Amin and broadcast over Radio Uganda. We’ll watch televised film. And we’ll read though a great number of archival files created by government officials. In the latter part of the course we will learn about the onward itineraries of the thousands of South Asians who were expelled from Uganda, focusing on the work and writing of Mahmood Mamdani, the father of New York City’s charismatic new mayor. 

Course Requirements:

Three short papers, one research project, occasional quiz.

Intended Audience:

This is an introductory course, and requires no prior knowledge. 

Class Format:

Lecture and seminar discussion

Sections.title: The Era of World War I
Sections.description:
This course examines British culture and politics from 1901 through the beginning of the Second World War, with particular attention to changes in political participation and structure; cultural and political debates; changes and continuities in everyday life; technology and media; new party politics; and fascism and other histories of violence.   Throughout the course, both constitutional and cultural histories of gender, sexuality, race, ethnicity, regions, and nations (e.g. England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales as well as Britain) are explored.  It highlights how some of these histories have on-going, even urgent, relevance in the present. 

The course spends considerable time on the First World War, including how difficult it is to specify a point at which it “ended,” even a more than a hundred years later.  It also consistently engages with the relation between the history of “Britain” and the British empire, and thus raises questions about the very term “British history.”

No previous knowledge of British history is assumed or required and students from all majors are welcome.

Sections.title: Rebels and Outlaws
Sections.description:
This course examines the world of revolts, popular protests, and outlawry in medieval Europe, with a focus on England, France, Italy, and the Spanish kingdoms between the thirteenth and the fifteenth centuries. These territories witnessed a number of massive uprisings during this period, in addition to numerous minor rebellions, in which peasants and townspeople rose in arms against lords, urban elites, and other authority figures. This course examines some of these events in detail. Building on a range of primary sources, such as chronicles, courts records, and pardon letters, we will examine the circumstances in which medieval revolts broke out, the rebels' aims and ideas, the place of women in popular protests, and the connections between some rebellious movements and attacks against Jewish communities. We will also analyze the representations of revolt in medieval texts, draw connections between the figure of the rebel and that of the outlaw, and reflect on the challenges for studying popular uprisings based on sources that—more often than not—were produced by the rebels' enemies.

Sections.title: Russia and the Soviet Union
Sections.description:
From the earliest times, the polities of the East Slavs, and, later, Russia, attempted to find a way in a competitive international environment despite disadvantages and challenges. Even as the largest country in the world (by territory), the Russian Empire and then the Soviet Union were confronted by rival states that threatened -- and felt threatened by -- the colossus that stretched from central Europe to the Pacific Ocean.

Russia's modern history is of radical social experiments, the rise of a Great Power, and then the descent into defeat. Yet, this is the country that provided an influential model of a kind of state socialism, and it played a key role in defeating Nazi Germany, before becoming one of the great antagonists of the Cold War.

Another striking paradigm is that Russia, always “late to the table” in European culture, and so different in its history from Western-European cultural patterns, has, despite (perhaps, in part, because of) its evident disadvantages and its frequent claim of a distinct path, made stunning and very original contributions to world literature, music, and the arts.

This course explores the extraordinary history of the East Slavs before modern times, then of the Russian Empire, later of the Soviet Union, and now of today’s Russian Federation, with some reference to the fourteen other states that emerged in 1991 from the collapse of the Union: Ukraine, Belarus’, the countries of “Central Asia”, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and the Baltic republics.

The course is interdisciplinary; the story is told from different perspectives, through the lenses of a number of invited lecturers from various departments and schools, bringing together the methodologies of the Social Sciences and the Humanities.

The humorist Will Rogers once said, "Russia is a country that no matter what you say about it, it's true. Even if it's a lie, it's true. If it's about Russia." Come and find out what really is true and what might be false about the country that Winston Churchill famously called "a riddle wrapped in a mystery inside an enigma."

Sections.title: Women/Gender in African Hist
Sections.description:
Who were the female warriors of West Africa? How did new ideas about masculinity influence Kenyan resistance to British colonialism? What role did motherhood play in the kingdoms of ancient Uganda, and how did sex and marriage help South African kings recruit male soldiers? How have ideas about gender changed in recent times? In this class, we explore the ways historic African societies thought about gender, and about the social categories many of us take for granted: man, woman, wife, mother. Ideas about what defines a man or woman, what they can do, and how they should behave differed widely over time and between societies in African history, and some of those ideas shaped the ways communities governed, defended, and provided for themselves. This course explores the range of possibilities in African history for living as a gendered person and the ways that gendered shaped social life from food production to healing to governance.

Sections.title: The Fate of the Jews,1933-1949
Sections.description:
The Holocaust — the persecution and murder of approximately six million Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators between 1933 and 1945 — was one of the most horrific events in the history of the world. The atrocities committed in the heart of the twentieth-century threw into question the very notion of human progress, and continue to haunt humanity to this day. We have all seen images and films about the Holocaust, or have read literature and diaries from the time, but mostly we shy away from confronting the bigger questions that the Holocaust forces us to ask about ourselves and our history. This course will better equip students with the skills and knowledge they need to interpret representations of the Holocaust by grounding students with the factual basis on which these representations are made. Students will learn to interpret some of the most important historical facts about the Holocaust, to evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of contending explanations regarding the causes and effects of the Holocaust, and to contextualize the Holocaust.

Sections.title: Black Feminism(s)
Sections.description:
What is Black Feminism? In this course, we will explore the history of Black women’s gendered and racial politics in the United States and, in particular, how their beliefs and experiences have differed from other groups. How have Black women pushed back against and attempted to reshape traditional, Eurocentric, “white feminist” politics? How have Black Feminist responses to racism diverged from and challenged mainstream and Black masculinist political scripts? We will explore these questions as well as representations of Black women’s sexuality and political activism. Course readings are drawn from a variety of disciplines and time periods with the goal of exposing students to the history of Black Feminist thought and the breadth of Black Feminist scholarship, activism, and methodologies. By the end of the semester, students will be conversant in the major concepts of Black Feminism and Black Women’s Studies and have developed the analytical tools to understand how race, gender, and class interact to produce the unique experiences of Black women in the United States.

You will listen along with supplementary readings.  This course will be 2 hours weekly, as well as office hours, videos responding to student questions, videos that introduce context for assignments and readings.  Students will create discussions posts, respond to each other and Instructor, and will take collective notes on readings via Perusal. The course will follow the ADERABA podcast and students will create a podcast in teams/pairs for final assignment.

Sections.title: Hot Topics in the Talmud
Sections.description:
This is a 2 credit online course during the second half of the term.

What even is Talmud? One answer is that it's a collection of the teachings of Jewish sages living in the ancient Galilee and Iraq (ca. 1st century to 7th centuries CE). Another answer is that it's THE foundational source for "traditional" Judaism. Yet another answer is that it's a weird, wacky, surprising, fascinating, and yes sometimes boring collection of teachings and narratives about rabbis, witches, demons, and spirits; medical advice, magic, astrology, theology, "law," and more. Come, let's read this "classic" together through a number of Hot Topics: sexuality, gender, abortion, demons, ecology, magic, imperialism, race, and more. Don't worry we won't read the boring parts.

Sections.title: French Fascism: Past & Present
Sections.description:
This course offers an in-depth exploration of the evolution of fascist thought in France from the early twentieth century to the present day. Students will first examine the historical context in which fascism arose, focusing on the rise of the far-right movements in the interwar period, and the impact of World War II on French society and politics. The second half of the course delves into the far-right's evolution in the wake of the Holocaust and the decline of the French colonial empire. From there, students will learn about the present-day French far-right’s connections to American and European forms of anti-semitism, Islamophobia, anti-intellectualism, and anti-Black hatred.

Key topics will include the influence of prominent far-right figures over the past century, the role of digital and print media, and the legacy of fascist thought in post-war France. The course will also explore recent resurgences of far-right nationalism, analyzing their connections to historical fascist movements.

Learning Outcomes:

Analyze the historical development of fascism in France.
Evaluate the interplay between fascist movements and broader societal changes.
Critically assess the legacy of fascism in contemporary French political and cultural contexts.
Engage in informed discussions regarding the resurgent far-right movements in France today.

Sections.title: Hist of Amer South in Film&Lit
Sections.description:
The American South has long been an enigma: racial violence, class conflict, intraregional strife, and intolerance lay beneath a veneer of solidarity and homogeneity. This course examines the contradictions within southern society and culture through a range of novels that deal with region’s past from the colonial era to the present. Reading iconic authors will help us understand the region in all its complexity. Through class discussions, extensive reading, and the writing of short essays we will mix an understanding of history with an appreciation for literature.

Sections.title: Jews, Power, & Identity
Sections.description: This course focuses on the history of Jews in Europe and the Mediterranean region from the tenth to the seventeenth centuries, with a particular focus on their experiences as a minority group within Islamic and Christian societies. We will explore the forces and traditions that shaped Jewish life, examine the attitudes of Christians and Muslims towards Jewish communities, and analyze how Jews maintained their identity while facing exclusion and periods of persecution. Throughout the semester, students will work closely with primary sources, including court records and letters documenting the lives of ordinary Jewish individuals. Students will gain insight into how the experience of being a minority shaped the history of Jews over the span of eight centuries. No prior knowledge of Judaism or Jewish history is required.

Sections.title: Law and Empire
Sections.description:
This course provides an introduction to the study of law and empire, and focuses on the role of law in early-modern and modern European empires globally.  We approach the topic from social, cultural and legal historical perspectives and explore working with (written and unwritten) archives of law produced in a colonial context. A broad range of issues will be discussed, including custom, religious law, legal pluralism, and the construction/negotiation of racial, cultural and gender identities in the colonial legal context. We importantly center the litigants and their agency, uses of justice and legal strategies, as well as other actors of law, such as judges, clerks, and translators. We move into the various spaces where law was produced, executed, imposed and opposed, such as courtrooms, ships, swamps, borders, prisons, and banishment islands. And we examine the long-term developments and long-lasting legacies of law into the postcolonial by assessing the long histories of international law, property, and constitutions after decolonization.

Sections.title: Global Cultural Encounters
Sections.description:
What is the difference between cultural appreciation, cultural hybridity, and cultural appropriation? In this discussion-based class we will study several moments of “first encounters” between Westerners and non-Westerners from 1800 to the present. We will focus specifically on sites of encounters where different groups of people have met, ranging from a battlefield or a colonial outpost to more unconventional places such as an opera house, a science lab, a museum, a soccer field, or a restaurant.

In thinking about these encounters and the ways in which global structures intersected with and shaped local histories, we will ask a wide range of questions, including (but not limited to) the following: what conditions led to different kinds of encounters between Europeans and non-Europeans? How did these cultural encounters create possibilities for understanding or misunderstanding throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries? How have cultural encounters reshaped the arts around the world? 

By thinking critically about the function of cultural encounters throughout history, we will better understand how powerful discourses about empire, migration, race, gender, and nationality have created the world we live in today.

Course Requirements:

Papers, presentations

Sections.title: Islamic Mysticism
Sections.description: This course examines the rise, formation and subsequent development of Islamic asceticism-mysticism (Sufism). It focuses on Sufism’s practices, doctrines, literature and institutions from the 8th century C.E. up to the present. We will also discuss various approaches to Sufism by Western and Muslim academics as well as criticism of Sufi teachings and practices by some influential pre-modern Muslim theologians. We will pay special attention to the variegated sociopolitical roles that individuals and institutions associated with Sufism have played in pre-modern, modern, and contemporary Muslim societies. As far as the most recent developments are concerned, we will analyze the conflict between the “fundamentalist” (Salafi) and Sufi interpretations of Islam and the important part that it plays in current debates about Islamic “orthodoxy” and the future of Islam in Muslim societies and Muslim diaspora worldwide. Finally, we will explore the impact of Sufi teachings, practices and literary production on Western societies and cultures.

Sections.title: Treaty Ports & Col in E Asia
Sections.description:
Following China’s defeat in the Opium War (1839–42), the Treaty of Nanking forcibly opened five coastal cities to foreign trade and residency. These "treaty ports" soon multiplied, eventually spreading to Japan and Korea. Yet, while they represented a brief historical footnote for Japan and Korea, in China, they served as the primary contact zone with the West for over a century. The legacy of these ports remains deeply contentious: they were simultaneously engines of urban prosperity, contrasting sharply with the agrarian hinterland, and bastions of foreign privilege that ignited China’s first nationalist movements.

This course examines the treaty port system through both seminal and contemporary scholarship, supplemented by primary sources. While the focus remains on China from 1790 to 1950, we will integrate comparative perspectives from Japan, Korea, and Vietnam to better understand this unique era of maritime and colonial history.

Course Requirements:

Sections.title: IHP: U-M Athletics
Sections.description:
Sports at the University of Michigan are intertwined with U-M’s broader institutional history in interesting and often unexpected ways. This course sees U-M athletics as providing a window into larger phenomena and asks students to explore its deeper origins, including an assessment of the entanglements between athletics and medical science, the impact of race and gender on opportunity, and the authority of governance structures like the NCAA and the Big Ten. What can understand when we consider athletics as an object of intellectual inquiry? What do sports tell us about U-M’s past and how might sports help us develop better futures?


To answer those questions, we will be developing a podcast series and an oral history database connected to the Inclusive History Project, a presidential initiative that seeks to evaluate U-M’s institutional past with an eye to equity, with the goal of learning how to present historical research to public audiences. This course is open to undergraduates, both majors and non-majors, who have an interest in conducting historical research. It satisfies History’s Junior/Senior Colloquium requirement.


This semester, we’ll be focusing on the experiences of the first generation of athletes to experience Title IX.

Course Requirements:

Class Format:

Sections.title: Siberia!ConquestCoal&LaborCamp
Sections.description:
Siberia spreads across Eurasia, from the Ural Mountains to the Pacific Ocean. Its frozen taiga and tundra are the historical home of shamans, reindeer herders and dogsledders, the peoples of the North. It is rich in furbearing animals, diamonds, coal, nickel, and other natural resources. With their initial encounter in the sixteenth century, Russian colonizers brought death, subjugation, and environmental destruction to the region. At the same time, Siberia’s inhospitable landscape offered convenient sites for exile of criminals and political dissidents. During the Soviet period, it housed Stalin’s system of forced labor camps, the gulag. And yet, in the Russian imagination, Siberia also remains a land of freedom and opportunity, an equivalent to the US Wild West.

This course will trace the history of Siberia up to the present day. We will explore the lifeways of the people of the North, the dynamics of imperial conquest and colonization, the tensions of inter-imperial competition with China, Japan, and the United States, and the development of the exile system. We will also trace the natural riches that drew developers, and the environmental ruin that followed.

Readings will include history, anthropology, environmental studies, and fiction. The sublime landscape and the harsh world of the gulag have long inspired the greatest writers of the Russian canon: Dostoevsky, Chekhov, Solzhenitsyn, and others writing today. 

History Majors, this class fulfills the European regional distribution, and ULWR requirements.

Course Requirements:

Multiple short papers building to an extended research project.

Intended Audience:

Junior and Senior History Majors. Others are welcome, depending on availability of openings. Please contact the instructor with any questions.

Sections.title: Modern Scottish Culture
Sections.description:
The Scottish moral philosopher Adam Smith claimed that the true wealth of the nation lay in its culture; more recent writers have argued that contemporary Scottish politics, including questions about independence, have been infused or even driven by cultural activity in a variety of forms. But cultural history is not just the story of how poets, theatre-makers, musicians, engineers, architects, film-makers, and other cultural actors work and may shape political life, but also how reading, seeing, hearing, and participating in cultural activity of all kinds — from sports to churches to raves — are ways in which Scottish people think and act. A multiplicity of histories, languages, and landscapes are spaces of cultural and political work--e.g., relations between, economics and film-making, politics and science fiction, poetry and demands for Scottish independence, and revisions and rebuttals of claims about Scottishness.

In this course, we explore Scottish cultural activity from the late 19th century to the present—including imagined futures -— through literature of many kinds, visual arts of many kinds, performances of many kinds, music of many kinds, and criticism of many kinds. The shared material of the course includes drama, film, fiction, poetry, music, landscape works, creative engagements with science and technology, the visual arts, and political theory. Students will undertake research explorations which will allow them to explore and share interests. 

Course Requirements:

Sections.title: Making the Mod Mediterranean
Sections.description:
The contemporary Mediterranean region represents a critical laboratory for issues such as migration, religion, mass tourism, authoritarianism, and environmental change. This course offers students the opportunity to explore and research historical processes, such as colonialism and war, that have defined the modern Mediterranean as a key strategic zone of political, cultural and economic transition. In developing research projects tailored around their interests, students will be encouraged to think broadly about what constitutes historical sources, including visual materials (paintings, photos, films), landscapes, and oral testimonies.

Sections.title: Transnational History of Drugs
Sections.description:
This course examines the global journey of drugs, with a particular focus on the Americas and the world’s most popular narcotics. Students will explore how societies’ relationships with substances—ranging from coca and cannabis to opium and alcohol—have shifted through time and across borders. We’ll delve into the forces of trade, culture, and science that have shaped attitudes toward intoxicants, as well as how governments and communities have sought to regulate them. The course highlights the complex intersections of power, economics, and identity that drive the transnational movement of drugs. The course will also examine how major narcotics have molded history from ancient rituals to present-day debates.

Course Requirements:

This course is run like a seminar and requires student participation based on the common readings. There is a term paper (15-20 pages) based on original research due at the end of the semester. There will be a series of shorter assignments that will help students prepare to write their term paper. Additionally, students will be required to write short reading responses on weekly basis. 

Intended Audience:

This course is designed for students of any major who are interested in drugs from a historical perspective and want to improve their research and writing skills.

Sections.title: Comp Reparation in US & Europe
Sections.description:
This upper-level seminar considers the question of how we, as members of a society and nation, remember parts of our past that we would rather forget by examining two cases studies -- one close to home, the United States, and one at more of a remove, Germany. We will compare the start-stop efforts in the U.S. to grapple with the legacy of slavery with West Germany’s slow but eventual coming to terms with the Holocaust. This comparison will provide us with useful tools for teasing apart a more complicated set of ideas that often gets subsumed under the term “reparations.” We will then consider the role of history itself in the work of reckoning and explore ways to contribute to the historical understanding of institutionalized harms within our surrounding communities.

Course Requirements:

In-class writing, discussion participation, research project

Intended Audience:

History majors, students interested in Germany, the Holocaust, memory culture, the U.S., reckoning with slavery

Sections.title: Japan to 1700
Sections.description:
This course covers the complex and intriguing history of the Japanese archipelago from about 300 BCE to 1700 CE. Have you wondered if  today's tenno (emperor) really descends from the Sun Goddess; if the samurai flaunted bushido and committed harakiri; if today’s manga originates from a 12th century scroll of wrestling animals; or if there is any truth to "Ghost of Tsushima"? You might find answers for these and many other questions in this course that examines the patterns of transformation along the twin axes of time and theme in more than a millennium of premodern history of Japan.

You will learn about captivating major themes, outlined below, along the evolving timeline:

  1. prehistoric creation of land and deities; (prehistory)
  2. ancient state-making with tools from the continent; (6-8th centuries)
  3. aristocrats’ aesthetic cultural power and prestige; (8-11th centuries)
  4. political rise of the samurai; (12-14th centuries)
  5. medieval militarism supported by land and urban economy (13-15th centuries)
  6. growing gender inequity in times of violence; (14-16th centuries)
  7. rising autonomy of the commoners; (14-16th centuries)
  8. Portuguese and Spanish trader-missionaries; (16-17th centuries)
  9. country-at-war (sengoku), final peace settlement, and invasion of Korea; (16th century)
  10. unification and early modern cultural extravaganza; (16-18th centuries)
  11. environment and climate, blood and pollution, sexuality and religion, family and gender, death and dying, and cultural diversity and prestige. (throughout)
  12. new and alternative interpretations of Japanese history

Course Requirements:

Attendance, completion of reading assignments, in-class exercise, including interpretation of sources, quizzes, and final written or oral exam. Graduate students registered under HISTORY 592: an additional paper or completion of another chosen project.

Intended Audience:

Sections.title: Modern Mexico
Sections.description:
In 1821 Mexico declared independence from the Spanish crown. Yet from the dawn of nationhood through much of the twentieth century, Mexico’s polity remained profoundly divided along racial, cultural, class, and ideological lines. In recent years, the ongoing cartel-related violence, the rise in poverty, along with the effects of the Covid-19 pandemic have again exposed many of these century-old fissures. What did it mean, socially, culturally, and politically, to be a Mexican nation? This course examines the history of modern Mexico, from the end of colonialism to the recent war on drugs. It invites students to probe the roots of its internal divisions as well as the outside influences that shaped Mexico as a nation. We will immerse ourselves in the changing world of Mexicans from all walks of life using lectures and assignments that draw on an array of historical documents—from state decrees, murals, religious iconography, to popular music. Our course will also pay special attention to the crucial relationship with the United States.

This graduate section is designed to complement the undergraduate course History 363: The History of Modern Mexico. It offers PhD and MA students an introduction to significant texts and debates in Mexican historiography, alongside an exploration of the broader narrative of modern Mexican history. Additionally, students will gain insight into the organization and structure of an undergraduate lecture course through the assigned readings and course format. Attendance at both the undergraduate lectures and the weekly graduate seminar meetings is mandatory. In addition to regular attendance and active participation in seminar discussions, students are required to write, at the end of the semester, a historiographical essay (20 pages) on a topic of their choice, selected in consultation with the instructor.

Course Requirements:

Midterm, final, two short papers

Intended Audience:

Non-majors and majors

Class Format:

Sections.title: Histories of Change
Sections.description:
What is Change? How do we think about it? What do we expect? Who tells of “change” and when?

“Conversion” is a seductive idea, offering our seminar a mighty beginning, but also an invitation. We’ll explore prominent incidents of cultural and religious transformation in Late Antiquity, Medieval Europe, Spanish America and insular Asia that have contributed to —and locked us within?— powerful terms of reference. And we’ll also look to break free, expanding our vocabulary, our thinking tools and sense of possibility. We’ll consider the ways in which individual identities and group allegiances are formed and asserted even as they remain dynamic, and keep our interpretative eye trained on processes of translation, on gradual emergence and re-invention. We will move about in terms of time period and geographical space, our historical grounding drawing from an array of other disciplines to inform our interpretation of change, most notably literature, anthropology, and art history. 

A series of short, creative assignments encourage students to regard themselves —which is to say, our own lives, our own noticings, memories, and surroundings— as emergent and changing, and thus intertwined with the very transformations and tellings we discern in the past.

Course Requirements:

Series of creative assignments, explorations, and reflections, and a culminating research project

Intended Audience:

"Conversions”  is a joint offering: it is an upper-level undergraduate course (HISTORY 487), to which graduate students are also welcomed to enroll (HISTORY 594).

Sections.title: Histories of Gender in Africa
Sections.description:
When anthropologist Ifi Amadiume published Male Daughters, Female Husbands in 1987, it represented the first work of academic ethnography written by a West African woman about women and gender in West Africa. In her original introduction, Amadiume decried decades of Western scholarship, first by colonial-era ethnologists and then by modern feminists, essentializing sex roles and depicting West African society in terms of culturally-rooted patriarchy. In the decades since, scholars have sought to disrupt western frameworks and scholarship on the histories of gender in Africa have moved to explore, critique, and rewrite the roles of women, households, marriage, rites of passage, and motherhood, and, increasingly, the roles of men as gendered subjects. Recent works consider the construction and production of gender far beyond domestic realms to identify the “unmarked categories” (Lindsay and Miescher, 2003) of masculinity and femininity that appear across domains of life in historical contexts. This course surveys women’s and gender history in Africa in all regions of the continent and spanning the distant past to twentieth century. While the focus is on Africa, students from all fields are welcome. This is a readings course and culminates in a 15-20 page historiographical essay.

Sections.title: Global Slaveries
Sections.description: Orlando Patterson’s 1982 comparative book on slavery (Slavery and Social Death) drew attention to the importance of the study of global slaveries. The seminar explores this challenge in collaboration with four faculty who work on slavery in multiple geographies and temporalities. As a first iteration of the Global Slaveries Seminar, we will collectively explore the different practices and gendered constructions of the free and the unfree in the history of slavery before and after European imperialism and the Atlantic slave trade. Often told as a linear story of slavery from the Roman estate to the American plantation we will instead move thematically across the variety of forms of slavery in the Mediterranean, Africa, Middle East and Americas to reexamine our assumptions about what slavery means and how it works in five modules: Reproduction/Family/Sexuality, Labor/Law, Diaspora, Narrative & Materiality/Objects.

Sections.title: American Carceral State
Sections.description: Drawing from the latest and most cutting-edge historical scholarship on America’s carceral state –studies on the history of incarceration, prisoner rights, the war on drugs, prison labor, sentencing, policing, immigration detention, etc.--this course will ask students to look very closely at historical context and political moment when considering the origins of logics of the criminal legal system of this country, and how it evolved over time.  In addition to studying the history of American carceral state, this course also helps students to rethink current scholarly understandings of numerous other major developments in American history—everything from the origins of urban crisis, to the rise of the New Right, to the collapse of the Welfare state, to the impact of deindustrialization, to the role of privatization in America, to the rise and fall of the nation’s public education system, and so many more. In short, whether a graduate student is inherently interested in the history of crime, punishment and prisons or not, this course will get them thinking about the intellectual questions they are interested in, in new ways.

Sections.title: Conquest & Capital-Iberian Emp
Sections.description: At the end of the first volume of Capital, Marx develops the concept of primitive accumulation to explain the historical transition from feudalism to capitalism. Criticizing political economists like Adam Smith, Marx argues that this process cannot be understood as a morality tale in which everyone gets what they deserve—a diligent and frugal few become capitalists while the lazy and profligate multitudes are reduced to proletarians. Rather, the rise of capitalism is a violent history of expropriation that is “written in the annals of mankind in letters of blood and fire” (875). He goes on the explain that Spanish and Portuguese colonialism, including the conquest and colonization of the Americas as well as the transatlantic slave trade, play a key role in this process. This seminar explores this colonial dimension of primitive accumulation by engaging directly with these “letters of blood and fire” in their historical and intellectual context. After introducing the concept of primitive accumulation and some of the debates it has generated in the Marxist tradition, we will read a series of primary sources from the Iberian empires that address questions such as the justification of conquest, slavery and the slave trade, the nature of money and merchant capital. Authors may include Francisco de Vitoria, Bartolomé de las Casas, Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda, Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo, José de Acosta, Philip Nichols, Thomas Gage, and Hugo Grotius. This course will be taught in English and all readings will be available in English translation.

Sections.title: Black Hist in Washtenaw Cty
Sections.description:
This graduate research seminar is designed to enable students to develop their historical research, critical analysis, and writing skills through collaborative approaches to research methods and practices. Students will work in groups to research and write public historical narratives—pamphlets, blog posts, podcasts, online exhibits, etc.—on topics related to the history of African American communities and of racially discriminatory practices in Washtenaw County from the county’s founding in the early 19th century through to the present. On a monthly basis, students in this class will also participate in meetings of Rackham’s Reparative Justice Research Group, an interdisciplinary faculty-student collaborative. Students will also have the opportunity to contribute their research to the research group’s report on racial harms in Washtenaw County which is due to be submitted to the County Commission’s Advisory Committee on Reparations in June, 2027. Finally, graduate students in history may use this class to write a single-author research paper that fulfills one of the department’s research seminar requirements.

Research projects in this course will build on four ongoing public history initiatives:

1) The African American Cultural and Historical Museum of Washtenaw County: aachm.org

2) The Black Washtenaw County Collaboratory: blackwashtenawcounty.org

3) Justice InDeed: justiceindeedmi.org

4) South Adams Street @1900: An Historic Ypsilanti African American Neighborhood: southadamstreet1900.wordpress.com

Sections.title: Birth of the Digital
Sections.description:
How Transistors Transform Society and Science

Modern humans live in two worlds – the physical and the digital – but considering the arc of human history this duality emerged in a flash.  What happened?  In large part, a simple switching device invented in the 1940s – the transistor – is responsible for disrupting how we live and how science advances.  Transistors shrank exponentially in both size and cost since their creation, to the point where a single computer chip today has 15 times as many transistors as there are people on planet Earth.  


This introductory survey course reveals The Pattern on the Stone, the foundational elements of digital computing explained in a book of the same name by Danny Hillis, a pioneer in computing education and parallel computing.  Students are introduced to logic gates and their hierarchical organization to create computing circuits and communication networks.  Topics surveyed may include: early analog and human computers, systems and models, interoperability and standards, scaling and parallel computing, encryption and cryptography, heuristics and algorithms, Turing machines, machine learning, quantum computing, and the politics of computer chips.  Along the way, Michigan’s roles in development of computing will be highlighted.  The close relationship between computing and mathematics is revealed through a few specific examples such as the sine, power-law, and sigmoid functions.  Students will learn through readings, in-class exercises and discussions, quizzes aimed at reinforcing readings, and essays.  No prior experience with computing is needed, but prior experience with the digital is a given.

Course Requirements:

Class meetings will involve lectures combined with in-class exercises and discussion. The latter may include think-pair-share around prompts appropriate for the topic at hand. Grading will be based on a combination of assessments, including quizzes aimed at reinforcement of readings, short essays, completion of in-class exercises, and participation in class discussions.

Intended Audience:

This course seeks to attract liberal arts students interested in understanding computers but who may have little or no prior experience in computer programming. Honors 202 is open to first- and second-year students in the Honors Program only. Discussion section 002 must be taken with the lecture to count as an Honors Core course.

Sections.title: Care, Control, & Institutions
Sections.description:
Why do institutions that promise care—schools, hospitals, shelters, zoos, and prisons—also regulate behavior, enforce norms, and manage risk? This seminar examines the complex relationship between care and control in modern institutions. Using tools from the social sciences, students will investigate how institutional policies, training materials, mission statements, and everyday administrative language shape how people are categorized, managed, and understood.

Rather than treating institutions as neutral systems, the course asks students to analyze them as sites of power, decision-making, and social organization. Through case studies drawn from education, medicine, criminal justice, and animal institutions, we will explore questions such as: What does it mean for an institution to “care” for someone? How do rules and policies construct ideas about safety, responsibility, and risk? And how do institutional practices shape the identities and experiences of the people—and animals—within them?

The seminar introduces students to influential thinkers who have studied institutions and social power, including works by Michel Foucault, Erving Goffman, and Dorothy E. Smith. Alongside these readings, we will examine cultural portrayals of life inside institutions through memoir, film, and contemporary media. Possible works include Dead Poets Society, The Shawshank Redemption, The Spirit Catches You and You Fall Down, Blackfish, One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest and Girl, Interrupted.

Course Requirements:

Designed as a small Honors seminar, the course emphasizes discussion, collaborative inquiry, and methodological reflection, offering students an opportunity to explore how social scientists study institutions and how critical analysis can illuminate the systems that structure everyday life.

Intended Audience:

First- and second-year students in LSA Honors Program. This course is not open to students outside of the LSA Honors Program.

Class Format:

Assignments emphasize both theory and method. Students will conduct an institutional artifact analysis (examining documents such as mission statements, intake forms, or codes of conduct), complete a comparative case study exploring the relationship between stated institutional values and everyday practices, and develop a policy or genre rewrite designed to make visible the tensions between care, authority, and responsibility.

Sections.title: Around Wrld 15wks: Politics
Sections.description: This course examines some of the world’s most pressing political and social issues and key concepts in international studies and human geography. From the comfort of our seminar room, we will explore the world in fifteen weeks by focusing on different issues in different world regions. Students will investigate themes including: migration, urbanization, environmentalism, political economy, and globalization. A series of case studies ground our planetary explorations. Stories from the Mediterranean Sea will challenge us to think about migration and nationalism. Break dancers and ecologists in South Africa, will push us to reflect on the legacies of colonialism. Documentary film and fiction from Southeast Asia will shed an intimate light on the inequities of an urbanizing world. Treks into the Amazon will allow us to ask critical questions about environmental justice. At once global, regional, and local, this seminar will deepen our understanding of the global processes that impact people's everyday lives.

Sections.title: Digital Futures
Sections.description:
Our futures seem increasingly digital. From politics to work, from romance to family, people around the world are grappling with how digital media technologies seep into the nooks and crannies of their everyday lives. The dominance of the digital both provokes panic about the harmful corporate and political forces they are unleashing and inspires hope about the capacity of activists to create better futures. In either case, the emphasis is on the power of technology. But how do communities and social movements around the world think and do about digital media’s promises or perils? This course goes beyond both the hysteria and the hype to examine the global social life and futures of digital technologies.

What assumptions about self and society do technology workers and corporations encode as universally valid and “culture-free”? What role do media play in shaping our collective sense of what is beautiful, true, or just? How are digital technologies implicated in shoring up racist systems or in creating space for resisting them? How is AI enabling ethno-nationalism and state violence against minorities around the world?

Each week, we answer these questions through reading about concrete case studies from a wide array of global contexts, from the Philippines to Iran to India as well as the United States, and by viewing and discussing documentaries about media worlds and experiences. Throughout, we explore what an anthropological, people-centered approach offers to understand our digital futures.

*This course will meet together with ANTHRCUL 237

Intended Audience:

This class is open to students from all majors, has no prerequisites, and non-majors would not be at any disadvantage.

Sections.title: Social Media in India & the US
Sections.description:
What is the relationship between artistic modernism and political independence? How did the creation of new nation states transform the art institutional landscape across South Asia? What kinds of relationships between form and politics emerged in the wake of significant events like the Partition of India? These are just some of the questions we will explore in this course, as we study artistic practices as well as the institutions and networks of modernism in the Subcontinent following the end of colonial rule. We will critically interrogate the position of the postcolonial artist, and how larger socio-political developments interacted with formal expression and the choice of materials.

The role and development of technologies of production and circulation will be underscored, as will the changing contexts of patronage and exhibition. We will conclude at the turn of the century, evaluating the conditions for the proliferation of 'postmodernist' practices across media, while diagnosing the advent of the so-called "global contemporary." The course will provide both theoretical tools and significant case studies in analyzing relationships between politics and artistic form.

Sections.title: Conflict, Violence, & War
Sections.description:
This is an advanced course for undergraduate students in political science and international studies. The course will introduce students to key topics, theories, analytical approaches and empirical findings in conflict studies. We take a global view and discuss what we know about the causes, dynamics and consequences of different form of political violence, such as war, state repression, revolutions, and terrorism. We will look at how various questions have been answered within international relations and comparative politics, such as: Why do wars break out? Why do states repress? Why do people join insurgencies? Is the world becoming more peaceful or more violent? How and why does political violence vary in form and severity across time, space and between different actors? What are some of the consequences of political violence and war for states, communities, and individuals? What stops violence and war in the international system and within countries? We will draw on examples of historical and contemporary conflicts and discuss broader international patterns of violence over time. The course will have a combination of lectures and discussion sessions.

Sections.title: International Cinema
Sections.description:
Are you bored with movies based on spectacular effects, unimaginative scripts, and expected morality conclusions? If you seek more challenge for your intellect, this course will keep you on your toes for most of the semester. This course will expose you to some of the most relevant, beautiful, and unexpected international films of the 20th and 21st centuries, from 1945 to the present day. We will screen and discuss the complex, intriguing, and sometimes unsettling topics that these films raise, like social restraints and expectations, intimate desires, or prohibited emotions - things that make us human, but whose social control frequently contributes to our discontent, or even unhappiness.

Why is it important to discuss emotions and their suppression today? In the world that creates an imperative of enjoyment and pleasure in service of capitalist consumption, while being entirely dismissive of their complexities, we will focus on the cinematic narratives that place them in their center, and discuss them alongside intellectual texts that attempt to explain our confusion with our reality.

Films include: In the Mood for Love (Hong Kong, 2000), Drive My Car (Japan, 2021), Raise the Red Lantern (China, 1997), Separation (Iran, 2011).

Theorists we will read include Ahmed, Foucault, Berlant, Massumi, and others.

This class will meet together with COMPLIT 362.001.

Course Requirements:

Most assignments will include an active incorporation of AI, and testing of its abilities. 

No mid-terms, no final exam. Final project envisioned as a group presentation.

Participation in class discussions expected of all students. 

Testing: super easy online pop-up quizzes related to film content.

Sections.title: Dismantle Discourse Discovery
Sections.description:
During the 15th to 18th centuries, Europeans made direct ties to Africa, the Americas, and Asia-an era known as the “Age of Discovery.” They profited from imported goods and ideas. Scientific “discovery” was an instrument of imperial domination, and a justification for colonial efforts as benevolent. What was the European worldview in the early modern period that enabled this behavior and approach? What knowledge was imported to Europe, what was left behind? What purposes - commercial, scientific, and ideological - did these so-called “discoveries” serve? And how did the advancement of Natural History itself act as a justification for further colonial projects? This course will discuss what we know of the indigenous knowledge before contact, which Indigenous ideas Europeans rejected and/or exploited and why, and how the import of plants, medicines, foods, etc., altered life back in Europe. We will work with ancient and early modern texts, images, and collections (i.e., Wunderkammer), critiquing the rhetorical approach of “Discovery” and its lingering presence in the legacy of Humanities as an intellectual and academic pursuit today.

This course will meet together with RCHUMS 315.001

Sections.title: Sports in German Culture
Sections.description:
This course investigates the cultural significance of sports from the early 1800s (Turnvater Jahn) until today. We will explore the transition in interest from Turnen (gymnastics) to Fußball (soccer) as the most popular sports, and look at the history of German soccer from its local origins to the 2024 European Championships in Germany and the 2026 World Cup in the US, Canada, and Mexico. As recent disruptions during German league games continue to show, soccer fandom has also become a protest movement. We will examine the goals of these movements and look at the financial structure of league teams. Furthermore, we will address critical themes like diversity and inclusion in soccer while we also investigate the persistence of nationalism among fans. While soccer with its various tournaments will be the primary athletic discipline under discussion, we will also look at the Olympic games (1936, 1972) and their geopolitical context. Through the lens of sport, you will study the culture and history of one of the world’s most important countries, and you will acquire a solid knowledge of Germany today.

This course will meet together with GERMAN 303.001

Sections.title: Globalizing Consumer Cultures
Sections.description:
Consumer culture is now a global and transnational phenomenon, with people increasingly defining themselves through their consumer choices. Ever rising standards of living are also shared across more affluent populations globally, breaching environmental boundaries, even as almost half of the global population lives in poverty, unable to consume enough for their well-being. 

What do we mean by "consumption" and where are we headed as a consumer society? How does it change who we are and how we live? To answer these questions, we will draw on anthropological approaches to gift exchange, the commodity and commoditization, the body, and social/class distinctions. We will also look at the role of advertising and branding as cultural phenomenon — in places as similar and adverse as India, Hungary, South Korea, Vietnam, and Sweden. Several weeks of the course will be devoted to consumer cultures in the former Soviet states of Eastern Europe and Cuba. We will also discuss the role of consumption in religious practice, in environmental movements, and in the search for well-being. 

The course will introduce students to qualitative ethnographic methods, as well as to contextualizing social processes within political and economic shifts. 

This class will meet together with ANTHRCUL 328.001

results.title: Topics in International Security, Norms and Cooperation

Sections.title: International Security Affairs
Sections.description:
This course provides an overview of the main theories and issues in international security. This class discusses major events and trends in international security and draws on examples from current affairs. We will start with the approaches to the study of international security.

The second part examines the causes and consequences of war. We then discuss alliances, nuclear weapons, and terrorism. The class concludes with US grand strategy and international order. Upon completion of this course, students will be familiar with the theoretical frameworks that underpin contemporary political issues and apply these theories to current events.

* This course will meet together with POLSCI 372.001

Sections.title: International Organization
Sections.description:
This course provides an overview of the theory and function of international organizations. We begin with a review of the historic origins of the international system, paying attention to the establishment and role of international institutions. We then consider how international organizations may be useful and how these international organizations may influence state behavior. As we examine various international organizations, we ask the following questions: What are the obligations that countries take on when they join the IO? How do international politics and domestic politics affect the operations of the IO? What powers of enforcement does the organization have? The primary purpose of this course is to provide students with the analytical tools necessary to understand and assess current events and their impacts. Upon the completion of this course, students should have a strong knowledge of international organizations.

Course Requirements:

Evaluation will be based on regular participation in class discussion, individual presentation, assignments, midterm, and a final group project.

Sections.title: Gender, War, and Peace
Sections.description:
It is often observed that migration is at a historic high. But journalistic accounts tend to recycle old tropes without bringing new insight. This course considers the refugee experience from three very different perspectives in order to arrive at a deeper, more balanced, and holistic understanding. One perspective is that of asylum seekers and refugees themselves. Course readings therefore include the poetry, short stories, and autobiographical writings. A second perspective is that derived from government speeches and documents. A third perspective is provided by intergovernmental organizations that aim to manage migration. How do the metaphors, imagery, narrative tropes, and rhetorical strategies compare across these diverse sources? What gaps in understanding can be filled by considering all three types of sources? Course evaluation will be based on active participation in the seminar, two papers, and a group case study. As a result of taking this course, students will gain a more holistic understanding of international migration; acquire skills in analyzing various discourses; and be able to identify the tensions between how migrants see themselves and how they are seen by others.

Intended Audience:

International Studies Majors and Minors.

Sections.title: Global Politics of Work
Sections.description:
Aimed at advanced undergraduate and graduate students (400/500-level), this course will explore these questions by drawing on academic literature and practical case studies on bureaucratic reform from all over the world. We will examine reform efforts across a wide range of parts of government, from the core civil service to education, health, tax, regulation, environmental management, and other sectors. Our reading and discussion will seek to learn lessons spanning from the earliest creation of professionalized state bureaucracies in antiquity to the introduction of new management philosophies, digital tools, and artificial intelligence into the governments of today – as well as the many transformations public service institutions around the world have undergone in between.

*This course will meet together with ORGSTUDY 495.001.

Sections.title: Law and Empire
Sections.description:
This course explores the reconstruction of public health as a central factor for domestic and international actors to address in postwar transitions. First, we will examine how violence on the battlefield has direct and indirect effects on the health of individuals in the postwar era. War directly affects individuals overall well-being, ranging from the physical traumas suffered to the emergence of infectious diseases and mental problems. Civilians and soldiers alike suffer the short-term risks of morbidity and mortality when they cannot access basic nutrition, water, or health services. The next part of the course turns to the indirect effects, that the conflict has likely diminished or eliminated the underlying social systems and institutions that provided the population with basic health care services. The long-term costs include the diversion of essential resources to the fight and the massive rebuilding costs of the infrastructure to promote basic health outcomes. Finally, the course will consider whether the provision of public health and the attending professionals can reduce the likelihood of a return to violence. Examples covered in the course will include Syria, the former Yugoslavia, Uganda, and Sierra Leone.

In the course, students will critically assess various theoretical and policy perspectives to address the health consequences of fighting to arrive at a broader understanding of possible intervention strategies to restore a society’s well being.

Course Requirements:

INTLSTD 401 has no testing components. All assignments are written papers and will be submitted via Canvas throughout the semester.

Intended Audience:

International Studies Majors and Minors

Class Format:

We will have biweekly discussion sessions that require participation in various conversations. The course will also include short videos for students to watch at their convenience, prior to certain discussions and assignments.

Sections.title: Colonialism&Cultural Identity
Sections.description:
This course explores how the specific cultural identities of the colonizer and the colonized are produced by the colonial system and how the meaning of these cultural identities persist and change after formal decolonization has occurred. Students will examine the three colonial ideologies of global white supremacy throughout the semester: orientalism in the Middle East and Eurasia; anti-black racism in Africa and the Caribbean; and the anti-indigenous racism of settler colonialism. This course concludes by looking at the political project of formal decolonization and its implications for contemporary decolonized cultural identities in the present and future.

*This course will meet together with POLSCI 489

Intended Audience:

International Studies Majors and Minors

Sections.title: PoliticalEconGlbalCapitalism
Sections.description:
This course explores the fundamental strategies of capitalist imperialism, aiming to equip students with a political and economic understanding of the pressing challenges of global inequality we face today. Students will explore key concepts such as colonialism and neo-colonialism, global wages, the international division of labor, global trade, technology transfers, global finance and debt, foreign aid, and climate resources. Additionally, this course will delve into the anti-imperialist strategies that shed light on alternative international practices that can reduce global inequality.

Intended Audience:

International Studies Majors and Minors

Sections.title: Humanitarian Dilemmas
Sections.description:
This course follows the development of humanitarian action from its inception to the present. Today, we are witnessing a major transformation of humanitarian action. The geopolitical changes unfolding from the end of the Cold War and the global war on terrorism have profoundly shifted the environment in which humanitarian actions and interventions take place. These changes—and proposed ways of responding to them—are triggering heated debates about both philosophical and operational issues within the humanitarian community. Long-held principles, such as neutrality and impartiality are being questioned and at times even discarded. The range of humanitarian actors has broadened to include celebrities and for-profit firms. Some scholars contend that it is time to rethink the enterprise. Others believe that the present is not a time that calls for reconsidering basic principles. This class will challenge students to consider the basic principles, analytical frameworks, and activities required to protect the lives and dignity of people affected by crisis and conflict.

Intended Audience:

International Studies Majors and Minors.

Sections.title: Global Cultural Encounters
Sections.description:
Since the Age of Revolutions, various forms of transnational social justice advocacy have shaped the development of international law in the Americas. This course will trace the history of movements calling for shared understandings and regional protection of human rights. We will consider first the relationship between local and transnational social movements and diplomacy in the first half of the twentieth century, focusing particularly on the creation of the Inter-American Commission (and later, Court) on Human Rights (IACHR) in 1959. We will then trace the IACHR’s work and evaluate its impact, considering particularly its relationship to the work of human rights movements in the hemisphere during and after the Cold War.

In the final unit of the course, students will present actual cases that have been adjudicated by the IACHR in the twenty-first century, considering the intersecting roles of local and transnational social movements and international institutions in building inter-American human rights law. Topics may include torture and forced disappearance; political rights and freedom of speech; human trafficking and contemporary slavery; violence against women; reproductive rights; indigenous rights and racial discrimination; LGBTQ+ rights; and the rights of migrants and refugees.
Across Latin America, the IACHR became a touchstone for grass-roots groups and NGOs that struggled to build democratic societies in the final decades of the twentieth century, and then to pressure new democratic regimes to live up to their promise of social justice. Over the past decade, some nationalist regimes of both left and right have rejected universal norms and international institutions and sidelined or even repudiated the IACHR. It is a critical moment to reflect on its history.

*This course will meet together with HISTORY 407.001

Course Requirements:

Weekly online responses to readings, two group presentations, two short papers on the topic of the presentation (3-4 pages), and a final 5-page paper.

Sections.title: RacialAttitudes US&Arnd Wrld
Sections.description:
This seminar on racial attitudes is designed to examine the various controversies that surround the role of race or ethnicity in American society and in various countries around the world. For example, what is the source of our attitudes about race and racial policies? Are prejudices and negative stereotypes the result of pre-adult socialization? Or are they motivated by a desire to protect the privileges of the in-group and to preserve their position in the socio-economic hierarchy? What roles do societal elites (e.g., politicians, media figures, etc.) play in shaping racial attitudes? How, and under what circumstances, are racial attitudes associated with candidate preferences and policy preferences? How can racial animosities be diminished? How have racial attitudes changed overtime? This course will seek to answer these questions while also exploring the historical antecedents of racial conflict in the US, and internationally.

This class will meet together with POLSCI 496.002

Sections.title: Conflict-RelatedSexualViolence
Sections.description:
This course examines causes, dynamics, and consequences of sexual violence in repression and armed conflict. Sexual violence can be part of many types of political conflicts and repression, and affects both women, men, and children. This type of violence has also been recognized as an international security issue, and as atrocity crimes. How and why did the international community start to take this issue seriously, and how has the attention to this issue changed over time? How prevalent is conflict-related sexual violence globally? Which states and insurgents engage in sexual violence? What are the causes and consequences of conflict-related sexual violence? How can we prevent, stop sexual violence, or at least reduce such atrocities? These are some of the key questions in this course. Sexual violence can be a particularly difficult topic to study due to the sensitive nature of these crimes and the taboos surrounding them. This creates research challenges and ethical dilemmas, as well as challenges pertaining to how we think about justice and recovery. We will discuss various dilemmas and challenges, and how they might affect analyzes of conflict-related sexual violence.

This is a writing intensive course. Students will do several writing assignments over the course of the semester to practice critical research skills, academic writing, and writing for a wider audience.

Students will become familiar with US foreign policy toward China, US Cross-Strait policy, and Cross-Strait relations. By the end of the course, students should have a strong knowledge base about US-China-Taiwan relations, and be able to identify key elements and assess contemporary political events.

Met together with POLSCI 489. 013

Students are expected to participate in class discussions and presentations.
