Sections.title: The First 700 Years
Sections.description:
At the beginning of the 7th century, a new religion, Islam, appeared in Arabia and by the end of the century, Muslims had defeated the Byzantines and Persians and created an empire that stretched from Spain to India. For the next millennium, Islam glittered. Its caliphs, courts, and capitals were grander, more powerful, and more sophisticated than those of any medieval king, duke, or prince. In this course, we will trace the emergence and development of Islamic civilization from the birth of Muhammad, ca. 570, to the Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258. We will read the Qur’an and listen to its recitation; examine the career of the Prophet Muhammad; follow the course of the Arab conquests; explore the nature of the conflict between Sunnis and Shi?is; learn about the five pillars of Islam, law, theology, and Sufism; and assess the achievements of Muslim intellectuals in literature, art, science, and philosophy. 30 minutes at the end of each class will be devoted to the analysis of primary sources in English translation.  

This course pursues the following goals: a) to provide a comprehensive idea of the rise and early evolution of Islam and of the subsequent impact that Islamic doctrinal principles have had on the cultures and societies of the Muslim world and beyond; b) to show the amazing diversity of Islam’s interpretation and application by its followers across time and geographical space; c) to demonstrate the profound complexity and ambiguity of interaction between the world of Islam and Western societies. Finally, yet importantly, the course is designed in such a way as to foster in students' analytic skills through composing clearly reasoned responses to the topics covered in the course and critically discussing assigned readings. The ultimate goal of the course is to assist students in orienting themselves to the vast sea of information about Islam and Muslims and to enable them to form a balanced, fact-based and, to the extent possible, objective understanding of the complex subject. No previous knowledge required.

Course Requirements:

One-page essays (10%), Section participation (10%), Midterm I (20%), Midterm II (20%), and Final exam (40%)

Intended Audience:

Undergraduate students interested in the history, religions, and cultures of the Muslim world.

Class Format:

Two 90-minute meetings weekly.

It offers you a snapshot of contemporary Italy by exposing you to podcasts, video clips, and films; all while strengthening your grammatical skills and practicing real life situations. In each module you will be asked to practice looking for an apartment in Italy, writing formal emails, expressing your opinion about contemporary issues, writing a cover letter, preparing a resume, and looking for internships in non-profit organizations.

Sections.title: Ital Love Music-Opera to Trap
Sections.description:
How does music shape national identity? When does a song become a political act? And why does Italy so often sing its revolutions before living them? This course explores Italian music as both a cultural barometer and prophetic voice. We begin with opera and the Risorgimento, examining how composers such as Verdi became entwined with nationalist sentiment and political imagination. From there, we move through protest songs, canzone napoletana, postwar reconstruction and the rise of the cantautori, the cultural politics of Sanremo, the liberatory energies of disco and feminist movements, and the negotiations of migration, national identity, and globalization in contemporary pop and trap. Central to the course are weekly linguistic workshops dedicated to close work with song lyrics. Students will analyze vocabulary, syntax, metaphor, dialect, and register, unpacking how meaning is constructed across genres and historical moments. The course builds toward a collaborative final project in which students select a genre studied during the semester and creatively reinterpret it for the present.

Sections.title: Creation Myths
Sections.description: Where did the world come from, how did it come to be the way it is, and what is our purpose in it? Several stories in Genesis, the first book of the Bible, engage with these questions: the creation myth(s), Adam and Eve, Noah’s Ark, the Tower of Babel, and others. These stories often seem timeless today, but they have a history. Their authors drew on texts and traditions from elsewhere in the Near East, mostly Mesopotamia, reshaping them in fundamental ways and creating new and often revolutionary ideas about God, humankind, and the universe. This course is about reading famous Biblical stories together with their much less famous ancient Near Eastern counterparts, giving the Bible some historical context, and thinking about how stories can change and why that matters.

Sections.title: Russian Jews under Tsars & Sov
Sections.description:
More than a hundred years ago the Yiddish writer Sholem Aleichem wrote a series of stories about Tevye and his family. Today Tevye is famous all around the world as the protagonist of Fiddler on the Roof. In our class we will discuss the original text and its various screen adaptations, trying to understand how a sad story of a humble Jewish dairyman from a Ukrainian village at the turn of the twentieth century has become a heart-warming musical hit with a universal appeal. All materials and discussions will be conducted in English, no knowledge of Yiddish or Judaism is required.

Course Requirements:

The class will meet synchronously once a week on-line via Zoom. Assignments include response questions, quizzes and participation in discussion groups. Attendance is required.

Sections.title: French Fascism: Past & Present
Sections.description:
This course offers an in-depth exploration of the evolution of fascist thought in France from the early twentieth century to the present day. Students will first examine the historical context in which fascism arose, focusing on the rise of the far-right movements in the interwar period, and the impact of World War II on French society and politics. The second half of the course delves into the far-right's evolution in the wake of the Holocaust and the decline of the French colonial empire. From there, students will learn about the present-day French far-right’s connections to American and European forms of anti-semitism, Islamophobia, anti-intellectualism, and anti-Black hatred.

Key topics will include the influence of prominent far-right figures over the past century, the role of digital and print media, and the legacy of fascist thought in post-war France. The course will also explore recent resurgences of far-right nationalism, analyzing their connections to historical fascist movements.

Learning Outcomes: 

Analyze the historical development of fascism in France.
Evaluate the interplay between fascist movements and broader societal changes.
Critically assess the legacy of fascism in contemporary French political and cultural contexts.
Engage in informed discussions regarding the resurgent far-right movements in France today.

Sections.title: Partners in Learning
Sections.description:
This skills- and practice-based course prepares students to lead and facilitate effective conversations in collaborative settings. Students develop practical communication and leadership skills for running meetings, guiding group processes, and organizing dialogue to achieve goals such as creative exploration, problem-solving, decision-making, and team building.

Drawing in part on the Pedagogy of Partnership, a relational learning framework that emphasizes shared responsibility, attentive listening, and collaborative meaning-making, the course treats communication not only as presentation but as facilitation: the ability to structure conversations, engage participants, and move groups productively through disagreement, uncertainty, and complexity.

Sections.title: Hasidism
Sections.description:
This course traces the emergence of Hasidism from its eighteenth-century origins in Eastern Europe to its contemporary global presence, with particular attention to its mystical theology and its evolution into a major force within modern Orthodox Judaism. At the heart of the course is the vibrant world of Hasidic storytelling—narratives and hagiographic tales that open a window onto Hasidic society, models of piety, and the cultivation of joy in everyday life. We will also examine distinctive material expressions of Hasidism, from ritual objects and dress—such as the public Chabad menorah and the shtreimel—to the ways these forms respond to shifting historical, cultural, and political realities.

Through music, ritual practice, and lived experience, students will explore how Hasidism has sustained a dynamic religious culture and become one of the most influential Jewish movements of the modern era.

Sections.title: The Nazis and Art
Sections.description:
This course investigates the Nazis and the art they promoted, demeaned, destroyed, and plundered for purposes of propaganda, racism, power, and financial gain. We will explore the role of art critics who viewed modern art as a sign of the sickness and depravity of society and its artists, and will focus upon film, architecture, painting, and sculpture. Nazi plunder and the activities of the Monuments Men who searched for the stolen treasures takes us on a path of discovery, reading much like a detective story. False definitions of Aryan supremacy emerge from the fascinating study of Pseudo-Archaeology, imitated in popular culture by the "Raiders of the Lost Ark." The 1937 Munich exhibitions of Great German and Degenerate Art underscores how art was used to convey the racial hatred of Jews, Blacks, Asians, and homosexuals. Issues evolving from the Nazi looting of art and its restitution are explored through the study of legal case studies; and the course concludes with a debate on repatriation, an issue that looms large today in the museum world. One field trip to the Detroit Institute of Arts is an optional delight.

Sections.title: Hot Topics in the Talmud
Sections.description:
This is a 2 credit online course during the second half of the term.

What even is Talmud? One answer is that it's a collection of the teachings of Jewish sages living in the ancient Galilee and Iraq (ca. 1st century to 7th centuries CE). Another answer is that it's THE foundational source for "traditional" Judaism. Yet another answer is that it's a weird, wacky, surprising, fascinating, and yes sometimes boring collection of teachings and narratives about rabbis, witches, demons, and spirits; medical advice, magic, astrology, theology, "law," and more. Come, let's read this "classic" together through a number of Hot Topics: sexuality, gender, abortion, demons, ecology, magic, imperialism, race, and more. Don't worry we won't read the boring parts.

Sections.title: Hot Topics in Jewish Studies
Sections.description:
THIS IS A 1-CREDIT ASYNCHRONOUS COURSE FOR THE FIRST HALF OF THE TERM.

Come explore hot topics and conversations in Jewish Studies while learning about podcasting. We will consider issues such as reproduction, gender, environmentalism, law and religion, the state and nationalism, Judaism and the “West,” and more in this class. Each class will follow an episode of the  ADERABA podcast. You will listen along with supplementary readings.  This course will be 2 hours weekly, as well as office hours, videos responding to student questions, videos that introduce context for assignments and readings.  Students will create discussions posts, respond to each other and Instructor, and will take collective notes on readings via Perusal. The course will follow the ADERABA podcast and students will create a podcast in teams/pairs for final assignment.

Sections.title: The Fate of the Jews,1933-1949
Sections.description:
The Holocaust — the persecution and murder of approximately six million Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators between 1933 and 1945 — was one of the most horrific events in the history of the world. The atrocities committed in the heart of the twentieth-century threw into question the very notion of human progress, and continue to haunt humanity to this day. We have all seen images and films about the Holocaust, or have read literature and diaries from the time, but mostly we shy away from confronting the bigger questions that the Holocaust forces us to ask about ourselves and our history. This course will better equip students with the skills and knowledge they need to interpret representations of the Holocaust by grounding students with the factual basis on which these representations are made. Students will learn to interpret some of the most important historical facts about the Holocaust, to evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of contending explanations regarding the causes and effects of the Holocaust, and to contextualize the Holocaust.

Course Requirements:

Students will be evaluated on the basis of quizzes, writing assignments, and exams.

Intended Audience:

No data submitted

Class Format:

The course will be structured as a lecture with discussions.

This course considers the nature and evolutionary origin of laughter and of humor, especially rough humor and its relationships to identity, gender, death, and violence. Sections.title: Figurative Language
Sections.description:
In this discussion-based course, we will be examining the linguistic and psychological properties of figurative language. Idioms (hang out, hot dog, bite the dust), metaphors (Juliet is  the sun), and the like are not marginal phenomena confined to poetry or literature, but are  ubiquitous both in writing and in everyday conversation. Indeed, it has been estimated that  speakers use an average of four idioms and two novel metaphors in every minute of speech, and  that there are as many fixed expressions in English as there are ordinary words. Clearly,  figurative language is central to a great deal of actual language behavior, yet it is rarely discussed  extensively outside of the humanities. 

This semester, we will consider figurative language from many different perspectives,  beginning with exploring whether “literal” and “figurative” language indeed constitute distinct  phenomena, and if so, where we should draw the line between them. We will then spend  significant time on metaphors, idioms, and proverbs, as well as closely associated concepts such  as sarcasm, irony, and (verbal) humor. Along the way, we will consider morphological,  syntactic, semantic, and pragmatic aspects of figurative language, including experimental work  on how figurative language is processed in the mind; we will conclude by considering social  aspects of figurative language, including its role in societal and interpersonal discourse.

Sections.title: Dissecting Fear
Sections.description:
This class is about facing fear. What are you so afraid of? Things that go bump in the night. The monster. The witch. The dark forest. The old house and its creaking corners. But for what ends is our fear used? Why is our culture so preoccupied with the horror? What are the cultural values, imaginations, superstitions, and historic resonances that inform our fears? Is the horror real, or is it imagined? And perhaps the most pressing question of all: When we face the horrors of our cultural production, are we better able to face the horrors of our reality? In the words of Toni Morrison, “It is not so much that I’m afraid to face my fears, but that I fear what they reveal about me.” This course aims to do just that, to unmask the social commentary around our shared nightmares, and push us to engage with our deepest wells of thought in order to confront what lies beyond the shadowy edges of our perception, the things we would rather look away from. We will do all of this to better understand our human fears, desires, and atmosphere of fright. By dissecting fear we will become stronger scholars and writers, and dare I say, we may even become brave.

In this first year writing course, we will investigate these questions and more by primarily interacting with the genre of horror through fiction and film, often by placing our findings in conversation with historical documents and contemporary journalism. We’ll engage with short stories by Mariana Enriquez, Shirley Jackson, and others. We'll also engage with film, including contemporary horror pictures as well as horror classics. We will read theory and critique that will ground us in our understandings, and better equip you to respond to these fantasies of fear. This course takes an anti-racist approach—we will make it a point to question our biases and examine how dimensions of fear are impacted by who is telling the story, and who is afraid. In this way we will examine the historic links between fear and systemic imbalances of power. This course will guide you through all phases of the writing process, gaining you the necessary skill to locate and propel your personal voice (a powerful thing, nothing to fear in finding it!) to its ultimate potential, preparing you to communicate effectively not only with academic audiences, but across venues.

Intended Audience:

Participants in Lloyd Scholars for Writing and the Arts. Non-LSWA students welcome and may request permission to enroll pending availability. Contact LSWA@umich.edu.

Sections.title: Exploring Nature Writing
Sections.description:
This section of LSWA 125 will focus on nature writing. We will read artistically-inclined essays, poems, and short fiction that focus on humans’ connection to nature – a connection which is stereotyped as meditative and restorative but can also be exploitative, harsh, or threatening.

Our discussions will focus on the rhetorical goals of these writers. What do they want us to feel or think about nature? In what ways are their pieces advocacy pieces? How do these writers interact with science, if they do at all – are they representing botany, ecology, etc. explicitly? Faithfully? Or do they use science as a springboard to magical thinking or fantasy?

As part of the class, we will take short field trips to nearby parks.

Assignments in the class will include rhetorical analysis, reflections, and an original piece of nature writing designed by the student.

Intended Audience:

Participants in Lloyd Scholars for Writing and the Arts. Non-LSWA students welcome and may request permission to enroll pending availability. Contact LSWA@umich.edu.

Sections.title: Writing Genres
Sections.description:
We've grown so comfortable with algorithms predicting our preferences (sometimes unnervingly - looking at you, TikTok and Spotify Wrapped) that we overlook the strangeness of what the algorithms are predicting. They don't work without categories, and when it comes to art, particularly narrative art, categories can prove slippery and odd. But they can also entrance and illuminate! Noir, fantasy, romantic comedy, conspiracy thrillers, sports anime, horror, coming-of-age, isekai: we take categories like these for granted when we talk about film or literature, but what (if anything) do they have to do with how we imagine and narrate our own lives? In this section of LSWA 125, we will examine genre: what it means, why it must exist, whether anything exists outside of it, and how we use it to construct experience and knowledge as consumers, scholars, and people just trying to make sense of it all. Genres will elude us, and genres will even shift and transform into each other, but genres will also give us a glimpse into the history of ideas as well as history itself. Writing about genres will not only deepen your engagement with all sorts of texts, it will introduce you to larger and richer conversations about culture, art, and belief. Texts will include both literature and multimedia references both high and low, common and obscure, and skills will be developed in analysis, argument, narrative, multimodal techniques, and writing into and across academic curricula. You'll also have a chance to familiarize yourself with local purveyors and analysts of genre in all its forms! Tolerance for stylistic excess is encouraged but not required.

Sections.title: From Kansas to Munchkin Land
Sections.description:
Close your eyes and imagine that you were born completely without sight.  Now imagine that your sight was miraculously restored.  What would you “see”? Look at your hand and wiggle your fingers.  Is this what you expected your hand to look like?   Would you be able to comprehend the world around you or would everything be such a confusing mass of shapes, lines, colors, and textures that you would feel overwhelmed by the complexity of it all? 

In this course we will demystify the art of seeing.  Learning to draw and paint requires you to look at the world more closely and to record what you see more accurately.  Learning to see, not what you “think” you see, but what you actually see, is the key that can unlock the door to your inner vision.  Once you can access visual phenomena through drawing and painting you will find out how much there is to see and how complex and beautiful the world around you truly is.

During the first half of this course you will expand your visual literacy skills through focused drawing and painting exercises. For the second half you’ll be making your own original artwork based on research using primary works from the University of Michigan Museum of Art’s extensive collection.

No previous experience is necessary, however students will be expected to possess a positive attitude, willingness to learn from others, and a strong work ethic.

Note:  Mandatory attendance and active class participation required. Expect extensive outside work on homework assignments. Museum trips (TBA) will be required. This course satisfies LSWA course requirements for Fall 2026; however, this course is not limited to LSWA students—if you are not a member of LSWA please reach out to the instructor for an override. This course also satisfies LS&A’s Creative Expression requirement. Lab Supply Fee $150 covers all art supplies. (Students with financial need should contact lswa@umich.edu for fee waiver assistance.)

Please note: A portion of this course may require students to draw from live nude model(s).

Sections.title: Self-Portrait Puppetry
Sections.description:
The art of puppetry might be one of our oldest living art forms. Even the oldest known artworks—relatively recently discovered in caves dating back some 35,000 years ago—were likely drawn or painted long after the advent of shadow puppetry. Flickering shadows cast by fires on cave walls may have been the precursor to our contemporary understanding of moving images (i.e. movies) and perhaps led to the invention of kinetic hand-made sculptures, i.e. puppets.

Variations on ancient puppets have appeared throughout history and have blended into our contemporary lives, including the likes of Kermit the Frog and Big Bird, which may have provided kids with their earliest introduction to the art of puppetry. The fact that these characters were just made of cloth and foam rubber likely never crossed our inquisitive minds, not to mention the multitude of live artisans, writers, and actors who worked behind the scenes to anthropomorphize these fuzzy sacks of cotton batting and button eyes into believable beings who possessed real thoughts and emotions.

In this course we’ll introduce ourselves to a few different forms of small-scale puppetry using ourselves as both image and story. Through the various puppets we will create in this class, our personal stories will be mined for narrative possibilities while our likenesses (real or avatar) will be used to act out scenarios we’ll develop for each other. Required will be a sense of child’s play and curiosity combined with an openness and desire to bring to life inanimate objects for the purpose of discovering cognitive dimensions that are best revealed through the art of puppetry.

No previous experience is necessary, however students will be expected to possess a positive attitude, willingness to learn from others, and a strong work ethic.

Note:  Mandatory attendance and active class participation required. Expect extensive outside work on homework assignments. Museum trips (TBA) will be required. This course is not limited to LSWA students—if you are not a member of LSWA please reach out to the instructor for an override. Lab Supply Fee $75 covers all supplies. Sections.title: Intro to Algebraic Varieties
Sections.description:
Topic: Introduction to Algebraic Varieties

The goal of the course is to give an introduction to algebraic varieties over an algebraically closed field. The first part of the course will be devoted to establishing a dictionary between algebra and geometry, in the setting of algebraic subvarieties in the affine space and in the projective space. We will then discuss dimension theory, as well as the general notion of algebraic variety. Time permitting, we will discuss separatedness, properness, and smoothness, and will finish by describing aspects of the classical topology on complex algebraic varieties. All along, we will look at many classical examples (Grassmannians, determinantal varieties, toric varieties, etc). 

The prerequisite for this course is an advanced course in ring theory, such as Math 494 or 593. In particular, familiarity with ring quotients and rings of fractions will be assumed. We will build from scratch the commutative algebra results that will be needed.

Sections.title: Math of Microhydrodynamics
Sections.description:
Topic: Mathematics of Microhydrodynamics

This course will cover the mathematical theory of particulate and multiphase flows encountered in various engineering and natural processes. Computational techniques for simulating complex fluids will be reviewed. We will examine a wide range of applications, from flows in thin films, porous media, and microfluidic chips to flows around suspended particles. Topics covered will include:

  • Linearity and reversibility in Stokes flow, uniqueness, reciprocal theorem
  • Constitutive laws for simple and complex interfaces, both passive and active
  • Boundary integral equations
  • Differential geometry in 2D, simulation of bubbles, vesicles and active particles
  • Spherical harmonics, BIE analysis on spheres
  • Small deformation theory and application

Sections.title: Discrete subgroups of Lie grou
Sections.description:
Topic: Discrete subgroups of Lie groups

The course will focus on aspects of the theory of discrete subgroups of Lie groups. The exact topics to be covered will be determined in consultation with the students. Here are 3 possible foci for the course:

  1. Teichmuller theory: One may think of the Teichmuller space of marked hyperbolic surfaces as the universal cover of the much-studied moduli space of Riemann surfaces. We could discuss both the complex analytic and geometric sides of this theory.
  2. Dynamics of hyperbolic surfaces: The study of the dynamics of the geodesic flow of a hyperbolic surface serves as motivation for much of the theory of hyperbolic dynamics.
  3. Anosov representations: Here we will study the emerging theory of Anosov representations into higher rank semi-simple Lie groups, for example SL(d,R).

Notes will be provided and no textbook will be required.

Sections.title: Foundational Kinetic Theory
Sections.description:
Title: Foundational Kinetic Theory    

Kinetic theory, a legacy of Boltzmann and Maxwell, is the cornerstone of nonequilibrium statistical mechanics. In this course, we will be interested in the mathematically rigorous derivations of this theory starting from the first principles of physics. The prime example is deriving Boltzmann’s particle kinetic theory from Newtonian mechanics; another is deriving wave kinetic theory from the Hamiltonian nonlinear wave/dispersive dynamics. Such questions have a long history in mathematics, starting in Hilbert’s sixth problem from 1900, and have witnessed great progress in the past ten years, which we shall discuss in some depth.

Sections.title: K-stability
Sections.description:
Topic: K-stability

K-stability arose in complex differential geometry as a framework for algebro-geometric criteria ensuring that a smooth complex projective variety admits a “canonical” Kähler metric. More recently, it has developed into a subject in its own right within algebraic geometry, with important applications to moduli problems. In this course, we will study various aspects of K-stability.

Sections.title: Finite groups of Lie type
Sections.description:
Topic: Finite groups of Lie type

One of the cornerstone examples of the deep interactions between algebraic geometry and representation theory are Deligne--Lusztig varieties. These are subvarieties of the flag variety indexed by Weyl group elements, the cohomology of which captures the representation theory of finite groups of Lie type. This course will study finite groups of Lie type, the geometry of their associated Deligne--Lusztig varieties, and the ensuing representation theory.

Prerequisites: at least one course in each of representation theory, Lie theory, and algebraic geometry.

Sections.title: Cancer Immunology
Sections.description: Welcome to Cancer Immunology. This course explores how the immune system interacts with cancer, from natural anti-tumor defenses and mechanisms of immune evasion to modern immunotherapies. Topics include key immune cells in tumor control, tumor–immune crosstalk, immune checkpoint blockade, and cancer vaccines. Through discussion of classic and recent studies, students will examine the experimental foundations and clinical advances shaping cancer immunotherapy.

Sections.title: Microbiomes & Human Diversity
Sections.description:
This course explores the intersection of history, science, and society. Students will unravel biomedical misconceptions by examining how ideologies about human difference shaped modern research. We analyze how cutting-edge microbiome science can correct misconceptions about race, refine our understanding of human variation, and advance the future of health equity.

Students in this interactive and discussion-based course explore how contemporary social perspectives shape scientific inquiry and public engagement, with a focus on the intersection of history, science, and society in understanding human diversity and our relationship to our microbiomes. Students traverse both biological and social science scholarship through discussions and critical review of the literature. Topics discussed include: the impact of social and environmental forces on the microbiome and the implications for health; how humans influence microbial communities on ourselves, in the environment, and in the built environment. misconceptions around the origin of health disparities; the parallel development of science, biological determinism, and discriminatory ideologies during the Enlightenment era; key distinctions between concepts of ancestry, race, ethnicity, and genetic variation; the roles and responsibilities of scientists and medical practitioners and the critical relevance of these topics to the biomedical community; current research emphasizing the relationship between microbes and social equity.

Course Requirements:

Student performance will be assessed through a combination of quizzes, required readings, in-class discussions, projects, and writing assignments. Active participation is also an essential component of the course grade.  Students are expected to complete all assigned readings. Regular quizzes will be administered to assess understanding of key concepts and material covered in readings and lectures. Active and meaningful participation in in-class discussions is crucial. Students should come prepared to engage with the reading material and contribute thoughtfully to discussions. Assignments will emphasize practical applications of course concepts and may include presentations, group work, and written assignments. There are no formal written exams.

Intended Audience:

This course is designed for upper-level undergraduate or graduate students with interests in biological and biomedical sciences, especially microbiomes/microbiology. It is particularly beneficial for those planning careers in health, research, or medical professions with a desire to learn more about concepts related to cultural competency, health equity, and health justice.

Sections.description: This course will provide a comprehensive introduction to nanofabrication and nanomanufacturing technologies in the context of both fundamental engineering research and practical implementation. We will start our discussion from the state-of-the-art micro/nanofabrication technologies widely used in the current semiconductor (or electronic device) manufacturing industry and nanofab/device research labs. Afterwards, we will proceed to the emerging nanofabrication approaches based on new top-down and bottom-up principles as well as the critical issues associated with the upscaling of such technologies for ultimately realizing nanomanufacturing. We will also talk about the critical physical/chemical mechanisms involved in various nanofabrication approaches as well as important device applications (e.g., nanoelectronics, optoelectronics, MEMS, energy, nanofluidic biosensors, post-CMOS semiconductor technologies, and emerging neuromorphic computing systems etc.).

Sections.title: Comp Data-Driven Methds Engin
Sections.description: This course presents an introduction of computational and data-driven methods for conducting graduate-level research in engineering. The theme of the course centers around scientific learning, approached as an inverse problem. We will investigate non-probabilistic, probabilistic, and data-driven approaches for solving and accelerating the solution of inverse problems. These will entail topics of classification and regression with regularization and cross-validation; Bayesian inference using Markov chain Monte Carlo and variational Bayes; data-driven modeling with polynomial chaos, Karhunen-Loeve expansions, Gaussian processes, and neural networks. Lastly, we will introduce strategies for “what new data shoud we acquire?” via statistical experimental design, as well as active and reinforcement learning.

Sections.title: Pncp, Mats, MFG, Devi of Batts
Sections.description: This comprehensive course is designed to give students an in-depth understanding of various aspects of batteries, encompassing manufacturing processes. Beginning with exploring thermodynamics and electrochemistry, the course emphasizes lithium-ion batteries, which play a pivotal role in modern energy storage systems. It covers a broad spectrum of battery types, including lead-acid, nickel-metal hydride, metal-air, sodium-sulfur, and redox flow batteries, ensuring a well-rounded comprehension of battery technology. Throughout the course, students will learn about essential components such as electrode materials, electrolytes, separators, additives, and the intricate electrode-electrolyte interface. Furthermore, the curriculum thoroughly examines advanced electrochemical techniques, the incorporation of nanotechnology in battery materials, and the structural design of battery devices, providing students with a comprehensive understanding of battery systems, including their manufacturing processes. Given the increasing interest in lithium-ion (Li-ion) technology, the course addresses fundamental electrochemistry and materials science principles and offers insights into battery pack designs and performance characteristics. Moreover, it fosters discussions on innovative strategies to advance Li battery technology, preparing students to confront emerging challenges in the field. Ultimately, this course aims to equip students interested in battery research, development, and integration into electric vehicles (EVs) and various other applications with the knowledge and skills to effectively navigate this dynamic and rapidly evolving field. By offering a solid foundation in principles, materials, manufacturing, and devices of batteries, this course empowers students to make meaningful contributions to advancing energy storage technologies and their applications across diverse industries.

Sections.title: Manufacturing Processes
Sections.description: This course provides foundational knowledge and skills in smart additive manufacturing. Specifically, it will cover: additive manufacturing (AM) workflow, processes and applications; design and verification; material characterization and processing; monitoring, diagnostics and control; and lifecycle economic and environmental considerations, all with emphasis on practice. The connections of these topics to smart manufacturing technologies will be specifically highlighted. Hands-on labs and industrial case studies will be used to reinforce the course material. The course will be team-taught in five interconnected modules (each with a lab) described in the syllabus.

Sections.title: Struc Anlys, Dyn, Qual AI Mthd
Sections.description: This course introduces the engineering workflow used to design, analyze, and qualify structural systems operating under static and dynamic environments. Students learn how requirements and operational conditions translate into structural loads, safety margins, and qualification criteria. Core topics include structural analysis, modal and vibration analysis, random vibration and shock environments, and model-based simulation using finite element tools. The course also introduces experimental methods for structural testing, including strength testing, modal testing, and vibration testing, with an emphasis on interpreting discrepancies between simulation and experimental results. AI-augmented engineering methods are integrated throughout the course to support design exploration, simulation interpretation, and test data analysis, while emphasizing engineering judgment and model credibility. Students complete a team-based case study in which they design a structural component, perform simulations, develop a qualification strategy, and present analysis and testing plans.

Sections.title: Middle Ages & the Modern World
Sections.description: The years 1000 to 1500 saw a remarkable flowering of artistic forms that live on with enduring evocativeness in our modern lives. The epic, one of the oldest literary forms worldwide, was repurposed and renewed by medieval bards and Scandinavian skalds in forms that inspired some of the most successful popular culture of the twentieth century. Likewise, the poetry of longing and desire inherited from the ancients also became the basis for a wholly new relationship dynamic between young people and a novel vocabulary to go with it (including “chivalry” and “fin’amor,” better known today as “courtly love”). Focusing on literature, film, and, to a lesser extent, architecture, this course will examine in detail foundational medieval works and the continued popularity of their themes in our current-day culture.

Sections.title: Lovers&FightersEarlyEnglishLit
Sections.description:
This course will explore English literature from its beginnings in the late 600s up to and including William Shakespeare. We’ll read a lot of texts you’ve probably heard of and maybe not had a chance to study yet--like Beowulf, The Canterbury Tales, Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, The Faerie Queene, and Dr. Faustus. But also, we’ll dig into less-known texts like the first book we know to have been written in English by a woman and the speeches of Elizabeth I. As the course title suggests, we’ll spend time thinking about evolving representations of love--romantic and otherwise--and depictions of warriors. Both change a lot in English literature between the 600s and the 1600s; we’ll track and investigate those changes and, as we do, learn a lot about the historical and cultural contexts that shaped the earliest stories in English.

Course work includes short low-stakes writing assignments, a couple exams, and four 1200 word papers. Participation will be a requirement.

Sections.title: ThePlaysofWmShakespeare
Sections.description:
This is a course on the plays of William Shakespeare and the culture from which they emerged. Our primary focus will be on learning how to read Shakespeare and how to situate his work in the fascinating context of early modern London and England. The plays we will read include the following: Much Ado About Nothing, Henry the Fifth, Twelfth Night, Othello, King Lear, Macbeth, and The Tempest.

Students will learn about the divine rights of kings, philosophical skepticism, and the Protestant Reformation. They will also encounter how Shakespeare and his contemporaries approached social problems such as income inequality and poverty, and how early modern thinkers theorized race and sexuality. In that Shakespeare returns to these and other topics again and again, we will chart how his thinking evolves and shifts. We will also repeatedly reflect on the institution of marriage as it was understood in this period, the bonds that were thought to constitute friendship and family, and the broader questions of what it means to think historically and nationalistically as a writer. Throughout the semester, we will watch scenes from some of the many cinematic adaptations of Shakespeare's work.

Course Requirements:

Two papers will be assigned, as well as a final project that will ask students to engage with Shakespeare's works in ways that interest them. PDFs of all assigned readings will be made available on our Canvas site. There is no midterm in this course; neither is there a final exam.

Sections.title: Sex,Gndr,&Rlgn in CntrbryTales
Sections.description:
Canterbury Tales has something for every literary taste. Some tales are bawdy and contain jokes about sexuality; other tales praise virginity. The tales offer tongue-in-cheek treatments of gender roles, portrayals of gender ambiguity, and descriptions of gender reversals. Some tales are highly irreligious, while others appear serious works of Christian devotion, and still others leave us wondering about the values associated with Chaucer's religion. Reading through the tales, students will learn about class structure, fashion, music, and material culture in Chaucer's time. The Tales' language is a little more difficult than modern English, but the works are also wonderfully lively and fun.

Class meetings will involve discussion of Chaucer's text and the culture surrounding it, as well as some role playing and informal attempts at dramatic reading.

Sections.title: Plato Latinus
Sections.description:
In this course, we survey the receptions of Plato in Latin from Late Antiquity through the Renaissance, focusing on major writers whose creative adaptations of Plato’s dialogues allowed them to become soaring authors in their own right. This survey takes us through over one thousand years of literary experimentation, and from North Africa to Florence.

The class is designed to appeal to anyone who wants to gain a sense of one intellectual arc of the European tradition, while appreciating the diversity and aesthetic influences of Plato Latinus. The course will cover the following texts:
I. Macrobius, Commentary on Cicero’s De Republica VI aka ‘Dream of Scipio’
II. Martianus Capella Marriage of Philology and Mercury
III. John Scot Eriugena Periphyseon
IV. Nicolas Cusanus De docta ignorantia
V. Marsilio Ficino De amore (Commentary on Plato’s Symposium)
VI. Francesco Patrizi Discussiones


These works, some allegorical, some mystical, some commentaries, offered a running alternative (if not outright rejection of) scholasticism, Aristotelianism, and essentialism, on the one hand, and aligned themselves with polytheist cultural traditions of education, art, and above all, spiritual traditions on the other.


Students can also find adjacent works and or authors that might align more closely with their specific research interests, as for example, looking at the transmission of Neoplatonism back into Latin from Medieval Arab texts such as the translation of Proclus’ Elements of Theology.

Course Requirements:

Attendance and participation (25 %) Student presentations (25%) 'Conference' presentation (25%) Final paper (25%)

Intended Audience:

Graduate students in Classics, MEMS, Art History, History, Philosophy, and advanced UG students. No knowledge of Latin is required as the readings will be in English

Class Format:

The class will meet once a week and will be a survey of works in English, with students presenting on the second week after a topic is introduced. There will be an optional separate class meeting (an independent study LAT 599) for students interested in looking at the works in the original Latin.

Sections.title: Issues in Race & Ethnicity
Sections.description:
This course introduces students to the political, social, and cultural history of the Middle East, spanning from the emergence of written cultures in Mesopotamia and Egypt (c. 3200 BCE) to the early twenty-first century CE. The course lectures, readings,and visuals are geared toward providing students with a grounding in the historical avenues of demographic movement and cultural exchange, formations of power and authority, innovations in science and technology, and interactions with global events that have distinguished the diverse experiences and heritages of people who live or have lived in the lands between the Nile and Oxus Rivers, a region generally referred to as the "Middle East." Through this overview, students will gain an understanding of the significant impact that this region has had on the course of world events and cultural development from the Bronze Age to the present day.

Course Requirements:

Throughout the semester there will be two quizzes, a mid-term, and a cumulative final exam. Over the course of the term students will also compile an integrative and chronologically organized chart including key terms from the lectures.

Class Format:

Each week's work consists of two lecture classes and one discussion session. At each discussion session the student will submit a one-page synopsis/diary on the week's reading assignments. This exercise will help the student learn how to read critically, extract important information, and internalize the material covered, ultimately preparing them for the examinations.

Sections.title: The First 700 Years
Sections.description:
At the beginning of the 7th century, a new religion, Islam, appeared in Arabia and by the end of the century, Muslims had defeated the Byzantines and Persians and created an empire that stretched from Spain to India. For the next millennium, Islam glittered. Its caliphs, courts, and capitals were grander, more powerful, and more sophisticated than those of any medieval king, duke, or prince. In this course, we will trace the emergence and development of Islamic civilization from the birth of Muhammad, ca. 570, to the Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258. We will read the Qur’an and listen to its recitation; examine the career of the Prophet Muhammad; follow the course of the Arab conquests; explore the nature of the conflict between Sunnis and Shi?is; learn about the five pillars of Islam, law, theology, and Sufism; and assess the achievements of Muslim intellectuals in literature, art, science, and philosophy. 30 minutes at the end of each class will be devoted to the analysis of primary sources in English translation.  

This course pursues the following goals: a) to provide a comprehensive idea of the rise and early evolution of Islam and of the subsequent impact that Islamic doctrinal principles have had on the cultures and societies of the Muslim world and beyond; b) to show the amazing diversity of Islam’s interpretation and application by its followers across time and geographical space; c) to demonstrate the profound complexity and ambiguity of interaction between the world of Islam and Western societies. Finally, yet importantly, the course is designed in such a way as to foster in students' analytic skills through composing clearly reasoned responses to the topics covered in the course and critically discussing assigned readings. The ultimate goal of the course is to assist students in orienting themselves to the vast sea of information about Islam and Muslims and to enable them to form a balanced, fact-based and, to the extent possible, objective understanding of the complex subject. No previous knowledge required.

Course Requirements:

One-page essays (10%), Section participation (10%), Midterm I (20%), Midterm II (20%), and Final exam (40%)

Intended Audience:

Undergraduate students interested in the history, religions, and cultures of the Muslim world.

Class Format:

Two 90-minute meetings weekly.

Sections.title: Femnsm Wmns Mvmnts Arab Cultr
Sections.description:
You flee your home when the Ottoman Empire begins to crumble, crossing the Atlantic Ocean on a great steamship when you get your chance. Against all odds, you eventually put down new roots in Detroit, Michigan. At first, your life is relatively constricted: you stick to a few neighborhoods, hanging out mostly in coffeehouses, speaking your mother tongue, and smoking until the small hours of the morning with your compatriots. Sometimes, you even sleep in these places, where you also get your mail. But as time passes, your community grows, and so does its infrastructure. Some are drawn by the allure of work at the Ford factory; others by the growing Armenian, Arab, Turkish, Greek, Sephardic, Assyrian, and other communities that have already been established here. Your community, also, must change as it expands. And here is a great irony: Although you are quite different from these other Middle Eastern communities, and sometimes have fraught and conflicted relationships with them, you still share much in common from your Ottoman past that cannot always be shed, either. So: where do you go from here? 

This course takes an in-depth look at disparate peoples who left the Ottoman Empire for very different reasons, and eventually came to call Detroit their home, in roughly the first half of the twentieth century. Based on the Public Humanities project “The Middle East in Metro Detroit,” it brings multiple local histories together to tell different stories about the lives and afterlives of formerly Ottoman subjects in the Motor City. Over the semester, we will gain a solid understanding of the collapse of the Ottoman Empire and of early twentieth-century American history in Michigan. Students will also learn how to piece together different archival sources–from newspaper clippings to song recordings, from memoirs to letters and short films–to tell their own stories about this complex period in creative ways. Finally, the course will have a conversational dimension, with special invited guests, from the descendants of these communities, who still live and work in Detroit today. 

Course Requirements:

Class participation (25%), midterm (20%), short journal entries (15%), short creative assignment (15%), final short presentation (10%), and a related project (15%)

Class Format:

Two 90-minute seminars weekly.

Sections.title: Dismantling the Discourse of D
Sections.description: During the 15th to 18th centuries, Europeans made direct ties to Africa, the Americas, and Asia-an era known as the “Age of Discovery.” They profited from imported goods and ideas. Scientific “discovery” was an instrument of imperial domination, and a justification for colonial efforts as benevolent. What was the European worldview in the early modern period that enabled this behavior and approach? What knowledge was imported to Europe, what was left behind? What purposes - commercial, scientific, and ideological - did these so-called “discoveries” serve? And how did the advancement of Natural History itself act as a justification for further colonial projects? This course will discuss what we know of the indigenous knowledge before contact, which Indigenous ideas Europeans rejected and/or exploited and why, and how the import of plants, medicines, foods, etc., altered life back in Europe. We will work with ancient and early modern texts, images, and collections (i.e., Wunderkammer), critiquing the rhetorical approach of “Discovery” and its lingering presence in the legacy of Humanities as an intellectual and academic pursuit today.

Sections.title: Science of Art& Art of Science
Sections.description:
Today, we tend to think of the disciplines of science and art as separated by an impossible gap. Artists operate in the subjective arena of expressive culture, whereas scientists concern themselves with the rigorous pursuit of objectivity. This course takes this assumption as a point of departure only to turn it on its head: by thinking together with a wide range of objects produced in early modern Europe (ca. 1400-1800)—including the things we tend to associate with the idea of art like paintings and sculptures, but also a wide range of printed images, technological instruments, robotic automata, military architecture, and written accounts of ephemeral spectacles including fountains and fireworks—this class invites all interested students to learn about a context in which the roles of science and art were inextricably entangled. Set against the backdrop of physical and ideological conflict as well as the colonial expansion of European power, the narratives explored through lectures, in-class discussion, and written assignments will address the ways that the making of art was a central component to the creation of knowledge that is central to fields we know and practice today, including engineering, botany, ornithology, geology, medicine, and more.

Textbooks: All readings on Canvas

HISTART Distribution Requirements: Europe and the US, Early Modern

 

Course Requirements:

  • Engagement (15%)
  • In-class group presentation: Spaces of knowledge (15%)
  • Writing assignment 1: Art and Science Today (15%) Midterm (15%)
  • Writing assignment 2: Art and Science Now and Then (20%)
  • Final exam (20%)

Intended Audience:

Undergraduate

80-minute lectures per week

Sections.title: Wrt about Video Game Mus
Sections.description: Writing about music is nothing new; however, writing about video game music, or anything else having to do with video games, is a relatively recent development since the first mass-produced video games with sound in the 1970s. This course hones writing skills by particularly focusing on common types of writing that arise from a study of game audio. Weekly readings showcase a variety of topics in the discipline as well as a range of audiences and aims. In-person and virtual expert visits will augment class discussions. The course is built around iterative process, peer review, thoughtful discussion, and critical analysis. The focus of readings will change each time the class is offered; for Fall 2024, themes revolve around musical canons, voice in video games, live performance of video game music, and systemic issues within the field.

Sections.title: Western Music 1750 to present
Sections.description: This course traces the evolution of media technologies and their symbiotic intersections with musical creativity, music reception, and social experience. Beginning with the advent of music publishing, and extending through successive innovations in recording, radio, film and television, the Internet, and artificial intelligence, we will explore the impact of media developments on musical practices that range from the symphonic to sampling. We will also consider the influence of media dissemination on music commerce and mass culture, while pondering strategies employed by artists and audiences alike to manipulate media contexts, circumnavigate creative and distributive obstacles, and facilitate social change through musical exchange.

Sections.title: Hist Am Musical
Sections.description: This course uses musical analysis, theatre/performance studies, gender studies, and queer theory to investigate how American musical theatre of the past one hundred years has shaped - and been shaped by - ideas about gender and sexuality. We will study several musicals including but not limited to Show Boat, Anything GOes, Porgy and Bess, Oklahoma!, Lady in the Dark, West Side Story, Guys and Dolls, Gypsy, Funny Girl, Cabaret, Rent, Fun Home and A Strange Loop. In this discussion-based class, we will explore questions such as: How are gender, sexuality, and race intertwined onstage? Do queer musical theatre creators portray gender and sexuality differently in their shows? What can musical theatre fan culture teach us about the genre? No background in music, theatre, or gender & sexuality studies is required for this course.

Sections.title: Music & Media
Sections.description: In the face of converging oppressions, individuals, communities, and nations use the emotional, kinesthetic, and dynamic communicative abilities of music to sound out their liberation.In this course, students will explore the variety and ubiquity of liberatory popular music around the world. Throughout the course, students will attempt to answer the following questions: What is liberation? How does music liberate? Who does it liberate? In what contexts are artists compelled to write liberating music? In order to answer these questions, students will discuss readings, listenings, and audio-visual content organized through four main units: 1) authenticity, 2) distortion, 3) rhythm and rhyme, and 4) dance. Students will familiarize themselves with both US popular music and world popular music, from country to afropop to punk to reggaeton. As a distinctly musicological course, students will employ critical frameworks for writing, discussing, and presenting the sounds of cultural and historical trends. At the end of the course, they will develop a final project (college level paper, podcast, or musical composition).

Sections.title: Music and Our Digital Lives
Sections.description:
This course is a survey of the Music(s) of Black Americans from the era of slavery to the present. Through weekly listening and readings from the fields of academic music studies and Black studies, students will gain foundational knowledge of the creation, development, and performance of Black American musics across time, style, and place. In these discussions we will consider the socio-political and cultural implications of music in the lives of Black Americans while remaining attentive to the range of different experiences within Black American communities. 

Class Format:

Course meetings will consist of a combination of lecture, discussion, and group listening.

Sections.title: Global and Popular Music
Sections.description:
In this class we will delve into questions around streaming, virality, social media, internet culture, and AI technologies to better understand the inner workings of our digital music world.

Digital music is embedded in our daily routines: Spotify playlists pipe through grocery store speakers, streaming music fills our ears as we walk across campus, and viral hits accompany the videos we watch as we scroll during our downtime. How did we come to these listening practices? What technological developments brought us to this world of instantly available music? How is AI going to shape the musical world to come? In this class we will delve into questions around streaming, virality, social media, internet culture, and AI technologies to better understand the inner workings of our digital music world. This class will culminate in a final project that integrates AI music making, critical playlisting, and community-oriented creative writing.

Sections.title: Taylor Swift Songwriter
Sections.description: A chronological survey of music history from the period of Haydn and Mozart to the present.

Sections.title: Virgin Mary Europ Renaissance
Sections.description: How did different cultures encounter one another’s musical traditions in an age long before digital technology enabled instant access to music all over the globe? What impact did foreign musical encounters have on the development of musical styles and genres across the baroque and classical eras? This seminar examines music of the eighteenth century from a cross-cultural and global perspective, emphasizing music’s connection to broader historical developments, including colonialism, revolution, diplomacy, and commerce. We will analyze well-known musical works by Mozard and Haydn from this perspective in addition to music of non-Western cultures and works created by composers of historically underrepresented identities. This is a discussion-based course with a final research project, which will be developed and shared with the class at various stages throughout the semester. Students will read primary sources and current scholarship in musicology, ethnomusicology, music theory, eighteenth-century history, and literary studies.

Sections.title: Classical Music North India
Sections.description: Who was Fryderyk Chopin, and why has his music continued to fascinate composers, musicians, and listeners to this day? To address these questions, students will examine Chopin’s musical and cultural legacy from the nineteenth century to the present. We will ask how his life, split between Poland and France, gave rise to divergent narratives of his career and music. Students will also consider his influence on later composers including Debussy and Szymanowski, as well as his impact on piano performance and pedagogy. Finally, we will examine how Chopin’s cultural significance has been constructed through film, museums, the tourism industry, and the Chopin Competition in Warsaw.

Sections.title: HipHop Postcolonial
Sections.description:
This redesigned upper-level course explores the relationship between hip hop culture and postcolonial scholarship, examining the intersections of music, capitalism, and identity. The course emphasizes critical approaches, investigating how postcolonial dynamics—such as cultural resistance and re/articulation, identity formation, and transnational exchange—shape hip hop as a global phenomenon. Through music videos, lyrics, class discussions, reading and writing assignments, students will develop the tools necessary to critically engage with hip hop culture.

In the first unit, students will be introduced to foundational texts in hip hop scholarship and postcolonial theory, developing the critical vocabulary and conceptual frameworks necessary for analyzing hip hop. In the second unit, students will apply these approaches to study cases of global hip hop cultures, including creative activities that encourage both analytical and imaginative engagement. In the final unit, students will examine contemporary tensions between cultural resistance and commodification, reflecting on hip hop’s social, political, and economic significance today.

Key authors include W.E.B. Du Bois, Frantz Fanon, bell hooks, Tricia Rose, Paul Gilroy, Gayatri Spivak, Stuart Hall, and Juan Bautista Segales. By the end of the course, students will develop a sharper understanding of how capitalistic culture intersects with the musical worlds we inhabit, moving beyond a U.S.-centered perspective and gaining the ability to articulate the intersections between hip hop and postcolonial thought within this broader context.

Sections.title: Chinese 7 String Zither
Sections.description:
Through the examination of influential electronic musicians, gendered labor practices, advertising, and sound objects, this class will explore the historical relationships between musical technologies, gender, and sexuality.

This course delves into the historical relationships between music technology, gender, and sexuality. We will examine the work of influential electronic musicians; explore issues of labor in musical spaces; consider the ways advertising inflects gendered consumer behavior; and study historical conceptions sexuality and sound reproduction. Throughout the course we will ask: Why are some musical technologies tightly associated with masculinity? Why are women and non-binary people so often underrepresented in technological spaces like recording studios and electronic music composition programs? How do commercial and manufacturing histories factor into how we think about gender and technology? This discussion-based class will focus on the twentieth century and cover a range of musical cultures.

This is a project-based field and laboratory course aimed at capturing and documenting Michigan folk, ethnic, and immigrant music. Using state of the art audiovisual laboratory facilities based in the Ann and James Duderstadt Center, students will assist with the final stages of a feature video documentary on Michigan’s rich musical heritage as well as launching projects of individual interest. Working individually and in teams, students will acquire basic skills for conducting interviews, audio/video capture and editing, archiving, and learn about the ethical and practical issues associated with ethnomusicological fieldwork. Interested students from SMTD-PAT and Musicology; School of Art and Design; School of Information; and LSA Screen Arts and Culture, American Culture, Anthropology, and Communications are encouraged to enroll.

Sections.description:
Recent decades have seen the solidification of the fields of sound studies, sensory studies, and affect studies, and a rise in their importance in music studies. More recently, phenomenological approaches to the study of musical experience have garnered significant interest. The intersection of these areas of study with music studies has been highly productive, contributing significantly to our understanding of music cultures. In this seminar, we will explore some of these insights, focusing in particular on the entangled issues of aesthetics and ethics, to enhance our knowledge of the social, cultural, and political implications of music. Recognizing that music, sound, senses, affect, and experience are intimately bound up together, our readings and discussions will explore various aspects of their intertwinings. The scholarship we will engage with will be primarily from the disciplines of ethnomusicology, anthropology, and cultural studies. 

Course Requirements:

Course requirements will consist of reading all assigned readings, regular attendance, class participation, leading a class discussion, and writing and presenting a substantial research paper. Grades will be distributed equally across these requirements with a view to your contribution to the making of a successful seminar.

Intended Audience:

This seminar is for doctoral students only.

Sections.title: Native American and Indigenous
Sections.description:
Topic - Native American and Indigenous Knowledges

How and why do Native American and Indigenous ways of knowing and being in the world matter in the contemporary United States? In other words, how and why do these epistemologies matter? Epistemology is a fancy word for the study of how we know things. Native American and Indigenous knowledges are shaped by worldviews, which are in turn shaped by centuries and millenia of societies living in relationship with all living beings as well as the environment. Although Native American and Indigenous knowledges were targeted for erasure during the long decades of removal, dispossession, and de-culturation, the will to reclaim and celebrate those knowledges is now stronger than ever. 

In this course, we will engage with contemporary Native American and Indigenous Studies scholarship that centers Indigenous language-based ways of being and knowing. Authors may include scholars such as Robin Wall Kimmerer, Leanne Betasamosake Simpson, Daniel Wildcat, and Blaire Morseau. Furthermore, this body of scholarship challenges each of us to take account of our own place in the world, in terms of the places, peoples, and more-than-human entities that surround us, what kinds of relationships we nurture, and what our responsibilities are as stewards of knowledge, awareness, and understanding.

Course Objectives:

  1. You will be able to explain the concept of "Indigenous Epistemology" to someone new to this subject of study.
  2. You will be able to search out sources of information on Native American and Indigenous communities in the United States.
  3. You will be able to explain the concept of "positionality."
  4. You will be able to articulate your own positionally to Indigenous epistemologies, and to the places that you inhabit.
  5. You will be able to articulate what your responsibilities are to knowledges you acquire. 

Course Requirements:

  1. Readings are the core of the course content, and will be the focus of short written assignments, and student teams will be responsible for stewarding in-class discussion
  2. Attendance is expected. There will be an attendance policy on the syllabus.
  3. I and small group activities during class meetings. Please bring a laptop or tablet to class in order to participate in small group activities.
  4. A Term Project on a topic of your choice.
  5. There are no exams in this course. In place of a final exam, there will be a "Final Essay Experience" assignment, opened on the day of the final class meeting, and due at the end of the scheduled final examination period. 

This class, and my teaching style, asks that you cultivate an open mind, creative problem-solving thinking, and an adventurous sense of exploration.

Sections.title: Intro to Neural Circuits
Sections.description:
This class is designed for advanced undergraduate students and graduate students in Psychology, Neuroscience, Biomedical Engineering, Biophysics, Chemistry, and other related disciplines. Students will learn about the history of psychedelic drugs and how these psychedelic drugs impact the brain. We will cover the modern field of psychedelic medicine and understand how the immediate psychedelic effects of these drugs then give rise to long term neuroplasticity. We will cover these topics via discussion of recent primary literature as well as knowledge of the neuroscience and psychology topics in the parallel Introduction to Neural Circuits course (to ensure everyone is on the same page in terms of background material). By the end of the course students will be able to understand cutting-edge research on the mechanisms and possible utility of psychedelic drugs as medicine.

Course Requirements:

Our readings will be drawn from the Bear, Connors, Paradiso textbook, as well as primary literature, and the cost of the class is equivalent to the cost of this textbook (in the $51-$100 range). The course grade will be based on two exams, occasional quizzes and contributions to in-class discussions.

 

Class Meeting Time: in addition to attending the Psych 330 (Intro to Neural Circuits) lectures, for students enrolled in Psych 733.001, there will be one additional hour of class time devoted to primary literature discussions. The timing of this additional one hour of class time will be decided at the start of the semester to suit the schedule of all enrolled graduate students. Grades will be based on presentations and a final paper. Students who are more computationally focused can also choose to replace the final paper with a final data analysis project that focuses on making sense of psychedelic-related neural datasets.

Class Format:

This is a seminar class that emphasizes discussion of primary literature.

Sections.title: Educational Neuroscience
Sections.description: Education is evolving toward understanding differences in the way people learn, how best to tap into those differences, and how the environment influences human learning and cognition. Understanding how the brain works is central to the way we think about how best to educate people. This course covers topics in how neuroscience informs education and how education changes the developing brain. The study of education involves understanding what motivates learners, how youth develop, what cognitive strategies are best for learning. This course will help you to understand the neuroscience that intersects with education within the subfields developmental, cognitive, social, and clinical neuroscience.

Sections.description: This upper-level course will cover the fundamentals of cell lineage and genome state in the context of brain development. We will discuss techniques to profile the genome states along cell lineages in model organisms, to analyze brain development at the single cell level, including single cell RNA-sequencing and spatial transcriptomics—two ways to assess gene expression in individual cells. In the accompanying computer lab, we will learn how to analyze single cell gene expression data using a real dataset. Students without coding experiences or statistics background should expect devoting much more time to the course, especially the lab assignments.

Sections.title: Comp Mechanisms Parenting Behv
Sections.description:
This course provides an in-depth exploration of the mechanisms underlying parental behavior across the animal kingdom, including humans. Through lectures and discussions based on primary literature, we will examine the neuroendocrine, physiological, and neurobiological processes that drive parenting, while also considering social, environmental, and cultural influences. A strong emphasis will be placed on comparative studies across species and will consider how mechanisms influence parenting behaviors within an evolutionary framework. We will also explore how research on non-human parenting informs our understanding of human caregiving. By analyzing parenting from multiple perspectives, students will gain insight into the diverse strategies species use to achieve the common goal of raising offspring. This course will highlight the many ways parenting can be successfully achieved across different ecological and social contexts. Grades are primarily based on weekly readings and written discussion pieces, class attendance and active participation in group discussions, and a final written research proposal on a topic related to parental behavior. 

Course Requirements:

Final Research Project: 3 page research proposal final paper (in lieu of a final exam) 
Assignments: Several assignments contributing to the development of the final research project
Quizzes: 1-3 online quizzes throughout the course, based on lecture material 
Weekly Reflections: Short written reflections on assigned readings
Participation: Class attendance and active participation in group discussions

Intended Audience:

While there is no formal prerequisite for this course, it is recommended that students have some neuroscience background (e.g., PSYCH 220 - Introduction to Biopsychology or PSYCH 230 - Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience) and that students have taken PSYCH 337 - Hormones and Behavior and/or PSYCH 235 - Introduction to Evolution and Behavior.

Class Format:

Mix of lectures and small and large group discussions

Sections.title: Neuroimmunology: Nueral Func
Sections.description:
Neuroscience typically focuses on neurons, yet approximately half of all cells in the brain are glial cells, or specialized immune cells in the central nervous system. Neuroimmune cells and signaling are key components of normal neural function, response to illness, behavioral regulation, and contribute to mental health disorders including depression, and neurological disorders including Alzheimer’s disease and other neurodegenerative disorders. The objective of the course is to understand the importance and basic mechanisms of neuroimmune cells and signaling in neural function, behavior, and disease.
In this class, we will discuss neuroimmune cells, signaling, and interactions with neurons, and impact on behavior in the healthy brain and in disease states, and recent advances in technologies to probe neuroimmune processes. We primarily discuss basic research, but will also include some clinical and translational implications.

Some neuroscience background (Psych230 or similar) is recommended for this course

Course Requirements:

 Assessment will be based on in class group presentations, in class workshop exercises, and a final paper. Attendance is required for this course.

Class Format:

The course will include lecture and discussion-based workshops; and will primarily focus on primary literature and published review papers for readings.
